## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public, and we act merely as their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive. To keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including technical restrictions on automated searching.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files:* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals. We request that you use these files only for personal, non-commercial purposes.
+ *Refrain from automated querying:* Do not send automated searches of any sort to Google's system. If you are conducting research on <term>machine translation</term>, <term>optical character recognition</term> <note>OCR; the process of converting images of text into digital, searchable text</note>, or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to assist you.
+ *Maintain attribution:* The Google "watermark" you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.
+ *Keep it legal:* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still under copyright varies from country to country, and we cannot offer guidance on whether any specific use of a specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book's appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. The legal penalties for copyright infringement can be quite severe.

## Baron von Reichenbach's Researches

**On Magnetism, Electricity, Heat, Light, Crystallization, and Chemical Attraction in their relation to Vital Force. Translated and Edited (at the express desire of the author) by DR. GREGORY, of the University of Edinburgh. <term>8vo.</term> <note>Octavo; a book size</note> cloth, 12s. 6d.**

This work contains a detailed account of the researches and experiments made by <term>Baron von Reichenbach</term> to establish his discovery of a natural influence that is similar to, but essentially distinct from, the known <term>imponderables</term>—heat, electricity, and magnetism. This principle, named <term>ODYLE</term> by the author, is characterized by the effects it produces on the senses of touch and sight: 1. By exciting peculiar sensations in the human body; and 2. By displaying luminous emissions coming from the poles and sides of magnets.

The sources from which this force flows—which the author's investigations prove to pervade the entire material world—are observed to be chiefly the magnet, crystals, the human body, heat, electricity, friction, and chemical action. In a history of experiments repeated in a great variety of forms, the author traces this power from its numerous sources through its irritating effects on people possessing extraordinary sensory acuteness.

The sections on **THE ODYLIC LIGHT** present a series of experiments revealing the various forms, characters, and properties of the light given off by magnets. This magnet light appears, under different circumstances, as a glow, flames, fibrous downy light, sparks, and luminous nebulae, vapors, smoke, and clouds. (Illustrations are provided of these various forms.) Crystals, besides showing a specific action on the animal nerves, send out a delicate flame-like light from their poles. The odylic luminous phenomena are further remarkable for possessing polarity, appearing with constantly different properties at the opposite poles of magnets.

## The Steam Engine, Steam Navigation, Roads and Railways,

**Explained and Illustrated. A new edition, revised and completed to the present time. Illustrated with wood engravings. <term>12mo.</term> <note>Duodecimo; a book size</note> 8s. 6d., cloth. By DIONYSIUS LARDNER, D.C.L., &c. Formerly Professor of Natural Philosophy and Astronomy in University College, London.**

This work is intended to provide the general reader with the level of information regarding steam power and its principal applications that well-informed people desire to possess. It is written in language free of mathematical and mechanical technicalities so that the details of the machinery, and the physical principles on which they depend, will be intelligible to anyone with an ordinary education. In former editions, much space was occupied by historical and biographical matter, as well as by descriptions of engines that have long since become obsolete. Since these do not form a necessary link in the chain of invention, they may be considered unnecessary in a work of this kind. In the present edition, that space has been more usefully occupied with other material.

The second and third parts are completely new. In the third chapter of the second part, readers will find a review of the progress of Steam Navigation from its first establishment in 1812 to the present day. This chapter also contains a refutation of those absurd reports that have been widely circulated, falsely attributing to the author the opinion that an Atlantic voyage was impossible; these reports are the exact opposite of the opinions he actually expressed.

# EDITOR'S PREFACE.

---

This publication is the first volume of a work in which all the observations made until now by BARON VON REICHENBACH, concerning the very interesting and important subject it addresses, are to be permanently recorded; and, at the author's request, I have undertaken to present these researches to the British public as they are published.
The present volume, which includes everything that has been published in Germany so far, consists of two parts.
Part I is a new and improved edition of the portion of the work published by the author in *Liebig's Annalen* in March and May 1845; however, no essential changes have been made to it. It contains a general historical sketch and summary of all the investigations conducted up to the latter part of 1844, when it was written. It only includes the details that seemed necessary to establish the existence of the new "imponderable" force or influence, Odyle, and to trace it to the many sources from which it is found to flow. These sources include magnets, crystals, the human body, the sun, the moon, the stars, heat, electricity, friction,

<header>EDITOR'S PREFACE.</header>

chemical action, and the whole material universe; and the reader will find various interesting and valuable applications of the facts thus ascertained; for example, to the explanation of corpse-lights, the origin of many ghost stories, and further on, to dietetics, etc. None of these sources of <term>odyle</term> are treated fully or minutely in Part I. The experiments detailed in it were made on more than twelve sensitive persons, of whom half—those who exhibited the highest degree of sensitivity—were women affected with various diseases of the nervous system, while the remainder were strong, healthy men. It is necessary to mention this here because, in various passages written in 1844, the Author expresses the opinion he then held: that the sensitive state is essentially a morbid one, and that perfectly healthy persons are perhaps never sensitive. His subsequent research, as detailed in Part II, has proved the fallacy of this opinion; but the original passages remain and might puzzle the reader without this explanation.

<margin><unclear>~</unclear></margin>Early in 1846, I published an abstract of this First Part, which serves as a general summary of the investigations down to the end of 1844. My object in doing so was simply to direct the attention of my countrymen to these admirable researches; and to make the work more readable and popular, I condensed the translation into about half the size of the original, without, however, omitting any essential point. The abridged portions were those consisting of minute and often-repeated details of the experiments—undoubtedly necessary to the permanent value of the work as they encompass the evidence produced, but not required in all their details for the purpose of direct-

I was well aware, and mentioned in the preface to that Abstract, that I was not doing full justice to the Author by omitting any part of that evidence, but I felt convinced that, in the meantime, a more popular sketch would better answer the intended purpose.

The reception of the Abstract in this country, which was much more favorable than that accorded to the original on the Continent, has, I think, fully justified this abridgment. I now present to the public Part I in its full extent and in a permanent form; and I am persuaded that, upon comparison with the Abstract, it will be found that, in every point except for the full detail of *all* the numerous and similar experiments, the summary of Baron <term>von Reichenbach</term> was faithfully represented in that publication.

The very favorable manner in which my Abstract has been received in this country demands my warmest acknowledgments. Not only was the edition sold very rapidly, but ever since 1846, I have been favored with so many letters of inquiry concerning a new edition and expressing high approval of the work that I have found it quite impossible to return individual answers to nearly all of them. I beg here to apologize for all omissions, and to explain that I would have republished the Abstract long before this, had I not been in constant expectation of receiving the succeeding parts of his great work from the Author, which I had undertaken to publish in full. The present volume is, then, the commencement of that publication, which was delayed for reasons that are given

But I may state here that the most important of these is not sufficiently highlighted there; namely, the fact that the Author devoted more than three years, after publishing the summary in 1845, to a laborious and detailed study of all branches of the subject. The results of these three years of research (as far as they concern only one of these branches) are now presented in Part II, which, if it had been published much sooner, would necessarily have been far less complete than it is now.

It may be mentioned here that the Abstract of Part I was favorably reviewed in various scientific and literary journals, as well as in the daily press. Indeed, up to this time, I have not become aware of any scientific criticisms published in this country regarding the Author's research which require any notice from me here. This, as will be seen by the Author's Preface, forms a strong and favorable contrast with the reception given to Part I by various scientists in Germany. It is pleasing to reflect that a work so truly scientific in its character has, despite the startling nature of the facts recorded in it, received from the British public that respectful and appropriate attention to which it was justly entitled, given the established scientific reputation of its Author. It must be gratifying to the many English readers of the Abstract to know—and to this I can myself testify—that the late <term>BERZELIUS</term> took a very deep interest in the investigation and expressed, in a letter to the Editor, his conviction that it could not possibly have been in better hands than those of BARON <term>VON REICHENBACH</term>.

So much in reference to Part I.

<meta>This page continues the Editor’s Preface, detailing the structure and scientific claims of Part II of Baron von Reichenbach’s work.</meta>

<page-num>xi</page-num>
<header>EDITOR'S PREFACE.</header>

Part II consists of several sections. In the first, the Author lists by name more than fifty new <term>sensitive persons</term>, thirty-five of whom are perfectly healthy and vigorous. Among them, he has found all degrees of sensitiveness, even the highest, and their descriptions and statements show perfect consistency. It is unnecessary to enter into any detail here. In the second section, the author conducts a detailed comparison of the new influence, <term>odyle</term>, with known influences or <term>imponderables</term>—heat, electricity, and magnetism (proper). He demonstrates, in a very elegant and convincing way, both its great similarity to these and the striking differences that force him to distinguish it from them. These differences leave no choice, for now, but to give it a distinct place and name, although future discoveries may possibly allow us to relate *all* the imponderables to a common force. But that time is still distant; and, in any case, a name will be required for the new group of distinct phenomena, just as we find it necessary to apply the names of magnetism and electricity to two such groups whose close relationship and possibly common origin must be universally admitted. These sections constitute the Introduction.

And first, regarding the objects of inquiry. It may be safely stated that no well-ascertained fact, or series of facts, can possibly exist in nature that is not worthy of our earnest study. It is no answer to say that there are many facts of no practical value; for the fallacy of such an assertion has been too often proven by the unexpected application of apparently trifling facts to important purposes, both theoretical and practical. When **LIEBIG** and **SOUBEIRAN** first described a peculiar volatile fragrant liquid produced by the action of bleaching powder on alcohol, this fact was recorded and remained for many years in our manuals as a mere curiosity of science. Yet when the time came, this insignificant compound, in the hands of my accomplished colleague, **Dr. SIMPSON**, rose to the highest practical value as **CHLOROFORM**. Had *all* the properties of this substance been carefully studied at first, we would not have had to wait until 1846 or 1847 for this boon to suffering humanity. It would be easy to fill a volume with similar cases, from the Steam Engine to Gun Cotton, all proving the great truth that no natural fact is insignificant or unimportant.

Secondly; as to the question of whether the phenomena studied in this work are *facts* or not; I may safely leave this to the decision of the careful reader of the work. I shall only express my conviction that if these facts are not facts, then no facts exist in any department of science.

Thirdly; as to the mode of investigation adopted by the Author: it is the inductive method, the same to which we owe all the progress of modern science; and in which the conclusions are deduced from carefully observed phenomena, varied by experiments performed with due attention to accuracy. No other method is known by which natural phenomena, and especially obscure natural phenomena, can be investigated with any chance of success.

This method has been most diligently, laboriously, and successfully applied by the Author to a class of phenomena which might perhaps be considered at once more obscure and more interesting than those which form the objects of many other departments of science, if it could justly be said that one part of nature is more interesting than another. I feel compelled to say that, in the course of a life devoted to science, I have met with no research in which the true and universally approved rules of investigation have been more perfectly adhered to and followed through than in the ones before us; which, were it necessary, might serve as a model to all experimental inquirers.

The qualifications of the Author for such an inquiry are of the very highest kind. He possesses a thorough scientific education, combined with extensive knowledge. His life has been devoted to science, and to its application to the practical purposes of mankind.

The first objection is that his observations (in Part I) are made on diseased subjects and are therefore of no value. Everything here depends on *how* the facts occurring in diseased subjects are ascertained and examined. And it is not likely that they will soon be better observed than by the author.

But further, many of the best-established facts in medicine rest on the statements of nervous patients. If some hysterical subjects exhibit great uncertainty in their statements, and even occasionally a tendency to deceit, this is itself a symptom worthy of investigation; and if such things make our research more difficult, it should only stimulate us to increased care and accuracy in observing. There is one more point on which I would like to offer a few remarks. This is the connection between the Author’s research and the subjects of Somnambulism and Mesmerism.

It will be obvious to the attentive reader that the highest or extreme degree of sensitivity to this new influence is found in spontaneous somnambulists, though it is not confined to the somnambulistic state. Somnambulism takes its place, along with nervousness, spasms, catalepsy, etc., as an indication of a state of the system favorable to the development of sensitivity, *but it is not at all essential to it.* Spontaneous somnambulism occurs very frequently; so frequently, indeed, that it is only surprising that there should ever have been doubts about the possibility of inducing it by artificial means.

This leads us to what is called the mesmeric state, which is simply somnambulism produced artificially. Its existence in this form is now generally—I might even say universally—admitted; yet, until now, we could not in any way account for the fact that one human being is able to produce this state in another, and that, too, without contact. Now, the Author’s discoveries show us that a force or influence, analogous to heat, electricity, and magnetism, but distinct from all of them, exists in the human body; and that a large number of persons are more or less sensitive to this influence.

As for the cry of fraud and imposture, it is, in a scientific investigation, utterly inadmissible for the reasons stated earlier and many others. Let us for a moment try to imagine the possibility that all the hundreds and thousands who have been, and daily are, mesmerized, are all impostors, while all the operators—if not equally deceitful—are themselves deceived. Let us bear in mind that this accusation is commonly and recklessly brought by those who have never investigated the subject, not only against those who have, but also against persons of great ability and of unblemished character and honor, and generally without a shadow of evidence. If we do this, I think we must reach the conclusion that such a line of argument is as irrational, unjust, and dishonest in itself as it is lacking in any force against observed and established facts.

I am far from denying the possibility of attempts to deceive in mesmerism, especially when made the

Nature is more wonderful than any forgery of man's invention. I have repeatedly produced mesmeric phenomena myself in persons as incapable of deceit as any who can be found, even among skeptics. In short, without the most rigorous proof, the charge of fraud is not to be tolerated for a moment. But even if fraud were established in one or more cases, this would not affect other cases in which no fraud was probable, or even possible.

That there is something worthy of research in these phenomena, all who have either personally studied them or carefully read the existing evidence admit; the best security against fraud is the greatest possible knowledge of the subject, which can only be obtained by men of scientific training and a scientific turn of mind devoting their energies to it. If this is duly done, the cry of imposture will soon die away, and mesmerism

If there are any phenomena which, in a certain sense, we might be entitled to call incredible, they are those of clairvoyance. I do not claim to have seen these myself; and, because of their relatively rare occurrence, a rational skepticism is excusable here. But even in this part of the subject, the existing evidence—a great part of which rests on testimony of the highest character—cannot be dismissed by any amount of skepticism. We must carefully distinguish between the facts themselves and the various, often absurd, explanations and theories that unscientific observers seem to think it necessary to devise and insist on providing; while others, before admitting the facts, require them to be explained, as if the truth of a fact depended on our being able to account for it. All this is unscientific. There are facts of the most interesting kind connected with this part of the subject; and we need not doubt that, if studied in the right spirit, these facts will one day allow for a natural physical explanation, at least as far as any natural fact can be explained. Indeed, the example given above of the flames at the tips of the fingers proves that there is a physical cause for some of the mesmeric phenomena—as we shall sooner or later find there is for all of them. Furthermore, even clairvoyance has frequently occurred spontaneously, without the use of any mesmerizing process whatever, just as somnambulism and cataleptic rigidity have done, as we know from the best authority. It is, therefore, independent of mesmerism, a fact to be investigated according to the usual rules of science.

I have ventured to make this digression because I am firmly convinced that the example set by the Author—in thus studying the more obscure and difficult natural phenomena—will be followed, with the most desirable results, in the related subject of mesmerism. Until scientific men take the trouble to investigate mesmerism in this manner, they are not entitled to pronounce a hasty judgment, much less a harmful judgment, on the work of those who, perhaps with fewer qualifications but certainly with an equal love of truth, have undertaken the investigation which they have themselves neglected.

To return to the Author's experiments: he has, through the most detailed instructions, made it possible for everyone to repeat them. It is hardly necessary to point out that in repeating them, if we wish to obtain or verify his results, we must strictly follow the conditions. Indeed, this is so obviously necessary that I would not have mentioned it if the actions of certain physicians in Vienna—in what they intended to be an experimental refutation of the Author's conclusions—had not provided evidence that even educated men, who should be familiar with science, can violate this essential and simple rule in the most blatant manner. For some almost incredible details on this subject, I refer the reader to the Author's notes on page 354 and page 370.

I must now add that I have repeated some of the Author's experiments myself and have found, as was to be expected, that his account of the phenomena was perfectly accurate. For a few details, the reader is referred to Appendix (A).

# EDITOR'S PREFACE.

There is no difficulty in finding sensitive subjects; but it is not so easy to make good and trustworthy observations once we have found them.

I have reason to know that many people have made similar observations confirming those of the Author. One gentleman, well known as a lover of science, has favored me with some of his own, which will also be found in Appendix (B).

Those who have had, or may hereafter have, an opportunity to confirm, illustrate, or correct the observations of the Author will do me a very great favor by privately communicating the results they have obtained or may obtain. With their permission, I would like to add these results, or a selection of them, to future parts of this work. However, it would be even more desirable for such observers to publish their results separately.

Finally, regarding the translation, I have endeavored in every case to adhere strictly to the meaning of the Author. Because of the peculiarities of the German idiom or the Author’s characteristic style—which is not always easily translated—it has often been necessary to completely change the structure of a sentence. I have attempted to produce a readable English work, as far as the nature of the subject and the very frequent use of <term>technical terms</term> and necessary repetitions of nearly identical details would permit.

# AUTHOR'S PREFACE

->TO THE<-

## SECOND EDITION OF PART I.

---

The Seven Treatises that make up this work were intended to appear sequentially in the monthly issues of **Liebig** and **Wöhler's** Annalen der Chemie, and were sent to the editor in time for their publication to have begun in July 1844. However, accidental circumstances prevented this, and thus it happened that they were collected in two separate supplementary issues of the Annalen, and published for the first time in March and May 1845. This explains the somewhat unusual form in which they appear.

In this Second Edition, some things have been corrected; but, on the whole, the work has undergone no essential alteration. My research, continued without interruption since the work appeared, has confirmed and more strongly established the observations recorded in it. I have decided not to abandon the half-historical, half-systematic course which I followed in detailing my observations and presenting the views derived from them; for this is the real course of all natural science, in which the correction of former errors always keeps pace with the expansion of our knowledge.

It was easy to foresee that a matter of such a strange and peculiar kind as the subject covered in these researches would meet with objections; and I was prepared in advance for the necessity of defending my experiments, and the conclusions deduced from them, against both well-founded and groundless opposition and contradiction. The new field of investigation opened up here extends its boundaries so close to the defenses of existing and established doctrines, and comes in contact at so many points with all that is known of the Imponderables, that it was not expected that it would be allowed to take its place in the crowded domain of science without much resistance. Yet I was only prepared for rational judgment and criticism; for occasional failures in repeating my experiments, arising from errors in the necessary arrangements; for opposition to the conclusions deduced from these experiments; or for the announcement of different conclusions or deductions from the recorded facts. I was not, I confess, prepared for an attack (which every friend to science, possessed of good feeling and good manners, must agree with me in considering ill-bred in the extreme) made on my work and on myself personally by a **Dr. DUBOIS-REYMOND** in **KARSTEN’S** *Progress of Physiology in the year 1845*. This philosopher does not think it necessary in the slightest degree to examine my experiments and deductions; but, from his lofty eminence, titles my labors, courteously enough, “an absurd romance, to enter into the details of which would be fruitless, and to him impossible.” I have no doubt of the truth of both statements. It would be fruitless because he did not understand the work; and a foolish judgment on that

Either my statements contain natural truths, which have a constant existence in the physical world and must therefore sooner or later be acknowledged, covering the ignorant reviewer with disgrace; or they rest on great errors, in which case it must be easy for him to perform his duty of discovering and explaining these, and thus secure himself against the reproach of unconscientious carelessness regarding the reputation of his fellow man. Only narrow-mindedness and folly could, without reflection, expose themselves to both dangers at once.

It is in the nature of every experimental inquiry that it cannot be free from defects. It is *because* we feel these defects in our knowledge that we make experiments, in order to complete that knowledge through newly discovered and newly acquired information. But while thus employed, we observe ten—no, a hundred—new gaps or blanks; and the reader, on his part, probably observes a dozen which have escaped the notice of the experimenter; the reviewer perhaps detects many more. It is most desirable that these should all be publicly announced and brought under discussion, so that the Author or others may investigate the matter further on all sides, or fortify what he has already won against all doubts. This is advantageous to all, even to the discoverer of every new scientific fact. My labors will no more be found to be without defects than the work of men standing much higher than I do has ever been perfect, and least of all in the natural sciences. No one can have felt this more strongly than myself. Every notice of any deficiency, expressed with proper feeling, I shall thankfully receive and experimentally improve my work accordingly. But lofty insolence, stained, moreover, with the most glaring ignorance of the work reviewed, must be driven back and confined to its due limits. It is not only my interest, it is the interest of all those who labor and who write on scientific subjects, that such weeds should be rooted out and swept away, and not allowed to flourish in the garden of science.

Another reason why this research has been delayed for so long, and why the gropings in the dark seemed likely never to end, is this: those who attended to the subject, one after another, insisted on beginning to build the pyramid at its apex. They wished to do at first what they ought to have tried last—namely, to cure diseases. Before taking the smallest pains to acquire even the slightest knowledge of the inner nature of the deep-lying force, the effects of which they had observed, they were bent on making a trade of it! Then, in their operations, they stumbled upon somnambulism, clairvoyance, and even insanity; that is, they everywhere met with the manifestations of the force at their maximum intensity, complicated with states of disease that were both intense and previously inexplicable. While they stood amazed at these large-scale and high-intensity phenomena—the explanation of which they felt to be beyond their power—they neglected to inquire into its small and feeble beginnings, upon which alone the foundation for a truly scientific structure could be securely laid. We have not drawn our knowledge and our doctrines of electricity and sound from lightning and thunder; nor have we obtained our knowledge of the expansive force of steam from the eruptions of volcanoes. But just as our ancestors made up fables concerning these phenomena because they did not understand...

But this is not the path of research in natural science; and the latter class, in truth, sin more grievously against the progress of enlightenment than the former. It is, indeed, anything but honorable to our contemporaries that they obstinately adhere to a primitive state of blind ignorance in these matters, and will not perceive how fearfully they expose themselves by doing so.

All these innumerable answers to my questions agree so perfectly in all points that every rational doubt must yield to the evidence of truth; and in this beautiful agreement lies the guarantee for their essential trustworthiness.

# INTRODUCTION.

If we make downward passes with strong magnets—having a supporting power of about 10 lbs.—along the bodies of fifteen to twenty individuals without touching them, we will always find one or perhaps more among the number who feel affected by it in a peculiar way. The proportion of human beings who may be found to be sensitive in this manner is generally greater than we imagine. It sometimes happens that, in the number mentioned above, three or four sensitive persons are found; indeed, I am acquainted with an institution where, upon trial, out of 22 females assembled there, no fewer than 18 perceived the sensation caused by the passage of the magnet, more or less distinctly. The nature of this impression on such excitable persons—who may, however, often be justified in regarding themselves as perfectly healthy—is not easily described. It is unpleasant rather than agreeable, and is associated with a gentle feeling, sometimes of cold and at other times of warmth, which resembles a cool or tepid *aura* or current of air that they believe gently blows upon them. Occasionally they experience a dragging or pricking sensation, as well as <term>formication</term>; some complain very soon of a headache. Not only females, but also men in the prime of life, can be found who distinctly perceive this influence. It is sometimes felt very vividly by children.

# INTRODUCTION.

To produce this effect, it is not a matter of essential importance, but rather immaterial, whether we use a horseshoe magnet or a straight bar magnet, or whether we use one pole or the other, provided it is active and of nearly the strength mentioned above. The passes should be made from the head toward the feet and not too quickly. The magnet is carried as close to the surface as possible without actual contact with the clothing; and, to guard against the effect of imagination on either side, the passes may be made from the <term>occiput</term> (the back of the head) over the neck and back. The magnetized person is thus unaware whether a pass is in progress at any given moment, and his statements are free from bias.

Powerful men and healthy, strong women usually experience nothing when tested in this way. Yet I have met with such individuals who, although in vigorous and blooming health, felt themselves decidedly affected by the magnet. The sensitivity referred to here is more frequently observed in people of sedentary habits, even though they may still be regarded as perfectly healthy; this is particularly true for men who are continuously engaged in writing and for girls constantly employed in needlework, as well as for people who are depressed by secret grief, the financial cares of life, the loss of relatives, or disappointed ambition.

Following such people, who may be regarded as not being in full health, come those who are sickly or partially diseased. These are very often magnetically sensitive, especially those who are commonly said to have "weak nerves," who are easily terrified, or who have been agitated and shaken by fright. Then there are many actual patients suffering from countless kinds of disease, but more particularly in those cases where local or general spasms accompany the illness, or during abnormal development of the system at the period of puberty. This also includes those who are very strongly and disagreeably affected by certain odors, and most especially people suffering from <term>catalepsy</term>, <term>St. Vitus's dance</term>, and various forms of paralysis, many hysterical patients, and finally, without exception, the insane and spontaneous <term>somnambulists</term> (sleepwalkers). Thus, the sensitive subjects form a chain, from the healthy man or woman to the sleepwalker, of which the extreme links

...are represented by a powerful man and a feeble somnambulist. We may easily convince ourselves of this fact in every large hospital.

Therefore, the magnet appears to be an agent that *generally influences vital processes*; and while this property has been observed—and individual physicians have tried to apply it in various ways, hoping to derive a method of cure from it without, however, obtaining very distinct or satisfactory results—on the other hand, natural philosophers have not yet included it within the domain of physics. Natural science in general has avoided it everywhere until now because of the uncertainty of the observations made so far. Nevertheless, when viewed from this perspective, magnetism offers a profound and infinitely varied interest upon closer investigation. If some of these phenomena become mixed with those of vital action, this happens precisely and especially where the boundaries between the Organic and the Inorganic become blurred. While natural philosophers hesitated over whether to assign these phenomena to the province of physiology or physics, they were neglected by both sides. They were thus left to practical medicine and did not always fall into the best hands. In the following pages, I hope to succeed in untying some parts of the *Gordian Knot*; to unify a number of these phenomena under common viewpoints; and to bring them under established physical laws.

# FIRST TREATISE.

## LUMINOUS APPEARANCES AT THE POLES AND SIDES OF STRONG MAGNETS.

1. Those sensitive people who are actually or apparently in good health notice nothing unusual in the magnet beyond the sensations mentioned above, and can tolerate being near it without harmful effects. However, this is not the case for sensitive people who are ill. Depending on the nature of their illness, the magnet's effect on such people is sometimes pleasant and other times painfully unpleasant—occasionally to such a degree that fainting, cataleptic, and convulsive attacks occur with such violence that they may eventually become dangerous. In this latter group of cases, which also includes somnambulists, there is usually an added *extraordinary sharpness of the senses*; the patients acquire a remarkable sensitivity and strength in their sense of taste and smell; many types of food become as unbearable to them as the normally pleasant scents of flowers become offensive. They hear and understand what is said three or four rooms away; and they are often so sensitive to light that, while they cannot bear sunlight or firelight, they are able *in the dark* not only to recognize the outlines of objects but also to distinguish their colors accurately. This happens in such deep darkness that people who are not sensitive

# MAGNETIC LIGHT.

...are completely unable to perceive anything. These facts are quite generally known and require no proof here. Moreover, it is not as difficult to understand the possibility of such phenomena as it might first appear to many who imagine something incredible or supernatural in all such matters. Not only do most animals surpass civilized man in the sharpness of certain senses, but even savages—and consequently other human beings as well—frequently equal dogs and other animals in the sensitivity of their smell and hearing. Regarding vision, horses, cats, and owls are familiar examples of the visual system's ability to see reasonably well even on a dark night.

2. Through the kindness of a physician in Vienna, I was introduced in March 1844 to one of his patients, the daughter of Mr. Nowotny, a revenue officer at Landstrasse No. 471. She was a young woman of twenty-five who had suffered for eight years from increasing headaches and had then become afflicted with cataleptic fits, accompanied by both tonic and clonic <term>spasms</term>. In her, an intense sharpness of the senses had developed, so that she could not bear either sunlight or candlelight. During the darkness of night, she saw her room as if in twilight and clearly distinguished the colors of all objects in it, such as clothes. The magnet acted on this patient with extraordinary force in various ways, and in every respect she belonged to the highest class of sensitives; thus, she was in no way inferior in sensory sharpness to true somnambulists, although she was not a somnambulist herself.

Seeing all this, and reflecting that the aurora borealis appears to be nothing other than an electrical phenomenon caused by the earth's magnetism—the true nature of which we cannot yet explain, as no direct emissions of light from a magnet are known in physics—it occurred to me to test whether a person with such sharp vision as Mademoiselle Nowotny might be able to perceive some luminous appearance in connection with a magnet in absolute darkness. The possibility of this did not seem very remote to me; and if it were found to be so, it seemed likely to provide the key to the explanation of the northern lights.

3. The first preliminary experiment I had her father perform in my absence. To benefit from the greatest degree of darkness and an eye that had been accustomed to the lack of light for some time—so as to achieve the maximum possible enlargement of the pupil—I asked him, in the middle of the night, to hold my largest magnet before the patient: a nine-bar horseshoe magnet capable of lifting over 80 lbs., after removing the armature. This was done, and the next morning I was informed that the young woman *had actually perceived a distinct and permanent luminous appearance* as long as the magnet was open; but that it always disappeared whenever the armature was attached.

To obtain more certain and detailed information on this point, I arranged to repeat the experiment myself with some modifications. I did this the following night, trying it at a time when she had just awakened from a cataleptic fit and was, consequently, in her most sensitive state. To ensure accuracy, the windows were covered with thick curtains and the candles removed well before the fit ended.

The magnet was placed on a table about ten feet from the patient, with its poles pointed toward the ceiling, and the armature was then removed. None of the assistants were able to perceive anything at all; but the patient saw two luminous appearances, one at the tip of each pole. When the armature was attached, the lights disappeared and she saw nothing more; but upon removing it again, they reappeared as before. At the moment the armature was detached, they seemed to her to shine somewhat more brightly and then settle into a steady state of lesser brightness. These fiery appearances were of nearly the same size on each pole and showed no tendency to move toward each other. Close to the steel from which the light emanated, it appeared in the form of a luminous vapor surrounded by a kind of shining rays. MAGNETIC LIGHT.

...more beautiful than an ordinary flame; its color was purer, nearly white, and occasionally mixed with rainbow colors. It resembled the light of the sun more than that of a fire. The light was not uniformly diffused. In the middle of the edges of the magnetic poles, it was denser and more brilliant than toward the corners; but at the corners, the rays were collected into bundles that reached beyond the rest of the rays. I showed her a small electric spark, which she had never seen and could not have imagined. It appeared much bluer to her than the magnetic light, and it left a lasting, peculiar impression on the eye that disappeared very slowly.

The interest I could not help taking in the subject made it desirable to increase and vary the observations and to verify them, as much as possible, through repetition and careful manipulation. The patient’s health was improving; her sensitivity visibly diminished from day to day, and there was consequently no time to be lost. Two days later, I again tried the experiment with the assistance of her relatives. It was conducted in the same way and yielded the same results. After another day, we repeated it first with a weaker magnet without informing her of the change. She did not see the previous light as before, but observed only "two fiery threads," as she put it. These were obviously the edges of the magnet; they were the only parts visible to her because the light from this magnet was less vivid. When we then removed the armature from the strong magnet used first, she immediately recognized the former light in its previous shape and color. Some days later, during which her health had rapidly improved, the experiment was repeated, but by then even the light from the strong magnet did not appear to her as it had before. She saw the two lights less distinctly; they were smaller and somewhat flickering. They often seemed to sink and then rise again, sometimes almost vanishing and then returning after a short interval. The next night, she saw only the threads of fire, even on the strong magnet. On the following night, the phenomenon had become invisible to her, with the exception of two bright, lightning-like flashes that appeared and disappeared whenever I detached the armature.

In the course of my investigations, I had become acquainted with Dr. **LIPPICH**, a learned physician and Professor of Clinical Medicine at the University of Vienna; through his kindness, I was put in communication with one of his clinical patients. This was Mademoiselle **ANGELICA STURMANN**, aged 19, the daughter of a hotelkeeper in Prague, who suffered from pulmonary tubercles and had long been affected by the early stages of somnambulism, along with fits of tonic spasms and catalepsy. Upon testing, I found the effect of magnets on her to be so powerful that, in sensitivity, she far surpassed Mademoiselle **NOWOTNY**.

Immediately upon my removing the armature, she had been thrown into spasms and unconsciousness by the influence of the magnet. This offered little prospect of a successful result from my experiments, but they were not without some fruit. After an interval, the girl came to herself and told us that at the moment I disarmed the magnet, she saw a *fire flash* from it about as high as a small hand, which was white mixed with red and blue. She was on the point of examining it more closely when the effect of the magnet instantly deprived her of consciousness. I very much wished to repeat the experiment, and the patient was willing to allow it; however, the physician thought it likely to be harmful to his patient, and I was, of course, compelled to abandon the idea of further trials. 5. In another ward, **Dr. Lippich** showed me a lad of 18, a shoemaker's apprentice, who had, by fright and ill treatment, been thrown into convulsions, which continually recurred at intervals. 6. She was in perfect possession of her faculties, had never either walked or spoken in her sleep, and was an intelligent and clear-headed young woman. But when attacked by spasms, the appearance increased to her eyes in an extraordinary degree. The light was no longer confined to the poles, where it appeared much larger, but she now saw streams of light *from the whole surface of the steel*, weaker than at the poles, but exhibiting the whole magnet in a bright light. This produced in her, as also in **Mademoiselle Nowotny**, a lasting dazzling sensation in the eyes, which very slowly went off. We shall soon see how all these things are related together. In the meantime, I had now obtained the fourth confirmation of the existence of the magnetic light. But it was only now that I was to meet with by far the most remarkable and the clearest of those who observed these remarkable phenomena for me.

She was then in full strength, looking well, perfectly clear in her mind, and was in the habit of going alone through the crowded streets to visit her relatives. I invited her to my house, and she was kind enough to come as frequently as I wished, thus enabling me to use her extraordinary sensitivity to the magnet in conducting experiments with physical apparatus that could not conveniently be carried to other houses.

This patient combined in herself rare advantages: first, she saw the magnetic light as strongly and brightly as any patient confined to bed; second, during the intervals between her attacks, she was strong and healthy, could move about, and was very intelligent; finally, despite her high degree of sensitivity to the light, she could perfectly tolerate the approach of the magnet—as well, in fact, as healthy people. Little can be accomplished with such subjects, but Mademoiselle <term>Reichel</term> was able to carry out every investigation quietly and deliberately to the end. People of this temperament are invaluable for scientific research. 16. Let us now turn to the consideration of some of the properties of this magnetic light. That we cannot see it with the healthy eye is in itself far from surprising. When we reflect how vast a difference exists between sunlight and candlelight—the former of which WOLLASTON estimated as 5,560 times, and LESLIE even at 12,000 times more intense than the latter; when we see how feeble is the light from the flame of alcohol, wood-spirit, carbonic oxide, and pure hydrogen gases, as well as other combustibles, the flame of which is not only invisible to us in direct sunshine, but even partially escapes our notice in the diffused light of day; such enormous differences in the luminosity of different flames or lights render the step to absolute invisibility for our healthy organs no longer a wide one; and consequently the existence of such a light, invisible to ordinary sense, is not only possible, but easily conceivable. We cannot therefore be surprised to find that such lights exist, and that luminous emanations, too feeble to be, in general, visible to us, shine over the poles of magnets.

17. To convince myself, if possible, that it was really light, and not a phenomenon of a different nature perceived by sensitive persons, I wanted to conduct an experiment with the Daguerreotype to see whether it were possible to produce an impression on the prepared silver plate. For this experiment, I applied to my obliging friend, Mr. Karl Schuh, a private gentleman in Vienna devoted to physical science and known for his improvements on the gas-microscope and his skill with the Daguerreotype. He sealed an iodized silver plate, in front of which a magnet was placed, in a dark box; a similar plate was sealed in a dark drawer without any magnet at the same time. After some hours, he found the first plate, when exposed to mercury vapor, affected by light; the other was not. But the difference was not very great. To demonstrate it more fully, he placed the magnet opposite a prepared plate in a box, wrapped it in thick bedding, and took the most anxious precautions to exclude light during the experiment, of which I was myself a witness. It was allowed to remain for 64 hours, and then, in the dark, exposed to mercury vapor. The plate now showed the effect of light over its whole surface. From this it appeared that, provided other causes are not capable of affecting the prepared plate when exposed to them for a long time, *it must be a real light, although faint and slowly acting on the plate, which flows from the magnet.*

Since, however, we have learned from recent polar expeditions how low in the atmosphere the aurora often descends, the ingenious idea of <term>DAVY</term> has lost much of its probability. It has lost the foundation on which it rested—namely, the rarefied space—and along with this, the diffusion of free electricity, which he derives from our storms and applies to the explanation of the aurora. The certainty we possess that the aurora is only formed under the influence of the terrestrial magnetic poles; the total lack of knowledge until now of any direct emanation of light from the magnet; and the fact, now ascertained, that luminous emanations actually do proceed from the magnet (although invisible to ordinary sight and exhibiting a play of colors, especially white, yellow, and red, to sensitive persons)—all these considerations naturally lead us to suspect that the aurora may either be magnetism itself flowing from the polar regions, or a direct effect of such magnetism. We know that the appearance of the aurora produces a disturbing effect on the magnetic needles of entire countries, just as the magnetic flame, or the magnet from which it proceeds, also does at appropriate distances. But it is probably only the emanations from the magnet, and not the magnet itself, which act at a distance in this way; and if this is the case, the effects of deviation produced by the aurora will coincide with those of the magnet. If, finally, we compare the detailed appearances of the magnetic light as seen by sensitive persons with those of the aurora, the probability of this natural coincidence is obviously increased. 

The aurora is well known as a white arch of light—or, according to some, as a vaporous or misty mass of light at the polar horizon—from which there occurs a flickering, variable shooting of rays, collected in bundles, toward the equator. Its lines do have one prevailing direction, but they are not always straight or parallel to each other, appearing often somewhat curved and occasionally scintillating. Their color passes from the white of the arch to bluish, emerald green, and espe—

The same shooting of luminous rays, the same flickering, delicate, vapor-like flame running in curved lines, the same varied play of colors, the same red illumination of objects; all these things are described in the same way by the observers of the magnetic light. The observations are indeed not perfectly alike among themselves, but they agree on all the main points. The principal discrepancies concern chiefly the size of the flame, which is less essential; and they are easily explained by the different degrees of sensitivity to the magnetic light found in different sensitive persons. We see, for example, in the case of Mademoiselle MAIX, that depending on whether she was in her usual tranquil state or affected with spasms, she saw two different luminous appearances. In the former state, she saw only a light the width of a hand over the poles; in the latter, not only did this light appear much larger and more intense, but the entire magnet was surrounded with luminous emanations. In like manner, we find in the case of Mademoiselle NOWOTNY, that the magnetic light, in its apparent size, kept pace with the progress of her recovery; it appeared smaller from time to time as her disease diminished, until at last it eluded her observation. At one stage of her illness, she observed a kind of luminous vapor immediately over the steel, which the far more excitable Mademoiselle REICHEL never saw. From this luminous cloud, Mademoiselle NOWOTNY saw bundles of luminous rays proceed, just as Mademoiselle REICHEL saw similar bundles proceeding from the solid angles of the ends of weaker magnets. This luminous vapor or cloud next to the steel resembles to the highest degree the luminous arch of the aurora; and if Mademoiselle REICHEL did not see it, the cause probably is that in her observations, the much more flickering light and flames arising from the sides of the bars covered the luminous cloud, so that she could not, of course, perceive it. It may be expected that as her recovery advances, a period will arrive when these lateral flames will disappear to her eyes, and then the luminous vapor will become exposed and visible to her, as it was to Mademoiselle NOWOTNY.

MAGNETIC LIGHT.

It is this tranquil, light, vapor-like appearance that makes the resemblance to the aurora so close that we feel involuntarily led to admit the complete similarity between the aurora and the magnetic light. However, do not misunderstand me: I do not mean to say that I regard the identity of the two phenomena as demonstrated, for there lies a chasm, not yet filled, between light that is visible to all healthy eyes and that which is invisible. This chasm cannot even be filled by the assumption of a difference of intensity between the two phenomena. But I hold this much for certain, and I think myself entitled to express the conviction that a most remarkable analogy exists between them—so great, indeed, as to undeniably make the identity of magnetic light and the aurora highly probable.

## 22. RETROSPECT.

*a.* A strong magnet exerts a peculiar influence on many healthy and diseased persons; it is an agent that affects the vital force.*
*b.* Those who are highly sensitive to this influence or irritation frequently exhibit heightened acuteness of the senses and are then able to perceive light and flame-like appearances in the magnet. The strength and distinctness of this perception increase with the sensitivity of the observer and the darkness of the location.
*c.* In the latitude of Vienna, the negative pole (- M) produces the larger flame, and the positive pole (+ M) produces the smaller flame. Depending on the form and structure of the magnet, the flame at each pole divides into several flames of iridescent colors. Its form and color vary depending on whether the magnet is open or closed, a common steel magnet or an electromagnet, and whether it is free or under the influence of another magnet.
*d.* The positive and negative flames show no tendency to approach or unite with each other.

### CRYSTALS.

23. The physician who attended Miss NOWOTNY had repeated, in her case, even before I saw her, certain observations made by earlier physicians in cases of catalepsy. Specifically, these were: first, the fact which Dr. PETETIN of Lyons in 1788, as well as others, had noticed and published—that when a strong magnet was placed in contact with the hand, the hand adhered to the magnet just as a piece of iron does; and, secondly, that water which had been subjected to the action of a magnet (by passing the magnet several times along the vessel containing it) was immediately and clearly distinguished from ordinary water by the patient. This last fact was first observed and made known by MESMER; it has been often ridiculed and just as often reasserted. We shall see, in the course of the present investigation, how much of it is found to be true or false when it is subjected to the test of physical research.

The adhesion of a living limb to a magnet is a fact completely unknown in the sciences of physics and physiology, and few people have convinced themselves of it through actual visual demonstration; it is therefore necessary to explain and illustrate it here to some degree. When Miss NOWOTNY lay in a cataleptic state—without consciousness or motion, but without spasms—and a horseshoe magnet capable of supporting about 20 pounds was brought near her hand, the hand adhered so firmly to it that when the magnet was raised,

She remained utterly unconscious the entire time; but the attraction was so strong that when the magnet was moved toward her feet, farther than her arm could reach, she did not let it go. Instead, although insensible, she raised herself in bed and followed the magnet with her hand as far as she possibly could; so the effect was the same as if someone had seized her hand and, by this means, drew or bent her body forward toward her feet. When the magnet was at last moved so far that her body could not be moved or bent further to enable her to follow it, she was compelled to let it go; however, she then remained in the manner always observed in <term>cataleptics</term>—fixed and immovable in the position into which she had been brought. I saw this daily, from 6 to 8 p.m., at which time the fits of <term>catalepsy</term> occurred; and the fact was usually witnessed by eight to ten persons—physicians, <term>natural philosophers</term>, chemists, and others interested in the sciences. It would be of no essential advantage to refer to these persons specifically.

When I visited the patient at other times of the day, I found her fully conscious and cheerful, but the phenomena were the same. Her hand adhered to and followed the magnet exactly as it did in the insensible cataleptic state. The account she gave of the phenomenon at my request added little to my knowledge of it, or to my ability to explain its strangeness from a physical perspective. She described her sensations as an irresistible attraction which she felt herself involuntarily compelled to follow, and which she was forced to obey even against her will. It was an agreeable sensation combined with a soft cooling breeze or *<term>aura</term>*, which flowed downward from the magnet to her hand; the hand felt as if attracted to it and drawn forward by a thousand fine threads. Moreover, she said she had never perceived anything similar to it in her life before; the whole experience was a peculiar, indescribable feeling which, when the magnet was not too powerful, had something infinitely refreshing and agreeable about it.*

# MAGNETIC ATTRACTION

I later had the opportunity to observe exactly the same phenomenon in Mademoiselle REICHEL. Her illness was different from that of Mademoiselle NOWOTNY but was, like hers, complicated by cataleptic fits; her hand followed the magnet exactly as described above, both in the cataleptic and in the ordinary state. The same thing was reported to me by Professor LIPPICH as occurring at a certain stage of the illness of Mademoiselle STURMANN—though I was prevented from personally making the observation—and I have every reason to admit it.

I confess that at first I had doubts about the complete trustworthiness of the patient's statements and suspected the possibility of fraud, although this idea was directly opposed to the evident honesty of the family and the truthfulness of the patient. Therefore, I took various precautions: I blindfolded the patient's eyes during the cataleptic state and operated with the magnet in many different ways, etc. It is appropriate here to mention some of the tests to which I subjected the patient. Among others, I arranged with a friend that, upon a certain signal from me, he would alternately remove and replace the <term>armature</term> of a powerful magnet (capable of supporting 80 pounds) on the opposite side of the wall, behind where the patient lay in bed. He was to point the poles of the open magnet toward her while I stood at the bedside and observed her. The armature had hardly been removed when the patient became restless and complained that an open magnet must surely be lying near her, begging her friends to look for it and relieve her from her distress. She was always painfully affected by large magnets, whereas the effect of small ones was pleasant and cooling. The <term>armature</term> was then replaced without her knowledge, and she became calm again. When the experiment was secretly repeated, she became quite puzzled and could not imagine the source of these varying feelings of discomfort that attacked and then left her, just as if a magnet had been held out to her. Therefore, the magnet had acted on her through a stone wall without her being aware of its presence, exactly as it did when it was opened before her, according to the known laws of magnetism, which irresistibly penetrates all physical bodies. At last, we explained the mystery to her, and the experiment was repeated with her knowledge. It produced the same results: every time the <term>armature</term> was removed, the same restlessness and the shifting flush appeared, which I had seen come and go during the secret experiments.

M. BAUMGARTNER, formerly a Professor of Physics and a well-known scientist, performed another test for his own satisfaction, which was remarkably well-designed. Once the phenomena produced by the magnet and its peculiar effect on the patient had been shown to him repeatedly, he took a horse-shoe magnet of his own from his pocket. He told the bystanders, within the patient’s hearing, that this was the best and most powerful magnet in his collection of instruments and that he wanted to see how strong an effect it would have on the patient. To our astonishment, Mademoiselle NOWOTNY declared that she could not confirm this; on the contrary, she felt it was not only weaker than the weakest of all the magnets

24. I was invited by Professor LIPPICH to an experiment and actually saw the suspended needle deviate considerably. All sticking had now disappeared, and the needle remained motionless. In the previous experiment, the finely suspended needle had obviously stuck to traces of perspiration on the finger, and when the stickiness of this moisture was neutralized by the flour, all attraction instantly ceased. To be even more certain, I introduced the patient’s finger into the coil of a differential <term>galvanometer</term>. However, no induced current was detectable either when it was introduced or when it was withdrawn, and the <term>astatic needle</term> remained motionless.

25. From all this it follows that there is nothing of physical weight in the attraction exerted by the magnet on the hands and feet of <term>cataleptics</term>. This attraction has no weight-bearing power, cannot even attract iron filings, and is equally incapable of acting on a needle or inducing an electric current. Therefore, the arm, which in the <term>cataleptic</term> state followed the magnet, supported itself; its passive attraction clearly had a completely different meaning from the attraction of iron toward a magnet—or, more correctly, toward magnetically and oppositely polarized matter, in the sense previously attached to that expression.

But it is equally certain that a person in a state of cataleptic insensibility—a state which cannot be faked—not only has no free will, but has no will of any kind. Now, since the mechanical magnetic attraction exerted on persons in that state by the magnet is a fact which is not only established here by sufficient experience, but which may easily be confirmed and controlled in every large city where such patients may always be found, it acquires, in spite of its apparent anomalous nature, an established scientific existence and urgently demands further investigation. Not to explain it, but to make its character somewhat understandable, I may here refer to all the attractions and repulsions which vegetative life, in both animals and plants, continually carries out in a thousand forms, without us being able, at present, to either perceive or infer the existence of mutual attraction. A root penetrates with force deep into hard soil; it breaks and splits powerful mechanical obstacles. We see no signs of mutual attraction or repulsion that might drive it so forcefully; and yet the result happens. Similar forces carry the hand of a cataleptic patient toward the magnet; and this occurs whether or not we can initially understand and account for it.

# AND OTHER SUBSTANCES.

[Che]mists and natural philosophers viewed this with disgust. NOWOTNY always accurately, decisively, and without a single failure, distinguished a magnetized glass of water from one that was not magnetized. STURMANN, MAIX, REICHEL, ATZMANNSDORFER, and others—and when I even saw it in some of these to an even higher degree—I gave up my doubts and my resistance to a phenomenon whose actual existence could no longer be rationally doubted.

28. The strangeness of the phenomena was yet to reach the peak of incomprehensibility; specifically, when it appeared that not only the magnet but a simple magnetized glass of water possessed the power of drawing the hand of Madlle. NOWOTNY. This was indeed the case, though to a much lesser degree; yet her hand was unmistakably attracted, both in the cataleptic state and at all other times, by a glass of water previously acted upon by the magnet, so that a clear effort to follow it in every direction was evident.

29. Observing this, and being convinced that such a strange phenomenon could not exist in isolation in nature, I wanted to test whether what occurred with water might also be produced by other bodies. If this happened, I hoped to see it in such a variety of instances that scientific laws could be deduced from them. With this goal, all sorts of minerals, preparations, drugs, and objects of all kinds were subjected to the influence of the magnet and tested on the patient in the same way as the glass of water. I found, in fact, that all of them immediately acted on her, just as the magnetized water had done; they prompted the hand more or less powerfully to follow them, but with various differences in their manner of acting. Some caused general spasms throughout the whole body; others only in the arm; others only in the hand; and finally, others hardly caused any spasms at all.

# EFFECTS PRODUCED BY

although all had been equally magnetized. There must, therefore, exist a difference in the different kinds of matter employed, which it was necessary to take into account.

30. To investigate this difference, I now tried the experiment of bringing the same substances into contact with the hand of the patient, *in their natural state, and without having previously magnetized them*. To my surprise, they now acted on her with a force which was often only slightly inferior to that which they had exhibited when magnetized. The action, however, was not always accompanied by the drawing of the hand to follow the object. On the other hand, that other action, by which the patient had (Section 26) convulsively grasped the magnet in her hand, occurred frequently in various degrees of force. The method I pursued was this: I placed the different substances in the hand of the patient while she was in the unconscious <term>cataleptic state</term>, and observed the effects. I then repeated the experiments when she was in her usual conscious state and free from the <term>catalepsy</term> condition. In this comparative trial, it appeared that, in both cases, the effect was qualitatively the same, but was beyond comparison quantitatively more powerful during the <term>catalepsy</term> than at other times. The effect essentially consisted of this: that the different substances, when laid in the hand of the unconscious patient, either

*a.* Caused <term>tonic spasm</term> of the fingers, just as the magnet did, and forced them to clench themselves involuntarily, so that the substance was grasped in the hand. The substances which thus acted again subdivided themselves into those that at the same time drew the hand to follow them, and those that did not produce that effect: or

*b.* Appeared inert, excited no spasm, and left the hand motionless.

The first effect occurred with various degrees of energy in different substances. It either occurred instantly on contact or was more or less slowly and gradually produced. In the latter case, the fingers began to bend and gradually contracted more and more, until the hand was clenched in a state of <term>tonic spasm</term>. This was precisely what was observed when very weak magnets were laid in the hand of the patient while she was unconscious.

# UNMAGNETIZED BODIES.

31. When I compared the substances used, they arranged themselves, in relation to this effect, not according to the nature and composition of the bodies, nor according to the electrochemical series—not even according to their power of conducting electricity. Indeed, the same substance, in different specimens, acted differently: in one case producing the effect, and in the other not. This was observed in carbonate of lime, sugar, quartz, and many others. I next noticed that, *among the amorphous substances, there was not one* which acted so that the patient grasped it in her fingers; and on the other hand, *that all the bodies which produced that effect were crystallized*. Among the crystalline bodies tested, however, there were quite a few which had no action. When I then, omitting the amorphous substances, arranged all the crystallized bodies into two opposite groups—placing those which were inert in one, and those which acted on the hand like a magnet in the other—I found that the former, the inert group, included *all substances that were irregularly crystallized*, such as loaf sugar, Carrara marble, and dolomite; and also all substances *existing in masses composed of many groups of small crystals, running in various or opposite directions*, such as prehnite, wavellite, lumps of sugar of lead, masses of crystallized silver from Kongsberg, etc.; and that the other, the active group, contained *all single, detached crystals, and those where the crystals, if in groups, had their principal axes parallel or nearly so*, such as celestine, many kinds of gypsum, and fibrous red and brown hematite.

All these comparisons could be reduced to this: that granular crystalline limestone, compact quartz, and loaf sugar were inert; whereas a crystal of calcareous spar, a rock crystal, or a fine crystal of sugar candy—that is, detached crystals in general—when laid on the hand of the patient, instantly excited involuntary contraction, attracted the hand, caused it to become clenched, and to grasp the crystal, sometimes with the strongest tonic spasm. Here, therefore, we perceive in *single crystals* a *peculiar power*, a *fundamental force*, which had previously remained unobserved. This force, as far as it has yet been recognized, belongs to matter not as such, but by virtue of its form and state of aggregation. Pouillet, in Müller’s translation of his *Manual de Physique*, p. 167, expressly says: “that it has not previously been observed in ponderable matter <note>Matter having mass or weight.</note> that its form, or the arrangement of its molecules, is a cause of new forces acting at perceptible distances.”

But we see that the supposed case is the actual one here; matter must be crystallized, otherwise it does not act in the way described here.

32. When I then tried an active body—a crystal—by itself, I observed that the power of exciting spasms in the living organism was not possessed equally by all parts of its surface. There were points—and the patient easily recognized these—which had this power to a very feeble degree, or not at all; there were others in which it was found with increased intensity. It appeared that each crystal exhibited two such points in particular, which were the proper seat of the power. And these two points are, in each crystal, diametrically opposite to each other; they were, in fact, poles of the principal axis of the crystal. The action of both was similar, but that of one was stronger than the other. There was also this difference: from one, a cool—and from the other, a warm—soft *aura*, or apparent current of air, seemed to flow.

33. While I was endeavoring to pursue the manifestations of this force in different directions, I conducted an experiment by drawing the stronger pole of a moderate-sized crystal—specifically, a rock crystal nearly 2 inches thick and 7¾ inches long—downward along the inner surface of the patient’s hand. I made passes exactly as one does with a magnet when intending to cause ordinary sleep. I found the action *exactly equal to that of a small compass needle* which I used for comparison. It was 5½ inches long, less than ¼ inch broad, and about 4/100ths of an inch thick. It weighed about 184 grains <note>A unit of mass; 184 grains is approximately 11.9 grams.</note> and supported about twice its own weight. The needle produced the same effect. If I reversed the experiment, drawing the needle upward from the tip of the middle finger to the wrist, it produced an unpleasant, lukewarm sensation, which was obviously disagreeable to the patient. We possess some research by <term>HAUY</term>, <term>BIOT</term>, and especially an investigation by <term>COULOMB</term>, in which it is rendered probable, although not demonstrated, that perhaps all bodies either possess magnetism or are capable of becoming magnetic. One experiment was made with two needles of silver: one was of silver as pure as it could be made by chemical means; the other was of silver which had been melted with iron, and which, as no trace of iron could be detected in it by chemical reagents, might also be regarded as chemically pure. The latter, notwithstanding, acted on the magnet 416 times as powerfully as the former. It was concluded from this that it really contained a minute trace of iron, although chemistry could not detect it, and that, in general, inconceivably small proportions of iron were yet sufficient to give to another substance the capacity for magnetism; indeed, even the needle made from so-called chemically pure silver may still have retained a trace of that metal. (Gilbert’s Annalen, xii. p. 194). Coulomb leaves undecided the question of whether the substances he employed were free from iron; and Gilbert, with some reason, remarks that they could hardly have been so. The experiments consisted essentially of placing needles between magnetic poles and causing them to vibrate, both before they were placed between the poles and while in that position. The number of oscillations in equal times was always found to be smaller in the previous experiment than when the needle was between the poles, and the action of the magnet was thus established. But we must inquire: What was this action? and everyone will perceive that it allows for a threefold explanation. The first ascribes it to the presence of iron in the needles; the second to magnetism inherent in the substances; the third "to another analogous force," as Biot guessed. The resolution of these questions, as far as they refer to my investigations, seemed to me most likely to be achieved through a new and direct experiment. I had crystals, especially of gypsum, which acted as powerfully on all my patients as a bar magnet capable of supporting 4 to 6 lbs. Such a bar, suspended by a linen thread, instantly aligned itself with the plane of the magnetic meridian. If, then, the peculiar force residing in the crystal—which acted on the patients with equal power—were identical with the magnetic force residing in the bar, the crystal, when suspended, should also align itself with the plane of the meridian. To test this, I suspended various crystals free from iron—especially one of gypsum 1.5 inches long—by a silk fiber from a cocoon about a foot in length, and covered the whole with glass cylinders. After several hours had elapsed, the crystals had become quite motionless, but never in one direction more than another; they neither pointed to the north nor in any uniform direction whatsoever. If I rotated the support by ninety degrees, the crystal, after it had come to rest, was always found in a position angled 90° from its former one. I could, therefore, cause it to assume any direction I pleased. There was not, therefore, the slightest resistance to the torsion of the finest silk fiber; *and the peculiar force residing in crystals does not give to these bodies*
