On one hand, therefore, the relationship of magnets and crystals to the *animal nerve* was entirely identical; while, on the other hand, the relationship to iron, to the electric current, to magnetic poles, and to the magnetism of the earth was totally different in magnets and in crystals.

42. Thus much, then, is established: *That the polar force residing in crystals—which is recognized by its peculiar irritating action on the healthy and diseased animal nerve—is not identical to magnetic force as it is currently known.* It does not attract iron; it has no effect on the magnetic needle; even when powerful, it is unable to create the slightest trace of magnetic attraction for iron in the finest steel needle; it has no effect on the polar wire; it produces no induced current when placed in the coil of a galvanometer; and it does not obey the attraction of terrestrial magnetism.

43. But conversely, it has been shown *that the magnetic force—as we know it in the loadstone and the magnetic needle—is associated with that same force we have discovered in crystals.* For, since the magnet acts on the animal nerve in the same manner as crystals do, it possesses, along with those properties not found in crystals, that force which also resides in them.

44. From this it necessarily follows: *That the force of the magnet is not a single force, as has been previously assumed, but consists of two; because to the long-known force, a new, previously unknown, and decidedly distinct one must be added—namely, the force that resides in crystals.*

The phenomena presented by the magnet, therefore, naturally divide into two parts, which complicate each other in their manifestations; and it will be necessary to revise at least a part of the vast store of observations that science has collected regarding the magnet.

***

I wished to determine whether the new force could be conducted, whether bodies could be charged with it, and whether it could be concentrated; and whether, and to what extent, it had any analogy with magnetism and electricity, which can be conducted, transferred from one body to another, and concentrated. Since I currently possess no reagent for it except the nerves of healthy and diseased <term>sensitives</term>, and because the effect on the healthy subjects known to me thus far* was so weak that I could not distinguish different degrees of it with sufficient certainty in such people, I was forced to use the heightened sensitivity of the patients mentioned earlier. I had reason to be entirely satisfied with the results of this mode of investigation. For as the people with whose help I conducted it—although they were in the most widely different circumstances and suffering from various diseases—not only agreed in the accounts of their sensations but also made statements which, considered theoretically, were harmonious and consistent, I had every reason to consider these statements accurate and valuable. I am well aware of all the objections to which I expose myself by declaring this. But these have no weight with the sober investigator of nature, who only walks with firm and sure step within the limits of experience. All the observations we can collect regarding the external world must ultimately be learned through our senses, because we can only observe by means of them. We have only five senses and no more; but we know with certainty that in nature—both within us and around us—changes are happening every moment which we cannot perceive simply because we have no sense fitted for that perception. In every interval of time, even the shortest, countless electrical motions occur around us; yet we do not perceive them in the slightest degree. 48. I wished to determine the capacity for the charge of this new force. The charge, therefore, was not completed instantaneously, but increased during contact for a short time and then reached its maximum. *The capacity for the charge was therefore reached within a few minutes.*

Above that size, the power increased with the size of the crystal; however, the exact rate of increase could not be determined for the time being.

52. The electricity of crystals, as excited in tourmaline, boracite, and other minerals by heat, had no perceptible influence on the effect of the new force on the animal nerve. I heated these bodies to different temperatures, but *this produced no distinct change in the results*.

53. Is there no relation whatever between the magnetism of the earth and the direction of the force peculiar to crystals? If we consider the manner in which crystals are often grouped, we might be led to suppose that the two forces are, at least to a certain degree, independent of each other. Anyone who has ever seen a drusy cavity of quartz opened in a mine, and has examined it from all directions while *in situ*, cannot have failed to observe that the hollow is lined on all sides with crystals, the axes of which lie in all possible directions. But even in mineralogical cabinets we can make the same observation, as in the nodules of chalcedony, the interior hollow of which is covered with crystals of quartz and amethyst. I have never been able to detect in them the slightest preference for any one direction. Other crystallizations, again, which form radiating lines grouped around a common center—as in natrolite, zeolite, mesotype, arragonite, and pharmacolite—form radiating spherical bundles, the rays of which run in all directions and do not indicate the influence of any directing force. Artificial crystallizations, as they occur in our laboratories and factories, are in the same way thoroughly confused—as in prussiate of potash, alum, sugar-of-lead, and sugar-candy—which, in large crystallizing pans, deposit their crystals without preference for any one direction. This appears to agree with the indifference exhibited by a suspended crystal toward the magnetic needle and the polar wire. In this point of view, therefore, the new force, as far as concerns the direction of the crystals in which it resides, is independent of terrestrial magnetism.

54. If, then, the new force residing in crystals is on every side free from that attraction toward inorganic matter which distinguishes the magnet to such a high degree, it is, on the other hand, all the more surprising, and appears to claim the highest scientific interest, *that this force shares with that*

It had something of the form of a tulip, and, like one of its petals, or like the flame of a candle, beginning below with an arch directed outwards, but soon turning upwards and extending to the length of her finger. The color she again described as blue, passing above into perfect white, while a few scattered stripes, or threads of red light, ascended into the white. The flame was in motion, undulating and scintillating, and cast around it, on the surface where the crystal rested, an illumination extending over a circle of more than 6½ feet in diameter, exactly as in the case of a magnet; in which a flame-like appearance, and light radiating from it, can be distinguished with certainty. I now tested Mlle. REICHEL with various crystals in the dark. She considered the flame-like appearances singularly beautiful, surpassing even those of the magnet in beauty of color and regularity of form. She perceived the light, not only over the poles, but within the mass of the crystals. The flame over the poles she described almost exactly as Mlle. STURMANN had done; but the light in the crystals was, according to her, essentially different. It appeared in star-like forms, which, when the crystal was turned round, took other shapes. It was no doubt the crystalline structure, and the planes of cleavage in various directions, which caused the production of internal light and internal reflections; phenomena which cannot occur in the same way in a steel magnet. She made drawings of the lights in large and small crystals, which represent most surprising appearances. I intend to collect at a future period, for the sake of comparison, all the magnetic luminous phenomena with which I have become acquainted, and to provide, with this description, copies of Mlle. REICHEL’S drawings of the light from crystals. Mlle. MAIX, also, whose quiet and accurate method of observing I particularly valued, admired, during many sleepless nights during which I allowed the large rock crystal to stand on her stove, the beautiful spectacle of a whitish star of light the size of half a hand, at its point. Mlle. ATZMANNSDORFER pointed out, in a number of different crystals, in the dark, the luminous poles, and arranged them for me in a series, according to the intensity of the light.

Since, therefore, all the many crystals I tested showed the same reactions of the peculiar force manifested at their poles—just as they occur in their highest degree in a large rock crystal—we are led to the conclusion *that, in general, all crystals, like the magnet, emit a delicate, flame-like light from their poles*. This is not usually visible to the healthy eye, but it is visible to the heightened senses of nervous patients, whose senses are all in an extremely acute state. It is hardly necessary to mention that this phenomenon is probably connected with the development of light during crystallization, which has been frequently observed by chemists and has long been included in chemical systems. The nature of these emanations is not yet understood; they were assumed to be electrical because they somewhat resembled electric light, but without any direct proof of identity between them. Heinrich Rose, however, has recently shown that this light is not associated with the development of heat or electricity; neither the air thermometer nor the electroscope is affected in the slightest degree when immersed in crystallizing solutions of substances that give out the greatest amount of light while crystallizing, such as the double sulfate of potash and soda. (Poggendorff’s Annalen, Vol. 52, pp. 443, 585.) Now that we are acquainted with permanent luminous emanations from the poles of crystals—which as yet show no similarity to electric light, but, on the contrary, are decidedly distinct from it—it becomes even more than probable that the light produced by bodies while crystallizing belongs not to electricity, but to the development of the proper light of crystals; and that, during the sudden formation of solid crystals from the molecules suspended or dissolved in the liquid, circumstances may occur under which the light of crystals becomes so concentrated that it is visible to ordinary eyes. I do not enter here into the question of the nature of this light, which, like the sun, shines without intermission while the body from which it flows does not diminish in the smallest degree; whether it be a vibration communicated to fluid media surrounding the body, etc. The atoms, and even more so the molecules of matter, are believed to be polar; and we regard them as the ele-

We may ask: are the poles of the crystal an expression of this, just as the terminal plates of an open voltaic battery each represent the sum of one of the components of the electricity of all the individual elements? In the meantime, the observations made here on five different patients on many occasions—which agree so well among themselves—will soon be confirmed elsewhere and by other observers. 

But I would warn others not to perform these experiments with somnambulists while they are in a sleep-waking state. Instead, use either patients who are not subject to somnambulism or, when such people of sufficient sensitivity cannot be found, use somnambulists only when they are in their ordinary, fully conscious state. Use the sleep-waking state either not at all or, at most, as a means of verifying observations made in the ordinary state. In my research, I have never experimented with patients in a state of somnambulism; I have left them to the physician and have contented myself with the role of a spectator. To prevent mistakes and failure, I repeat that where one desires to replicate my experiments, the darkness must be complete and so dense that, even after remaining in it for a long time, one cannot perceive any trace of even a glimmer of light. Lastly, the crystal must be very large—if possible, no less than eight inches thick and of a proportionate length. In very sensitive patients, smaller crystals may indeed serve the purpose; as we have seen, Mlles. REICHEL and ATZMANNSDORFER saw light from almost all crystals, especially sulfates and fluorides, which always surpass rock crystal when they are of equal size.

### 57. RETROSPECT.

*a.* Every crystal, natural or artificial, exerts a specific action on the animal nerves, which is weak in the case of healthy subjects;* powerful in those affected with disease, especially of the nervous system; and most powerful in cases of catalepsy.
*b.* This force is seated chiefly in the axes of the crystals and is most powerful at the opposite ends of these: It is, therefore, **polar**.
*c.* Light, visible in the dark to sensitive eyes, is emitted from the poles.
*d.* In certain diseases, this force draws the hand into a kind of adhesion, resembling that of iron to a magnet.
*e.* It does not attract iron; causes no tendency in any bodies to assume a direction related to the magnetic polarity of the earth; has no action on the magnetic needle; induces no galvanic current in a wire; and is, therefore, **not** magnetism.
*f.* It may be transferred to, and collected in, other bodies by simple contact.
*g.* Bodies possess some degree of coercive or retaining power for it, but only for a short time, during which the charge gradually disappears.
*h.* It is conducted by different substances in different degrees, and better in proportion to the continuity of their structure.
*i.* The capacity for being charged with it is in direct proportion to the strength of the new force.
*k.* It is exhibited at opposite poles of different quality;

# THIRD TREATISE.

---

## AN ATTEMPT TO ESTABLISH FIXED PHYSICAL LAWS IN REGARD TO THE VARIABLE PHENOMENA, HITHERTO CLASSED UNDER THE NAME OF ANIMAL MAGNETISM.

58. I WILL now try to apply the laws established in the two preceding treatises to another class of observations related to those already described, and to give these observations a broader scope and a firmer foundation. Since time immemorial, certain enigmatic phenomena have been known that are produced by the magnet’s action on certain patients, and especially on <term>somnambulists</term>. In the last century, and probably earlier, it was observed that *similar effects could be produced without the magnet, and with the hands alone.* Given the state of knowledge reached so far, it was not possible to discover any certain connection between that power of the magnet and the similar power of the human hand or foot. It was equally impossible to recognize any regularity in the phenomena or to detect any law by which they were governed. The consequence was that all natural philosophers set the subject aside and neglected it, refusing to grant it a place among the physical sciences. Individual physicians and a few amateurs partly kept the tradition alive and partly increased the collection of incoherent observations. For lack of a better name, they called it Animal Magnetism, an expression that is all the more inappropriate because the phenomena included coincided

I have, in the first instance, avoided going deeply into this literature. I wished to keep my view and my judgment free and unprejudiced, and for the present, to build up my work on the foundation of my own experience. It seemed better to me to select my own path in the direction that natural philosophy usually pursues, which is not always that of medicine. The physician is chiefly concerned with the discovery of a means of cure; the natural philosopher with that of natural truths. The former has a tendency toward the concrete, the latter toward the abstract; and this original divergence is the reason why they have so far been so little able to combine in their research.

59. After I had proved the existence in crystals of a force which, in spite of all its differences, still exhibits an unmistakable analogy with magnetism; while, on the other hand, the so-called animal magnetism, despite essential differences, also allowed us to catch glimpses, through certain resemblances, of a surprising parallelism with magnetism; this apparent analogy led me to investigate whether anything—and how much—common to both could be ascertained, and whether laws might be discoverable to which animal magnetism is subject, just as the force in crystals appears to be. Since we may imagine crystallization to be the link uniting dead to living matter, I thought I might hope to provide, through experimental research, a point of union between animal magnetism and other departments of natural science, and perhaps supply it with that firm scientific foundation it had until now struggled in vain to attain.

60. In order to clear the way, it seemed to me above all things necessary to ascertain, as far as possible, the part played in these phenomena by the magnetism of the earth. With this in mind, I therefore tested healthy and sick persons; among others, M. SCHUH; M. SCHMIDT, a surgeon; and Mlles. NOWOTNY, STURMANN, MAIX, REICHEL, and ATZMANNSDORFER, under various circumstances and at various times.

61. M. SCHUH, in the house he then occupied, had a singular habit: when he awoke early in the morning, he regularly turned himself around in bed so that his feet were where he had laid his head during the night, and he would always fall asleep again. This second sleep was invariably much more refreshing to him than the entire previous night’s rest, contrary to the usual rule that the first sleep, especially before midnight, is the most refreshing. When he failed to obtain this morning sleep, he felt weary the whole succeeding day; this strange habit had long since become a necessity to him. I inquired about the position of his bed and found that it was placed so that the head was toward the south and the feet toward the north. By my advice, he positioned himself, upon going to bed, in the opposite direction—namely, with his head toward the north and his feet toward the south. From that day forward, he never felt the necessity of turning himself in bed in the morning. His sleep was good and strengthening, and he abandoned his old habit forever.

### THE HUMAN HAND ACTS

The parallelism between them is, as will be seen, complete; and the coincidence of the two forces in their collective manifestations is so **perfect**, that they are obviously identical. For the sake of clarity, I here place the results briefly together:

Passes made over <term>sensitive</term> persons with the hand act on them like passes made with the poles of crystals. § 79.

The force which acts here is <term>conductive</term> through all bodies, like the <term>crystalline force</term>. § 80.

Other bodies may be charged with it, as with the <term>crystalline force</term>. § 81.

The charge is soon dissipated, as with the <term>crystalline force</term>. § 82.

Bodies have a <term>coercive power</term> for both the one and the other force. § 83.

The capacity for receiving a charge, possessed by all substances, is alike in both cases. § 83.

The force in the human body is <term>polar</term>, like that in crystals. § 89.

It is indifferent to <term>terrestrial magnetism</term>, like the <term>crystalline force</term>. § 90.

It exerts, like the <term>crystalline force</term>, a mechanical attraction on the <term>sensitive</term> hand. § 91.

It exhibits <term>luminous appearances</term>, in kind and intensity, like those of crystals. § 93.

And thus we are led back to the opening proposition of this section, § 79; namely, that, in fact, the same force resides in the human hand which is found in crystals; and *that, consequently, the <term>crystalline force</term> and <term>animal magnetism</term> are thoroughly identical; so that the same laws which regulate the former apply also to the latter.*

## FOURTH TREATISE.

### FURTHER SOURCES OF THAT PECULIAR FORCE WHICH RESIDES IN THE MAGNET, IN CRYSTALS, AND IN THE HUMAN HAND.

96. In the preceding research, we have not become acquainted with all the sources of the enigmatic force which is the subject of our investigation. Indeed, the sources of it mentioned so far are not even the chief ones. Pursuing the matter, I have been led to other and very important sources of this influence. It is known that natural philosophers have long discussed the question of whether the solar rays are, or are not, capable of communicating magnetism to a steel needle. After Morichini, who published the first observations, the subject was treated chiefly by Mrs. Sommerville, Mr. Baumgartner, Configliaghi, and others. The memory of their research necessarily drew my attention to the part which the *sun* might possibly play in reference to the subject of these inquiries. The undeniable and long-known influence of the *moon* on patients affected with certain nervous diseases made it somewhat probable that a similar influence might belong to the *sun*.

97. I took advantage of the first clear sky to try some experiments in this direction with Mademoiselle Maix. I placed the end of a copper wire, about thirty-three feet in length, in her hand and allowed her to become accustomed to it. I then placed a long portion of the opposite end into the sun's rays outside the window. The patient instantly perceived the usual effects of

The room was warm, and the external air was somewhat cool. 99. I again varied the experiment by attaching wet instead of dry linen to the wire and proceeding as before. In this case, the action was accompanied by a disagreeable secondary sensation, like that which, according to the patient, moist air produced in her. But the primary sensation peculiar to the sun—namely, increasing warmth in the wire and the peculiar refreshing coolness which was perceived and spread from the wire over her whole system—was experienced with great vividness.

102. Similarly, early in my research, before I had recognized this peculiarity of the solar rays, I had frequently heard Mlle. STURMANN state that the sun made her feel cold—a statement that was incomprehensible to me at the time.

103. However, it was with Mlle. REICHEL that I was able to investigate the subject most accurately. Not only did a wire connected to an iron plate, copper plate, zinc plate, tinfoil, lead foil, strips of silver, gold leaf, German silver, or brass plate produce in her a peculiar sensation of cold when the metallic plate was exposed to sunshine; the same effect was also observed when linen, wool cloth, cotton, or silk attached to the wire were placed in the direct rays of the sun. All the sensitive nervous patients testified to this unanimously; they were as surprised as I was by the unexpected and apparently contradictory nature of these facts compared to ordinary experience. This apparent contradiction will be clearly explained in the following sections.

(§ 74.) At an earlier time, Mlle. **MAIX** had told me that she could not bear anyone who had just come out of strong sunshine to approach her bed. Some time previously, a whole group of friends who had been walking in bright sunshine came to visit her; however, the effect of their presence was so painful and distressing to her that she was unable to endure it and was forced to ask her friends to leave the room. This effect, she said, was simply that of the sun; not the pleasant coolness, but the sensation that makes a wire feel warm—in short, the sensation usually obtained from magnets, crystals, and so on.

109. After these experiments, and once I had left Mlle. **MAIX**, the girls in her family amused themselves by trying some experiments of their own. When I next saw them, they told me that the patient had found an iron key, which had been left in the sun’s rays for some time, to be as strongly magnetic as a bar magnet kept in the house. It did not attract physical iron, but the patient assured me that it affected her sensory perception exactly as a magnet does. It had, therefore, been charged with the new force by the sun. The power was not permanent but disappeared from the key after some time, just as the crystalline force disappears from bodies charged with it.

110. This observation led the girls to try another experiment, the result of which was remarkable. They placed a horse-shoe magnet, which had become weak in its physiological action, in the sunshine instead of restoring its power by the usual method of stroking it with another magnet; they had the satisfaction of being completely successful. The horse-shoe magnet was so remarkably strengthened in its action on the patient that, from that time forward, whenever a magnet lost its power or became weak, it was always placed in the sunshine to restore its activity. This is, in a way, a confirmation of the observations of **ZANTEDESCHI**. <note>Francesco Zantedeschi was an Italian physicist known for his work on electromagnetism.</note>

112. These facts, when combined, lead us to the law: *that the force of the solar rays, which corresponds to the crystalline force, may be communicated to other bodies.* And since these bodies become charged with it and retain the charge for a certain time, *they possess a certain degree of coercive power in reference to the force.*

113. Its conductivity is shown by the fact of its reaching the patient’s hand through copper and iron wire. I shall only add a few facts here. When I put one end of a piece of linen, with the usual precautions, into the hand of Mlle. REICHEL and moved the other end into the sunshine, the sensation of crystalline force soon penetrated to the hand and there excited coolness. The same result took place with woolen, cotton, or silk cloth, when tried in the same way. When these bodies were moved into the shade, the coolness disappeared in a few minutes, but always returned when they were again exposed to the sunshine. The conduction was most rapid through silk, less so in linen; still less in woolen, and slowest of all in cotton. A bar of wood, nearly twenty inches long, conducted the force of the solar ray quite rapidly. With a measure 6½ feet in length, it required more than half a minute before the action had passed from one end to the other. But even a glass tube, one end of which was in the sunshine, rapidly conducted the force of the sun to the other end. *Bodies, therefore, of all kinds, whether good conductors, bad conductors, or non-conductors of electricity, possess, without exception, the power of conducting the force derived from the solar rays.* Those bodies that are continuous in their structure, such as metals, glass, etc., conduct it easily and rapidly; those composed of detached parts, such as woolen and cotton cloth, do so somewhat more slowly and with more difficulty.

120. From all this, it follows that the moon’s light is not mere moonshine; although it yields us no heat, yet along with its light, it possesses a powerful force which *exhibits the same properties as that residing in crystals, etc. The moon is therefore a fifth source of this influence.*

### CHEMICAL ACTION. ELECTRICITY.

135. When we look back at the state of chemistry in the times of AGRICOLA, KUNKEL, and BRAND, we can form some idea of the relationship in which that science now stands to the subject of these researches. Scattered fragments of observations lie all around; but in what a state! I shall illustrate this with one example. For about seventy years, an apparatus has occasionally been used in medicine called the *magnetic baquet*. I can hardly venture to describe it, because it will prove an abomination to everyone accustomed to scientific investigation into natural truths. A wooden tub is filled with a hodgepodge of the most absurd and senseless kind, which is stirred around with magnetized water. An iron rod is now introduced, and from it, woolen threads are carried to various patients, who are thus to receive a health-bringing current of vital magnetism from the *baquet*. Now, this extraordinary mixture consists of iron slag, broken glass, steel filings, roots, iron ores, grains of corn, sulfur, sawdust, glass plates, wool, old iron, aromatic herbs, and mercury—all magnetized and mystically stratified. One naturally, and with reason, asks: Can anything conducive to health, or anything intelligible, proceed from such a diabolical cauldron? But how a magnetic effect should be exerted by such a stew, all natural philosophers will certainly agree with me in thinking it utterly incomprehen-

Was chemical action another source of the power residing in magnets, in crystals, in living men, in the sun, in heat, etc.?

137. To determine this, I took a glass of water, dissolved bicarbonate of soda in it, introduced the end of a copper wire five feet long into it, gave the other end to Mlle. It became so strong that it produced flushing of the face. It continued uniformly as long as the action lasted, and ceased when it stopped.

138. I had now seized the thread of the new force in a chemical process; but it was necessary to make quite sure.

# CHEMICAL ACTION.

I first had to address the objection that the electricity developed in the process had acted on the sensitive patient. Chemists do not agree whether, in a case such as the one described above, any electricity becomes free or not. LAVOISIER and LAPLACE, and more recently GMELIN, thought they had discovered the development of negative electricity during the decomposition of carbonate of lime by sulphuric acid. PFAFF and others deny this. Without counting up authorities here, I thought it safest, in this specific case, to appeal to direct experiment. I therefore attached a conducting wire to a <term>Bohnenberger's Electroscope</term> <note>A sensitive early instrument for detecting static electricity.</note> and introduced it into the liquid (which was isolated in a long-stemmed glass) in which I mixed the tartaric acid and bicarbonate of soda. The gold leaf did not move. I then attached the plates of the <term>condensator</term> <note>An early term for a capacitor, used to store an electrical charge.</note> and added fresh portions of the salt and acid to the water; but even then, upon separating the plates, not a trace of motion in the gold leaf could be detected. If, in such a violent action, free electricity is developed, it is not at all probable that it exists in such an inappreciably small quantity—at least, certainly not from the purely chemical part of the process. I must conclude, therefore, that electricity does not become free here, where it cannot enter into circulation; and that the portion of electricity set free by the chemical act is, according to known laws, rendered latent again at the moment of its production. The sensation in the patient's hand, therefore, cannot be caused by a current of electricity and clearly belongs to the class of phenomena investigated in this work.

She instantly felt the wire become seemingly warm, then hot, while a cool air diffused itself around the glass.

When I stirred it slowly in the dark, I myself saw bright flashes of light whenever the rod rubbed against the sugar. I could hardly consider these as electric, for here the external surface of the sugar was softened and half-dissolved. The light produced by rubbing together two pieces of sugar, chalk, etc., in the air is generally regarded as electric, but the proofs for this are very deficient. I placed freshly burnt quicklime in a saucer and allowed water to fall upon it. As soon as the internal movements connected with the slaking <note>The chemical process of hydrating quicklime to form slaked lime.</note> commenced and vapor began to rise, the whole mass of lime appeared to the observer to be white-hot, and a dull blue flame rose over it to the height of a hand. 150. The field of these researches opens up here to a vast and almost unlimited extent. But this can hardly surprise us; on the contrary, such a result was naturally to be expected and was dimly visible on the horizon when I made the first observations on crystals. Chemical action—in its various forms of solution, decomposition, combination, and changes in the grouping of the elementary molecules—is so closely related to the destruction and reconstruction of crystals that, as soon as such a force was seen to reside in crystals, it was clear it must have a necessary connection with those forces and actions which effect the union and the separation of the molecules of matter. It was therefore to be supposed, *à priori*, that chemical action would interact effectively here. I hope that it will provide us with a means of concentrating the new force and of making it more manageable than I have been able to do so far. I am limited, as of yet, to the sensitivity of sensitive persons; and it is to be hoped that, above all things, chemical action may yet supply us with what is currently a missing requirement <note>desideratum</note>: namely, a more convenient reagent for the new force, as well as a sure measure of its relative amount or intensity in different cases.

151. Let us now look back to the magnetic *baquet*. This strange and incomprehensible thing now loses its mysterious character, but only, no doubt, at the cost of becoming still more absurd and ridiculous than before. It is nothing other than a source of chemical action, produced, as it were, accidentally by the throwing together of almost any substances and continuing slowly and continuously. From it the desired force flows, just as heat is slowly diffused from a very slow fire. It is a slow current, derived from chemical action, of the peculiar influence which flows from magnets, crystals, the human hand, etc.; an influence very improperly called "Animal Magnetism" by the writers on the *baquet*. 153. All that I have said here of digestion applies, with a change of terms but with equal force, to *respiration*. We have thus traced the origin of the force which flows, in a polar form, from our hands and fingers as if from a magnet. We see where it is constantly renewed, and from where it, ever burning, blazes out from us. Chemical affinity, which is employed to an infinite extent in our bodies, produces, sets free, and supplies this force; and whenever and wherever we meet with it, we find it exhibiting its innate polarity.

They reached a firm layer of white lime, about as long and as broad as a grave and quite thick; and upon breaking through this, the bones of a human being were discovered. It was thus confirmed that someone had been buried there and covered with a thick layer of lime, as is usually done in times of pestilence, earthquakes, and similar calamities. The bones were taken out, the grave filled up, the lime mixed with earth and scattered abroad, and the surface leveled. When **Billing** was now brought back to the place, the apparition was no longer visible, and the nocturnal ghost had vanished forever.

It is hardly necessary to point out to the reader what I think of this story, which caused much discussion in Germany because it came to us on the authority of the most trustworthy man alive, and received from theologians and psychologists a thousand frightening interpretations. To my eyes, it belonged entirely to the domain of chemistry and allowed for a simple and clear scientific explanation. A human corpse is a rich field for chemical changes, for fermentation, putrefaction, gasification, and the interaction of all manner of affinities. A layer of dry quicklime, compressed into a deep pit, adds its own powerful affinities to organic matter and lays the foundation for a long and slow action of these affinities. Rainwater from above is added; the lime first crumbles into a mealy powder and afterwards is converted, by the water which trickles down to it, into a tallow-like outer mass through which the external air penetrates only slowly. Such masses of lime have been found buried in old ruined castles where they had lain for centuries; and yet the lime has been so fresh that it has been used for the mortar of new buildings. The carbonic acid of the air, indeed, penetrates to the lime, but so slowly that in such a place a chemical process occurs which may last for many years. The occurrence in **Pfeffel’s** garden was therefore quite according to natural laws; and since we know that a continual emanation of the flames of the crystalline force accompanies such processes, the fiery appearance is thus explained. It must have continued until the affinities of the lime for carbonic acid, and for the remains of organic matter in the bones, were satisfied, and

The conductor, in this case, was the transverse axis of the patient’s body, from one hand to the other, through the chest and arms.

173. Therefore, wherever <term>electricity</term> is generated so that it continues for some time, the peculiar force which I have tried to investigate in this work appears; *and <term>electricity</term> is thus the tenth source of it.*

### THE MATERIAL UNIVERSE.

174. The force which we are investigating here has now been seen proceeding from ten different, but always *special* sources. We shall now find it flowing from a *more general* source; we shall seek it in the <term>material universe</term>, and endeavor to ascertain something of the great and important part which it has to perform in nature.

175. Everyone knows that there are many persons on whom certain substances produce a peculiar effect, generally disagreeable, the results of which are often ludicrous. I do not allude here to the strange fancies, likings, or dislikings instinctively felt by pregnant women. But when we see people who cannot touch fur; others who cannot look at feathers; indeed, some who cannot endure the sight of butter, etc., etc., without feeling ill and faint when they are forced to do these things, we might, if we considered a single case, attribute it to a defective education. But experience has shown that such special <term>antipathies</term> always return in the same form, and with reference, in each case, to the same substances, in the most widely different persons and in the most widely distant countries. This proves that they are far from being always manifestations of ill-breeding or bad manners; and that they must proceed from some special cause, whether <term>objective</term> or <term>subjective</term>; further, that when they occur, they

In my extensive researches with very sensitive persons, I soon observed that there was something in common and some agreement in such antipathies, which, if pursued and compared, would certainly give hope of reducing the phenomena to a relationship of cause and effect, and thus enable us to approach nearer to the common but more hidden natural cause which produced them. I found that certain special sensations always presented themselves, and that, when I took care to clearly ascertain the feelings of the patient and reduced them to a common nomenclature, the apparent variety might be reduced to a few sensations which were constantly observed. And I soon found that these few might be brought under certain rules. They consisted of sensations of apparent heat or cold in different substances of the same temperature; of decidedly agreeable or unpleasant feelings, the latter reaching the point of exciting spasms; of sensations of pulsating pricking and dragging; and of painless <term>tonic spasms</term>.

193. To make the following experiments understandable, I must first provide an account of the layout of my house where they were conducted. The so-called castle is built such that, in the front, two parallel rows of nine rooms are connected by doors. When the doors are opened, each row creates a continuous straight line 160 feet long. Since there is a ten-foot-wide balcony at each end, and the balcony doors align with the others, I had a straight line of 180 feet from one balcony to the other where the air remained still. When it was necessary to use long wires, they could be run through the second row of rooms, conveniently providing a length of about 365 feet. I positioned Mlle. <term>REICHEL</term> at the end of one of the outer rooms and conducted experiments to determine the distance at which various objects affected her. First, to establish a baseline of measurement, I used <term>magnets</term>. With another magnet, having limbs about eight inches long and one and a half inches wide, I had to move to a distance of 60 feet. A heavy nine-bar <term>horse-shoe</term> magnet, which could support more than forty pounds at the time, affected her until I reached a distance of one hundred feet—the length of six rooms. force, in a more general and perhaps altered form. The concluding proposition, derived in § 178 from observations on Mlle. Nowotny alone, is now valid for all the persons tested; and I may now expand it as follows:—

*All solid bodies in contact with sufficiently sensitive individuals excite unique feelings, differing in intensity according to their chemical nature. These sensations are primarily those of an apparent change in temperature—such as cool, tepid, or warm—accompanied by a pleasant or disagreeable sensation that matches them more or less consistently. Finally, these reactions are in all respects similar to those produced by the force of magnets, crystals, the human hand, etc.*

To demonstrate that the cause of the phenomena just described is identical to the crystalline force, it is now necessary to study the other characteristics of that cause.

197. Is this universally diffused influence communicable to other bodies, or can they be "charged" with it—as I have often phrased it—without necessarily meaning to claim that it is a physical substance? A unique observation I made regarding Mlle. Maix leads to the answer to this question. Her sister, Barbara Maix, came to visit her. This young woman was apparently healthy, yet suffered from various nervous ailments. She took hold of her sister’s hand and had hardly done so when she jumped back trembling and let it go. “What in the world do you have in your hand that pricks me so?” she cried. There was nothing in the patient’s hand; however, she had held a piece of sulfur in it immediately before. Once this effect had gradually faded, it could be repeated at will as often as Mlle. Maix held a piece of sulfur in her hand for a short time. This clearly showed that the power to excite a pricking sensation is simply the result of transferring certain unknown properties of sulfur to the hand, which was then capable of acting on a second hand that was similarly sensitive to sulfur and other such substances. When I held sulfur for some time in my own hand and then took hold of Mlle. Maix's hand, she felt the same sensation and thus discovered what I had been holding.

198. Direct experiments proved this more decisively. I gave Mlle. MAIX the German silver rod, and when she was accustomed to it, I had her lay it down, and then I placed a piece of sulfur on it. 199. Experiments with Mlle. REICHEL gave similar results. I first repeated the experiment made by the MAIX sisters, without telling her about it. I held a roll of sulfur in my hand for five minutes. MAIX had observed in the hands of two different persons, and a striking indication of how much objective reality lies at the root of these phenomena. My hand, although I intentionally refrained from touching anything, was not in its natural state at the end of fifteen minutes; to the patient, it still felt as it did before, though to a lesser degree. It had therefore received a charge from the sulfur, which it retained for a considerable time and which was only slowly dissipated.

A pair of steel scissors, which by itself felt warm, was laid for a time on sulfur and then picked up by her. The scissors were now cool and caused the pricking sensation described above.

A glass tube, forty inches long and faintly warm by itself, was covered with sulfur at one end for a minute, and the other end was given to her. She found it was now very cool. Five minutes afterward it was still cool—more faintly, but quite perceptibly. At the end of half an hour, it had recovered its original slight warmth. Another glass tube, placed in contact with the outside of a bottle of sulfuric acid, produced the same effect.

In future treatises, I shall compare these together and endeavor to further develop them from many points of view, some of which I have only been able to indicate. Judges higher than myself will then perhaps undertake to pronounce a verdict on the whole investigation.

### RETROSPECT.

*a.* Not only magnets, crystals, the human hand, chemical action, etc., but all solid and liquid bodies, without exception, excite sensations of coolness or warmth, which are here synonymous with pleasant and disagreeable.

*b.* The acting force belongs not only to certain regular forms, or to peculiar conditions of matter, but resides in matter as such.

*c.* This force acts, not alone on contact, but also at a distance—as from the sun, moon, and stars, so from all matter.

# SEVENTH TREATISE.

---

## DUALISM IN THE PHENOMENA OF ODYLE.

216. The polar opposition in the magnet, the dualism in every crystalline form, and the symmetrical and sexual opposition in all living organisms naturally led me to suspect that something similar might be found to prevail here. The first indications of this that presented themselves were the constantly recurring sensations of warmth and coolness, and of agreeable and disagreeable feelings, which all sensitive persons—both healthy and diseased—perceived in all material substances. I found, indeed, that these people were not always in agreement regarding the sensations caused by the same object or material; but once they had assigned any substance its place among the warm or cold substances, they were almost invariably consistent with themselves in subsequent trials. There must, therefore, have been at work here objective differences in the objects tested and subjective differences in the observers (likely connected to the nature of their illness) which determined inconsistent results on one hand and constant results on the other. The attempt, therefore, to find a path that might lead me to a certain scientific truth by following the sensations of warmth and coolness was surrounded by many unique difficulties. These could only be overcome by patient perseverance.

217. The first question was this: What does the expression *warm* mean when used by sensitives? What does *cold* mean? Since the objects they examined were all of the same temperature, these words could not refer to an actual temperature or a real difference in temperature. Consequently, the expressions must be understood in a specific sense, distinct from their usual meaning. They imply *effects on the sense of touch, originating from an unknown cause, which are analogous to those of heat and cold.*

218. Mlle. STURMANN found a bottle of oxygen gas and a piece of sulphur both hot; Mlle. REICHEL found them both cold; and Mlle. MAIX felt them both to be hot when held in her hand, yet emitting a cool *aura* in every direction. They all agreed that they perceived a variation from the temperature of the air, but they gave different accounts when determining its degree. Three observers provided three different statements, yet all three remained consistent with their own perceptions every time the experiments were repeated.

219. From this, it clearly appeared that not only was the objective cause residing in matter present in different degrees in different substances, but also that different degrees of sensitivity occurred in different diseases. These variations in sensitivity might, in turn, cause merely quantitative differences in sensation—so that a substance acted more intensely on one patient than on another, perhaps over-exciting them—or they might lead to qualitative differences in results, such that a specific object might always appear warm to one person and always cold to another.

232. To confirm further the proposition established here, I shall now describe similar results obtained with healthy subjects, and particularly with Mr. Schuh, a student of physical science. When I placed my right hand in his left, after a few seconds, he felt an unpleasant sensation in his head; when I, in addition, placed my left hand in his right, this sensation rapidly increased, and in half a minute caused an undulating headache that soon became almost intolerable; after I had removed my hands, it continued for seven or eight minutes and then slowly disappeared. When I crossed my hands and took hold of his, he found it most disagreeable. Proceeding from the observation that right and left are to each other as negative to positive, I asked him to place his own right hand in his left, leaving out my hands. To the great surprise of himself, as well as of those present, he found that his headache instantly set in, and almost as severely as before; and that it ceased and returned, gradually, as he separated or joined his hands. His negative right hand formed with his positive left a kind of pair or simple arrangement (if I may use the terms of <term>galvanism</term>), and the circuit was closed by his arms and body, so that <term>polarisation</term>—or, if we may for the present adopt the word, the current—began, and soon acted on the brain. Several months later, he told me that he dared not, at any time, leave his hands together.

I particularly recommend this method of observation, as it is easy to manage, applicable to all cases, and very distinct for the sensitive observer. With two such rods of equal thickness, any two substances may be accurately compared. The trial with substances contained in vials and thus laid on the hand is only practical with such bodies that act very powerfully, such as sulfuric acid, potash, or caffeine. With more weakly acting substances it is unsuitable, because the glass varies greatly in its effect in different vials, and, according to its composition, is sometimes cold, sometimes warm, or sometimes neutral, and thus complicates the results. This often goes so far that weak substances, which are cool by themselves, may be felt even as warm through the glass, and *vice versa*. Salts and other bodies in the form of crystals must be powdered, even if only coarsely, before being tested. For no pure or unmixed result can be expected from a cluster of crystals, each of which is polar; some of the more powerful crystals act by their poles, and thus disturb the result. For example, the results from nitre and bichromate of potash were long contradictory until I ground them to powder, when they yielded a constantly cold sensation. But the powder must not be used until some hours after it has been ground, because the mortar and pestle have communicated their own state to it, which only gradually disappears. The percussion and friction also change its natural state, as the force derived from mechanical action—and perhaps also from electricity—is communicated to the powder. Finally, the substance must not, before trial, be left near others, especially powerful ones, which would charge it with their own influence, nor must they be exposed to sunshine or moonlight, nor held long in the hand. When several are compared, their temperature must be the same, etc. etc. Any of these rules, if neglected, would render the results more or less misleading, as is easily seen from the preceding pages.

242. Mlle. REICHEL further described all emanations from electrified bodies as cold, especially those from bodies that were positively electrified. The conductor, the glass, and the wood of the machine were all warm on their own; but when excited enough to produce sparks only 0.2 of an inch long, she felt them all as cold at a distance of ten or fifteen paces. The result was the same when, instead of electrifying a large surface, I allowed the electricity to be discharged directly from the conductor into the air through a point.

# DISTRIBUTION OF ODYLE

From the moment I woke up, although I remained in bed for hours reading, the odyle in my right hand increased until past the hour of breakfast and toward noon. # IN THE BODY DURING THE NIGHT.

Chymodyle is set free, if we choose to express it that way. It is a matter of absolute indifference how much or how little share we attribute to the vital force in these changes. There was no other way of managing it, for in order to obtain pure results, it was necessary that I should sleep exactly as I was accustomed to doing, and in my own bed. Figure 3, Plate II shows the result of different varied observations on me and on others. Then, as the morning twilight dissipates the darkness, the force rapidly rises, and fresh life flows into the organized world; odyle and vital force increase again during the whole day, as long as the sun shines.

Sleep is therefore a change in the functions and powers of our organs, but in no way the start of their inactivity; poets may use the comparison of sleep to death as a metaphor, but physiologists studying the phenomena of organic life cannot do so. Vitality is just as active during sleep as it is in the waking state; only its direction is changed. 275. Several <term>physiological truths</term> may be deduced from this last series of research. I shall only point out one rule here that is applicable to <term>dietetics</term>. If the day, with its sunlight and the rising <term>odyle</term> in the forehead and hands, is intended for the voluntary and intellectual functions of animals—while the night, with its falling <term>odyle</term> which then retreats to the <term>hindhead</term> <note>the back of the head</note>, is designed for involuntary, unconscious <term>vegetative functions</term>—then everything we do or omit that corresponds to this natural order must be favorable to our well-being. Conversely, everything that opposes it must be harmful. 

Now, as we have seen, the <term>digestion</term> of food favors the rise of <term>odyle</term> in the forehead and hands; the effect of the chemical changes of digestion is combined with that of the <term>solar rays</term>, and both promote the development of <term>odyle</term> and, consequently, the vital energies of the day. It is, therefore, advantageous for us to eat by day, as nature indicates. However, the effects of digestion continue for several hours. It might happen, then, that we eat at such an hour that digestion occurs after sunset, when the <term>odyle</term> in the forehead and hand is falling. The rise caused by digestion would then, in its effects, run directly counter to the fall caused by the setting of the sun, which would lead to a state of conflict or opposition in our bodily system. 

Consequently, we have here new theoretical reasons for, or explanations of, the old practical experience which dictates that we should not eat in the evening, and especially not for several hours before going to bed. If we do so anyway, the consequences are poor sleep with restless dreams—that is, a state of semi-consciousness, or half-activity of the forehead. We might indeed suppose that the <term>odyle</term> developed by digestion would then be carried to the <term>hindhead</term> and thus even promote sleep. Throughout the whole course of this present treatise, we have seen everywhere and without exception that the observed phenomena are in a state where <term>odyle</term> is recognized by its producing sensations of lukewarm heat or coolness. Under the circumstances in which we thus observe and perceive it, we can trace certain variations *very distinctly*. First, it is found in bodies *that have been charged with it from the outside*, when it proceeds from other substances. Through the contact or proximity of these, <term>odyle</term> has been communicated to or triggered in the first body, as seen in the effects of radiation from heavenly bodies and the effects of friction, chemical action, and heat. This change is temporary and of short duration. Second, it is permanently inherent in amorphous matter as such, though it is not very strongly marked in this case. Third, it is found associated with actual magnetism in amorphous bodies (such as magnetic steel) which *have been charged with both forces together*. This is not temporary, but remains in the body as long as it continues to be magnetic. (See § 23, <note>note</note>.) Fourth, it appears in certain bodies—such as crystals, plants, and animals—concentrated at *certain points*, and is then permanent.

In the first two cases, <term>odyle</term> appears to be uniformly distributed over bodies, *like a simple electric charge*. In the latter two cases, it is polarized *like a voltaic pile*. This occurs not only in the direction of one axis but, especially in organized structures, along many axes crossing each other.

*Therefore, <term>odyle</term> possesses a marked dualism, which has an unmistakable analogy with that of electricity.*

c. The warmer pole is generally positive and may be designated by + O. The cooler is negative and, consequently, marked — O.

d. The amorphous inorganic world forms a vast arrangement, at one end of which the most strongly odylo-positive body (at present potassium) is found, and at the other, the most powerfully odylo-negative body (at present oxygen). This arrangement ranges from the greatest apparent warmth to the greatest apparent cold, thus forming a series including all bodies.

i. Chemical action, as such, always produces directly — O.

m. In humans, the entire left side is positive, and the entire right side is negative. This polar opposition is most strongly marked in the hands and in the tips of the fingers.

# CONCLUSION.

---

If I collect and compare all the experiments and observations described in the preceding seven treatises, along with the deductions made from them, the following physical and physiological propositions present themselves:

**I.** The time-honored observation that the magnet has a noticeable effect on the human organism is neither a lie, nor a fraud, nor a superstition, as many philosophers nowadays mistakenly suppose and declare it to be; instead, it is a well-founded fact—a physico-physiological law of nature that loudly demands our attention.

**II.** It is a fairly easy task, and possible everywhere, to convince ourselves of the accuracy of this statement; for everywhere people may be found whose sleep is more or less disturbed by the moon, or who suffer from nervous disorders. Almost all of these individuals clearly perceive the specific action of a magnet when a pass is made with it from the head downwards. Even more numerous are the healthy and active persons who feel the magnet very intensely; many others feel it less clearly; many hardly perceive it; and finally, the majority do not perceive it at all. All those who perceive this effect—who seem to amount to a fourth or even a third of the people in this part of Europe—are included here under the general term “Sensitives.” § 60.

**III.** The perceptions of this action center around the senses of touch and sight; touch, in the form of sensations of apparent (§ 217) coolness and warmth,

<summary>The author concludes that the magnet's effect on the human body is a legitimate scientific fact rather than a superstition. He defines "Sensitives" as the significant portion of the population who can feel these magnetic effects through sensations like temperature or light.</summary>

**XXXVI.** Odyle, like heat, has the property of existing in two different states: one in which it is sluggish, being slowly communicated to and slowly passing through bodies; and another in which it is radiated to a distance (§§ 193, 254). In this latter form, it is instantly felt by healthy sensitives, without any noticeable delay, at the distance of the length of an entire suite of rooms away from magnets, crystals, the human body (§ 254), and the hands. All bodies and processes that spread odyle over other bodies by slow conduction also radiate it in all directions at the same time, though with varying strength; this is seen in friction, electricity, heat, chemical action, and bodies in general (§ 201). Odylic rays penetrate through clothes, bedding, boards, and walls (§ 23, <note>see note</note>), yet clearly with less ease than magnetism and with a certain degree of slowness. The conduction and charging of odyle from one body to another through mere proximity, without contact—such as from the poles of magnets and crystals, from the hands, or from amorphous bodies high in the series, like sulphur, etc., etc.—all seem to depend on the radiation of odyle; and this explanation also applies to the so-called magnetizing of sensitive persons.

Metals placed within the sphere of electrical action produce the most vivid phenomena. § 168.

Perceiving the odylic light cannot depend solely on a unique sharpness of vision, because all those who are capable of seeing it are, without exception, also possessed of that unique sensitivity which enables them to recognize odylic impressions through the sense of touch. They can distinguish between the odylic sensations of warmth and coolness, as well as between the pleasant and offensive feelings they experience; and these sensations are consistent. Now, since these different powers of perception are always present together in certain individuals—namely, in sensitives—we must regard them as associated. They seem to depend on a unique disposition of the entire nervous system, the nature of which is unknown, rather than on any specific condition of individual sense organs.

**XXXIX.** The odylic light of amorphous bodies is a type of faint external and internal glow, apparently extending through the entire mass. Elementary bodies, especially metals, shine most vividly (§ 206); compounds—such as oxides, sulfides, iodides, hydrocarbons, silicates, and salts of all kinds—different varieties of glass, and even the walls of a room; in short, all things emit light (§ 206).

It exhibits all the colors of the rainbow (§§ 9, 13), but red predominates in the flame from the positive pole, and blue in the flame from the negative pole. ## INTRODUCTION.

---

277. It has been objected to me that the five girls whom I have chiefly employed as my reagents for the new force are not sufficient, where the goal is to establish important truths in natural science with certainty. I proceeded to act on this principle and exerted myself to expand my investigations over a greater number of persons, in various states of health and in various conditions of life. In this way, more than two years have been spent, and to that extent the following treatise—containing a detailed investigation into the properties of the odylic light, *as exhibited by magnets*—has necessarily been delayed. But it now appears with a group of NEARLY SIXTY SENSITIVE PERSONS AS WITNESSES: male and female, mothers and young women, children and elderly persons, those of low and high rank, poor and rich, feeble and vigorous, diseased and healthy, women during menstruation and during pregnancy; and thus we have representatives of so great a variety of physical conditions that little more can be desired. The most essential addition, however, to the previous observations obtained by this expansion of my research will probably be found in this: that *perfectly healthy, strong persons* take their places in the list of sensitives; that persons who were never ill and have spent their lives in continual hard physical labor perceive the peculiar sensations and the luminous phenomena which I have described in these researches, exactly in the same

It seems important to me to explain my reasons for using these terms in the way that I have.

In the electrochemical system introduced by Baron **Berzelius** into natural science—and by means of which he gave chemistry the form it still retains—we proceed, as is well known, from the polarity of the voltaic pile of zinc and copper. We regard the electricity of the zinc pole as *positive*, because its properties agree with those of the electricity produced by rubbing zinc amalgam on glass, which has long been called positive. We are further agreed in designating as negative all those bodies which *especially* appear at the positive pole when their compounds are decomposed by voltaic electricity,<note>It is necessary here to use a qualification, such as *especially*, because, with the exception of the extremes—oxygen (fluorine?) and potassium—all the elements in the series may appear at either pole. Thus, for example, when sulfuric acid is decomposed, oxygen appears at the *positive* pole and sulfur at the negative pole; but when sulfide of potassium is decomposed, sulfur appears at the positive pole and potassium at the negative pole. This last occurs with all metallic sulfides; hence sulfur, though positive in regard to oxygen, chlorine, etc., is considered a negative element in general.—W. G.</note> and *vice versa*. 

Proceeding with this clue, I have endeavored to investigate the <term>odylic phenomena</term> which appear, on the one hand, in <term>electro-positive</term> bodies and, on the other, in <term>electro-negative</term> bodies. The great and well-marked differences between them in regard to <term>odyle</term>—as I have ascertained and described these in previous treatises—I have further encountered in the poles of crystals, magnets, living beings, etc. There has certainly presented itself a parallel between certain properties of one pole of such polar bodies and the same properties in one of the series of non-polar bodies (positive or negative, as just mentioned), and *vice versa*: the same parallelism exists between the properties of the other pole and those of the other series of non-polar bodies. Now, I have assumed that those poles with properties running parallel to those of the electro-negative bodies possess the same polar value, and I have designated them <term>odylo-negative</term>, and *vice versa*. That pole in our magnetic needles which points to the south, and which I have uniformly called the *southward* pole, is the one which, considered in reference to <term>odyle</term>, produces the same effects as...

### **A.—BETWEEN ODYLE AND HEAT.**

*a.* Odylic emanations cause feelings of coolness and warmth in all sensitive individuals, sometimes even icy cold and burning heat; that is, they trigger sensations *apparently* identical to those named. However, when directed at a thermometer, that instrument is not affected in the slightest degree; even the thermoscope of NOBILI <note>An early 19th-century instrument used to detect minute changes in temperature, developed by Leopoldo Nobili.</note> remains motionless. Neither the cold-producing nor the heat-producing poles of crystals affect these instruments at all.

*b.* There are many cases in which heat and odyle produce diametrically opposite effects. A right hand feels cool when acting upon sensitives, but it *always* affects a delicate thermoscope with warmth. The solar rays trigger a sensation of cold in sensitives, but they warm the thermometer. Moonlight is felt as vividly warm by a sensitive person, but it produces no clear effect on the thermoscope. Glowing charcoal and the flames of all burning bodies radiate cold with remarkable intensity to sensitive nerves, but they radiate heat to the thermometer. In chemical processes, cold emanations are produced that are perceptible to sensitives, whereas the thermoscope often or generally indicates the release of heat.

*c.* The conductivity of odyle through metals far surpasses the limits of heat conductivity. A copper wire of considerable length—60 or 70 feet or more—when charged with odyle at one end, produces odylic changes of sensation at the other. However, if heated, the heat will only be conducted along the wire for a few inches. The same is true

## B.—BETWEEN ODYLE AND ELECTRICITY.

<term>Odylic phenomena</term> often occur where electrical phenomena either do not appear, or, as far as we know, do not exist. This is the case, for example, with sunshine, moonlight, the <term>spectra</term> of different kinds of light after transmission through glass, crystals, the human hand, and, in part, chemical processes.

*a.* <term>Odyle</term> distributes itself through the mass of any body charged with it; a hollow ball of metal, for example, glows when charged with <term>odyle</term>, not only on its own surface, but internally. A glass of water tastes to the <term>sensitive</term> equally <term>odylized</term> in every drop; and the water retains its new properties entirely, even when poured into another glass. (§ 107). Free electricity settles itself only on the surface. <term>Odyle</term> may be for a time communicated to all bodies, including the air within a room; whereas Dr. FARADAY could not collect electricity anywhere in a room prepared for the purpose, as the whole amount instantly escaped through the surface of the walls, etc.

*b.* When a body is charged with <term>odyle</term>, the free <term>odyle</term> adheres to it, so that it is not rapidly removed from the body, but requires some time—from a quarter of an hour to several hours—before it is dissipated by contact with other bodies. Free electricity is instantly removed from a body charged with it by contact with another, such as the finger.

*c.* Odyle may be communicated to, and to a certain degree accumulated in, bodies that are not insulated. Electricity can only be communicated to and condensed in insulated bodies, and not at all in those that are not insulated.

*d.* All bodies, provided they have a continuous structure, are nearly equally good conductors of <term>odyle</term>; only those that are not as coherent, such as woolen and cotton cloth, etc., are less perfect conductors. Electricity is only well conducted by metals; it is slowly conducted by many other substances, and by some not at all. The conduction of <term>odyle</term> through the best conductors, such as metallic wires, occurs slowly; twenty to forty seconds are required for its passage through a wire fifty or sixty yards long. Electricity flashes through distances a million times greater in an interval too short to be measured.

*e.* All bodies are permeable to <term>odyle</term>; there are, indeed, slight differences among bodies, but these are trifling. There are many bodies nearly devoid of permeability for electricity, which present insurmountable obstacles to its passage.

*f.* Action at a distance occurs much more powerfully and from much farther away when electricity excites or induces <term>odyle</term> in other bodies than when electricity induces an electric state in them. Thus, a conductor feebly charged with electricity—only enough to give sparks 0.2 of an inch long—excites a vivid current of <term>odyle</term> in a wire at six and a half feet (§ 169); whereas a charged conductor at that distance can produce no such induced *electrical* state in another conductor.

*g.* The excitement of <term>odyle</term> by means of electricity is not instantaneous; it always requires a noticeable amount of time, frequently thirty seconds or more. This is true both for the effects on the sense of touch and for luminous phenomena. An <term>electrophorus</term>, excited by the strokes of a piece of fur, is electrified long before the <term>odylic flame</term> appears. An electrified wire, and one through which a <term>galvanic current</term> is passing, only begins to glow odylically when the current has lasted for some time, or some seconds after the shock of a <term>Leyden phial</term> has passed through it. ### C.—BETWEEN ODYLE AND MAGNETISM.

<term>Odyle</term> is produced and vividly manifested in a multitude of cases in which magnetism, properly so called, is nowhere observed or is not yet known to exist; such as, in part, during chemical changes, in vital changes, in crystals, in the case of friction, in the spectra of solar and lunar rays and of candlelight, in polarized light, and in the amorphous material world collectively.
*a.* In the vast majority of cases, <term>odyle</term> is developed alone without magnetism. Magnetism never appears alone, but is always associated with <term>odyle</term>.
*b.* Where magnetism is supposed, but not generally admitted, to exist—as in the sun’s rays or the moon’s rays—it is, at all events, so feeble that the fact of its presence is still highly doubtful. But in these very cases, <term>odyle</term> appears with a power and variety of effect which is truly astonishing, and even appears capable, in certain cases, of shaking life to its very foundations.
*c.* The obscuring of the sun or moon by mist or clouds instantly and very decidedly diminishes their effects on <term>sensitives</term>. Magnetism is arrested by nothing, and least of all by vapors.
*d.* All solid and liquid bodies may be charged with <term>odyle</term> in the very same manner: metals, steel, salts, glass of various kinds, silk, resin, and water; all, with minor differences of degree, may be charged with <term>odyle</term>. Magnetism can only be communicated to a very few bodies; and we do not know if <term>diamagnetism</term> can be communicated at all.
*e.* When bodies are charged with <term>odyle</term>, they act on <term>sensitives</term> exactly like a magnet. But they possess not the slightest trace of magnetism proper, and do not attract even the smallest particle of iron filings.

The differences which, according to the above comparison, exist between <term>odyle</term> and heat, electricity, and magnetism, have not only not diminished in the course of the investigations made after the writing of § 276, but have, on the contrary, become even more prominent. We shall find this to be even more the case in the treatises next to follow. They are, in many points, so strong and marked that the necessity for a special name for the new force appears more irresistible than ever. *Under the term <term>odyle</term>, I collect and unite all the physical phenomena occurring in the course of these researches which cannot be categorized under any of the previously recognized <term>imponderables</term>; and also the <term>vis occulta</term> <note>hidden force</note>, which produces them.* It remains for future investigation to determine whether, and to what extent, these phenomena can be distributed among, or transferred to, the known forces mentioned above. But a deeper insight into the essence of these things than we now possess is necessary before such a result can be expected.

Everyone is nearly convinced that electricity and magnetism are essentially one; no one doubts that the same force acts in the one case in a half-free state, and in the other, in a half-combined or latent state. We hourly look for the grand discovery by which their identity will be proved, and both will be brought under one common concept. But we shall never be able to dispense with either of the words, electricity or magnetism. And exactly in the same way, we shall never be able to do without the word <term>odyle</term>, or some equivalent term on the adoption of which men may agree. Such a term must always be required to embrace a mass of phenomena which cannot, with propriety or accuracy, be recorded except as a peculiar group.

## LUMINOUS PHENOMENA.

### THE ODYLIC LUMINOUS PHENOMENA SEEN OVER THE MAGNET.

280. In all these cases, I have only mentioned the phenomena *generally*, because I was endeavoring to identify characteristics indicating the presence and activity of odyle, and was able to establish these by proving the existence of the luminous phenomena. ### HISTORICAL DEVELOPMENT OF THE FACT OF THE ODYLIC LIGHT SEEN OVER MAGNETS, CONSIDERED GENERALLY.

283. 284. All these observations were made in 1844. During 1845, 1846, and 1847, I collected a much larger number, having devoted myself uninterruptedly to the study of this attractive subject during those years. I shall now present those that simply serve to further prove and establish the fact of the existence of light playing over the magnet. But I must explicitly remark here that this is primarily intended for readers who do not consider the observations already given to be sufficient to convince them, and who think it necessary to have a very large number of witnesses testifying to the physical phenomenon of the luminous emanations from magnets. I follow the order of the ability to see the light, beginning with those cases in which it was feeblest, and proceeding to those in which the power was most strongly developed; I proceed from the healthy sensitives progressively to the delicate, the sickly, and lastly to the highly sensitive patients who are permanently in bad health.

### A. HEALTHY SENSITIVES.

285. Among these there were a few possessing to a very marked degree the power of perceiving the impressions on the sense of feeling made by the odylic influence, but who could not see the magnetic light; others who saw the light, though feebly; and some, who saw it very easily, and with such distinctness and precision, *that they surpassed in this respect not only many patients, but also some actual somnambulists.*

286. **Dr. FRIEDRICH** from Munich, a young and healthy physician, of whom I had heard that he was subject to sleep-walking, was so kind as to permit me to test his power, and to go with me into a dark chamber which I had prepared expressly for these experiments. I found him decidedly, though feebly, sensitive. He saw light from other objects, but not from magnets.

287. **M. EDUARD HUETTER**, proprietor of the bookselling establishment of the heirs of **ANTON DOLL** in Vienna, a robust, young, and perfectly healthy man, was in many ways sensitive to odylic impressions, but had no power of seeing magnetic light, with the exception of a feeble and uncertain gleam in the dark from a small but strong horseshoe magnet.

288. **MAXIMILIAN KRUEGER**, a boy of twelve, in the orphan house of Vienna, very sensitive to other odylic impressions, was not able to perceive any light whatever from magnets in the dark.

289. **M. CARL RÖSSNER**, Imperial Councillor and Professor of Architecture in the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, forty-two years of age, singularly sensitive to all the other
