I frequently encountered the same thing, especially among men, and to a remarkable degree in Dr. DIESING, Curator in the Imperial Cabinet of Natural History in Vienna. He was in the highest degree sensitive to odylic feelings, but utterly insensitive to all the luminous phenomena, even after four hours spent in complete darkness.

Here, therefore, are five decidedly sensitive persons who could hardly, or not at all, perceive the light that flows from the magnet. From this, we must conclude that odylic sensitivity is not always combined with the power of seeing luminous phenomena. However, these cases are certainly exceptions.

290\. I have already often spoken of Mr. KARL SCHUH when treating the perception of the feelings excited by odyle. In reference to the luminous appearances, he stands at the bottom of the scale. He does not see the magnetic flame, but in total darkness, he can clearly recognize the form of the magnets. Therefore, he perceives—though feebly—the light emissions from the mass of metal, though not in the form of a flame. This is what I have called the **odylic glow**, and it forms the first degree in the perception of these luminous phenomena.

291\. The Chevalier HUBERT VON RAINER, from Klagenfurt, twenty-four years of age and a barrister, is a man overflowing with health and vigor; he has never been ill and knows neither headaches nor stomach pain. His sensitivity, as concerns odylic feelings, is very marked; however, he was only able to recognize the magnetic light with certainty at the moment when I removed the armature <note>The iron bar placed across the poles of a magnet.</note>, when he saw a flash of light.

CONSTANTIN DELHEZ**, forty years of age, a French Philologist residing in Vienna, healthy but highly sensitive, after being an hour and a half in the dark chamber, saw bar magnets glowing with a vaporous light. In a five-bar horseshoe, this light or flame was stronger at the negative and weaker at the positive pole. In an electromagnet, he saw both poles covered with a pale light, two inches high and two inches wide.

297. **Baroness PAULINE VON NATORP**, in Vienna, a mother of two children, young and very intelligent, of fair complexion, saw the flash when small horseshoe magnets were disarmed, and a continuous light on the northward limb. In larger magnets, she saw the flame, sometimes only from one and at other times from both poles, like a luminous vapor nearly four inches high. In large magnets of lower magnetic intensity, she saw over the poles only a feebly luminous thin vapor or smoke.

# WITNESSES TO THE LIGHT

298. **M. DEMETER TIRKA**, a Greek wholesale merchant in Vienna, forty years of age, known for his love of the plastic fine arts, of powerful build, and—with the exception of an occasional headache—perfectly healthy throughout his life, saw a flash of light above the northward pole of both a small and a large horseshoe magnet when I removed the armature. A three-bar horseshoe showed a continuous light over the same pole, but no light on the southward pole. A heavy nine-bar horseshoe did not show him a distinct flame anywhere, but all objects close to it were clearly illuminated.

299. **MADAME SYLVIA VON VARADY**, wife of the Imperial Court Councillor, **M. Strongly magnetic bars eight inches in length showed lights 0.8 of an inch high at the poles.

300. **M. When I attached the armature and then suddenly removed it, they rose higher in the first moment, but immediately fell back to their original size. At first, he did not see a nine-bar horseshoe; but very soon he perceived, when the magnet was open, a very thin, widely spread light flickering over the poles, sixteen inches wide and forty inches high. He did not describe it as a flame, but as a general, very delicate luminous appearance, visible in the surrounding darkness. He saw a small pocket horseshoe magnet more distinctly covered with flame-like lights than the nine-bar horseshoe. Its magnetism was

### B. DELICATE OR SICKLY SENSITIVES.

320. Under this category, I include all those who can go about their occupations like healthy people, yet are, from time to time, affected by discomfort and illness, forcing them to stay in their room or their bed.

321. Ms. **SUSANNA NATHER**, thirty-seven years of age, is the daughter of an officer from Basel. I found her ill in a convent in Vienna, showing all the symptoms of highly-marked sensitivity. It was remarkable that, despite her very great sensitivity to everything that affected the sense of touch, she could never see the magnetic light. We find, therefore, highly sensitive persons who occasionally suffer from severe nervous ailments, yet whose organs of vision are not able to perceive the <term>odylic light</term>, while we have many perfectly healthy persons who, with the utmost ease and clarity, see these phenomena.

This is precisely how, in both France and Germany, the truly interesting phenomena of <term>somnambulism</term> have been covered with disgrace and rendered shameful in public opinion. I was myself present when our worthy Professor, Dr. LIPPICH, administered a severe and well-deserved rebuke to the physician, but, as the sequel too clearly proved, it had no effect. I know well that, despite all this, enough people will remain to whom all I have done will not seem sufficient; for there are such things as *irrational doubts*; there is *absurd incredulity*; and lastly, there is also *evil-minded skepticism.*<note>A small association of Vienna physicians has recently given us a deplorable example of this. I sincerely pity these gentlemen (of whom there are at least twenty-three, all doctors and professors of medicine) because, in the course of twenty-two sittings, they did not know how to approach the truth and gradually lost themselves and their sensitives in such a monstrous labyrinth of confusion that the whole investigation finally collapsed into mere lies and imposture. I will not name names. When we read the report which they published in November and December 1846, under the protection of the Journal of the Society of Physicians in Vienna, we cannot avoid a feeling of pain when reflecting that men of such ability—who could have rendered essential service to science if they had chosen—have wasted their powers in a manner so deplorably useless, and even obviously harmful to the progress of knowledge. For, instead of confirming and discovering any truths, they have—through a series of very poorly conducted experiments—arrived at the most absurd and perverted conclusions, and done their best to once again shroud in doubt and obscurity facts that might be regarded as established. I will not fail, as the course of my work leads me to notice these blunders, to do them full justice in notes. I do not believe that they require contradiction in the eyes of those who understand scientific research, for to such people they refute themselves by their own absurdity; however, it is my duty to protect foreigners and those unfamiliar with these subjects from the delusions that these poorly executed experiments are intended to foster.—R.</note> These I am unable, and do not wish, to refute. I only concern myself with thoughtful, reflecting, and rationally judging people—those who are friends to the quiet progress of science. Such persons will, I trust, be satisfied with the evidence presented here, insofar as it supports the fundamental proposition *that light emanates from magnets in the dark*, and that many people (though not all), both healthy and sick, perceive this light clearly and with certainty.

Through this kind of collective evidence, we obtain the following *well-established leading propositions:*

**a. Every steel magnet gives out light independently; it is odylic light in the general sense. It appears under different forms, and in these it exhibits different degrees of intensity, different colors, different degrees of thinness or density, and different kinds of motion.**

**b. Not every eye can perceive the light.** *Only a certain class of persons can do so,* the individuals of which may be either healthy or diseased. Certain morbid states increase this power to a high degree, but the same or nearly the same degree of it is also now and then found in healthy persons.

c. *The odylic light is very feeble,* and is so overpowered, or, as it were, "killed" by every other light, that it is rendered invisible. In order to see it distinctly, therefore, the eye must be prepared by remaining *for one or more hours in absolute darkness.* The slightest trace of light that penetrates into a room darkened for the purpose almost always renders the observation of the light impossible, and at all events makes it uncertain.

335. In order to establish, as firmly as possible, the fundamental position that light—that is, a new, hitherto unknown phenomenon, not reconcilable with our existing notions of magnetism, and whether it be ordinary light or light possessed of other peculiar and inherent properties—does emanate from the magnet, I was resolved to spare no labor. And I felt the more bound to confirm it by all the means at my disposal, because as yet we do not possess any visible proof of the same cogency as we can employ in other physical experiments so as to represent it generally. But having once fixed and established it as a natural law by the inductive method, and with the enumeration of a superabundantly great number of indisputable special cases, I do not think it necessary for the future—and it would certainly be regarded as a tiresome and useless superfluity—to corroborate all the further observations on this subject, in its measureless extent and every detail and peculiarity of each separate division of it, by adducing, as I have hitherto done, several dozen experiments which only repeat and confirm what has already been shown.

I would request the reader to judge the account given here of my further research into the phenomena of odylic light in its various forms, with reference to the principles just listed.

## FORMS OF THE EMANATIONS OF ODYLIC LIGHT IN THE MAGNET.

336. The odylic light of magnets appears, as far as my research currently extends, in five forms, which appear distinct to the eyes of sensitive persons. These are—
1. The odylic glow.
2. Odylic flames.
3. Threads, fibers, or feathery down.
4. Luminous vapor or smoke.
5. Scintillations.

We shall consider each of these forms of odylic light in turn.

### 1. ODYLIC GLOW ON STEEL MAGNETS.

337. We have seen that one of the first and most general phenomena observed by almost all <term>sensitives</term> in complete and long-continued darkness is a peculiar kind of luminous state, in which steel magnets appear as if feebly glowing or red-hot, and which I do not know how to call anything other than the *odylic glow*. I have already spoken of the nature and appearance of this glow in the preceding treatises, and have publicly produced the names of more than fifty earlier and later eyewitnesses

338. In the dark chamber, I showed a simple bar magnet, one and a half feet long, to the boy STEPHAN KOLLAR. It was lying in the magnetic meridian, with its north pole in the normal position toward the north. He saw only one-third of the bar glowing—specifically, the part including the north pole. The remaining two-thirds escaped him, so that he only had occasional glimpses of them. I showed the same bar, under the same circumstances, to the healthy <term>sensitives</term> Mlle. ZINKEL, Mme. BAUER, Dr. NIED, Baron OBERLAENDER, Mme. von VARADY, M. RABE, Mme. von PEICHICH, and many others. They saw it glowing throughout, strongest at the poles and diminishing toward the middle. However, the color of the glow was not the same everywhere. The northern half glowed with a bluish light, and the southern with a yellow-red light, which matches the colors of the flames on the opposite poles. Mlle. ZINKEL also described the division between the colors as unequal: the northern bluish half was somewhat shorter, and the opposite one was longer. I inverted the bar, placing the south or positive pole toward the north and the north or negative pole toward the south, so that the poles of the bar were in the same position as those of the earth. The colors of the glow now became somewhat turbid and were modified to some degree. The reddish half of the bar was now toward the north and the bluish half toward the south; but the blue was duller than before and had a tinge of red, while the yellowish-red was turbid and mixed with much grey. The northern half was again the shorter of the two. In every change of position and intensity of color, the half that happened to point toward the north was, therefore, always the shorter. I now took *an open horse-shoe magnet*. Professor RAGSKY, M. SCHUH, Chevalier von RAINER, M. HUETTER, and M. DELHEZ saw the limbs toward the poles only in a feeble, dark grey light. I placed both poles in the meridian before more highly sensitive persons, first pointing both northward, then southward. In the former case, they saw the blue glow of the north pole

(I borrow the terms *conformable* and *unconformable* from geologists and miners, who call a stratification opposed to that of the general lie of the surfaces in a mine unconformable, in contradistinction to the conformable stratification which forms the general parallelism. In the same way, I call that position of a bar or horseshoe, or any other form of magnet, conformable, in which the northward pole lies toward the north, the southward toward the south, and the opposite position unconformable). I performed the experiments with Mme. KIENESBERGER, with a three-bar horseshoe, placing the poles upward, and turning them alternately to the north or to the south. I therefore omit the repetition of the description of them. These phenomena kept, in some degree, pace with the respective intensities of the magnetism of the earth, and of that of a bar magnet; concerning which M. GAUSS has taught us that, in our latitude, they are to each other inversely as the weight of one-eighth of a cubic meter of the earth’s mass and that of a steel bar weighing one pound.

# ODYLIC GLOW ON STEEL MAGNETS.

In other words, the magnetism of a common steel-bar magnet is, in our latitude, generally more intense than that of the Earth and outweighs it so greatly that the former cannot be overpowered by the latter during an experiment. Yet the Earth’s magnetism makes its presence known insofar as the colors of the magnet's odylic glow visibly lose clearness and purity in unconformable positions. We know that, because of the connection between magnetism and odyle, these allied phenomena always appear together in magnets, of which we have seen many examples.

339. A similar result was obtained in a later trial in which I set up a twenty-inch bar magnet *vertically* before Mlle. **ZINKEL**, with the north pole facing upward. When a simple horseshoe magnet was used, both poles retained their colors whether pointed vertically upward or downward, but they varied in tint and intensity. However, in all the trials, the magnetism of the bar and its associated odylic state overpowered the Earth's to a certain extent; this was consistently more pronounced the stronger the magnet employed.

344. The odylic *polarities*, therefore, *are reversed* when several like poles are brought together or coupled. They then form alternating strata, and this occurs despite the *magnetism proper, which is not reversed*. In this case, therefore, magneto-negative poles were seen in a red odylic glow, and magneto-positive poles yielded a blue odylic glow, but they were alternately stratified with negative magnetic poles in the normal blue glow and positive magnetic poles in their normal red glow.

This very striking phenomenon is one of the very obvious distinctions between magnetism and odyle that present themselves to the enquirer.

With the view of intensifying this phenomenon, I brought a bar magnet, *twenty inches long*, near to the sides of the horseshoe, using *unlike poles*. But the result did not correspond to my expectation. When I brought the northward pole of the bar near the southward pole of the horseshoe, at about two inches from it, the red glow of the latter was indeed perceptibly increased; but the alternation of colors in the lamellae disappeared, and Mlle. **ZINKEL** saw nothing but a series of red plates. I next wanted to test the effect that *crystalline poles* might have in a similar experiment; for as the bar magnet, acting on the magnetism of the horseshoe, interfered with and destroyed the luminous odylic phenomena, it was quite conceivable that an unmixed odylic influence might affect the odylic appearances presented by the compound horseshoe in quite a different way. The result proved, in fact, to be quite different from that obtained with the bar magnet. For when I brought the positive (southward) pole of a very large rock crystal from the side to within about four inches of the northward pole of the horseshoe, the stratified bands not only did not lose any brightness or contrast of colors, but the blue of the alternate lamellae increased greatly in distinctness and beauty, while the red turned to grayish red. On the opposite side, *mutatis mutandis*, the red lamellae acquired a finer and brighter color than before, while the blue ones became decidedly grayish blue.

But when I brought like poles of the crystal and the horseshoe near to each other—north to north, south to south—all the odylic glow belonging to the northward or southward poles respectively became dark and even disappeared; while, on the contrary, the glow of the opposite polarity was enlivened and intensified. That is, when the northward or negative pole of the crystal was brought near the same pole of the horseshoe, the glow of all the blue bands disappeared to the observer, Mlle. ZINKEL, while that of the red bands became brighter; and if the southward poles were brought near each other, the opposite result took place.

<header>EFFECT OF THE ARMATURE ON THE</header>

This led me to try the effect of the *odylic poles of the animal body*. I turned first my right and then my left side *towards the compound positive or southward limb of the horseshoe*. In neither case was the odylic glow extinguished; on the contrary, in the first case, the red lamellae increased in the intensity of light and color, while the blue became darker; in the second, the blue became brighter and the red darker. When I did the same at the *negative limb*, my left side caused increased brightness of the red lamellae and a dullness of the blue; my right side intensified the blue lamellae and rendered the red darker. Each pole of my body, therefore, increased the light and color of the opposite pole and diminished those of the similar pole; this generally heightened, for Mlle. Zinkel, the contrast of colors in the stratified bands.

*From these observations it follows that the influence of the magnet on the colors of the odylic glow in steel magnets is quite different from that of the odyle of crystals or of the human body. In other words, odyle, when coupled with magnetism proper, has a different effect on the phenomena of the odylic glow in steel magnets than that produced by odyle when not associated with magnetism—as it emanates, for example, from crystals and from the living human frame.*

345. The closing of the magnetic circuit, by attaching the *armature*, had a powerful influence on the strength and distribution of the odylic glow in steel magnets. It has been already frequently stated that when the magnets are open, the glow is strongest towards the poles and weakest in the middle, in the shorter or magnetic axis; but when the armature is attached, the appearances are changed. In the dark chamber, before Mlle. Zinkel, I attached the armature to a simple horseshoe, standing vertically. The first thing she noted was that the armature, which previously, like iron in general, showed a feeble whitish glow, now became much more luminous; and next, that the color of its light changed, dividing into two halves: a bluish and a reddish. 347. In regard to *intensity*, the luminous appearances on the closed magnet are not constant in their distribution on the different parts, but vary in different ways. On one hand, this is because the magnetism of the earth, and probably other agents—such as terrestrial and atmospheric electricity, sunlight, human hands, and other substances near the magnets which diffuse odyle—act on them to a greater or lesser degree. On the other hand, it is because magnetism and odyle are naturally distributed unequally over a magnet, as a consequence of their own peculiar attractions and repulsions. All these influences act, now on one side, now on the other, and displace the odylic poles and the force of their luminous energy more or less. It will never be an easy matter, in all time to come, to calculate the effects due to all these factors. But I have, in the meantime, collected some observations, which I include below.

348. **Mme. CÆCILIA BAUER** saw a number of magnets lying on a table in the dark, but observed that they differed much in the intensity of their glow. Many appeared beautiful and bright, while others were dull, cloudy, and deadened. I arranged them according to her account of the intensity of the light, from the dullest to the brightest. On examining them in daylight, it appeared that the intensities of light did not correspond with the weights supported by magnets of different sizes, but uniformly with the magnetic intensity. Simple horseshoes, which affected the needle at a great distance, glowed brighter than a nine-bar horseshoe, which carried ten times more iron but did not act on the needle at so great a distance.—*The intensity of the glow was therefore in proportion to the magnetic intensity.*

349. All sensitives possessed of a tolerable power of perception for the light saw bar magnets as brighter at the poles than at the magnetic axis. This was the case with **Mlles. REICHEL, WEIGAND, ATZMANNSDORFER, GLASER, Baroness VON VARADY, M. RABE, Baron VON OBERLAENDER, Baroness VON NA-**

...the armature, glowing brightest. Mme. KIENESBERGER, BARONESS VON AUGUSTIN, and Mlle. ATZMANNSDORFER saw, in every case tried with them, that the poles were brighter than the armature. It seemed to me that in all cases where the ends of the armatures were well-fitted to the poles and well-polished, and thus offered many points of contact, the poles were dimmer and the armature brighter. This was because the armature then conducted the magnetism more perfectly and discharged the poles more rapidly and completely. The faster the conduction, the dimmer the light was at the poles; the slower the conduction, the greater was the accumulation of magnetism and odyle at the poles, and the brighter their light. The light in the armature is probably always the same, but in one case it is overpowered by that of the poles, while in the other, it exceeds that light in intensity.

354. When I closed a horseshoe magnet, not with its armature but with another horseshoe, the results were somewhat modified. Both curves indeed became rapidly brighter, but did not now surpass the poles in light intensity; on the contrary, the light of the poles was still superior to that of the curves. Mlle. PAUER and Mlle. ZINKEL, two perfectly healthy, exact, and trustworthy observers, saw this distinctly. While closing the magnet with the armature gave greater intensity to the curve, closing it with a horseshoe magnet still left the poles brighter than the curves.

355. We can see the cause of this difference. When two horseshoe magnets close each other, a double quantity of magnetism and of odyle must be conducted through both at the same time. The opposite poles also excite and set in motion, when in contact, a still greater amount of magnetism and odyle. There is, therefore, on the one hand, a much larger amount of these imponderable influences brought into circulation; on the other hand, the channel through which they must pass has become less open, for soft iron is a much better conductor for them than steel, which has such great coercive power over them. Now, the armature is made of soft iron, but the horseshoe supplying its place is made of hardened steel. Again, the armature is only one-tenth the length of the horseshoe; consequently

# AFFECTED BY THEIR POSITION.

...the former permits a rapid passage, the latter one ten times slower. Thus, a much larger amount of the imponderable influences must pass through a more difficult channel when a horseshoe is closed by another horseshoe instead of an armature. The consequence is that the imponderables, impeded in their egress, accumulate at the poles and then, of course, produce a brighter odylic glow. This somewhat interrupted or retarded state of circulation approaches that of the entirely interrupted circuit in the open horseshoe, when no means of egress are provided; and in that case, we know that the polar glow is the brightest and far surpasses that of the curve. All this, therefore, agrees well with theory.

356. We have already seen how powerful an influence the position of the magnets regarding north and south exerts on the *colors of the glow*. The *intensity of the glow* is also affected by this circumstance. All the sensitives *saw in every bar magnet* placed conformably that both poles glowed beyond comparison brighter than in one placed inconformably, in which the glow was dull and turbid. The magnetism and the odyle of the terrestrial poles, in the former case, act along with and reinforce the odylic emanations of the bar; in the others, they act contrary to and thus enfeeble these emanations, with the force of both terrestrial poles disturbing the phenomena. This simple experiment has been repeated so many hundred times and is so often necessarily cited in describing others that I shall not waste any space here enumerating the names of observers. There is sometimes more complication in the case of *horseshoe magnets*; we have already considered them with reference to this point when open (§ 338); I shall here state the observations made on closed horseshoes.

A. When a closed horseshoe lay in the meridian with the poles turned northward, the northward or negative pole was brighter and the opposite pole was duller. With the poles turned southward, the intensities were reversed: the northward pole was duller and the southward was brighter.

B. When the magnet stood vertically, closed, and the limbs were conformably placed with *the poles being upwards*, Mlle. Zinkel saw the poles become brighter and the curve become duller.

# EFFECTS OF POSITION ON THE ODYLIC GLOW.

Taken together, therefore, the *curves* and poles of a closed horseshoe glowed brighter when turned upwards or towards the west, and less brightly when turned downwards or towards the east (see § 536).

357. These experiments were repeated many different times with simple and compound horseshoes, and Mlle. Zinkel always gave the same consistent account of the phenomena. These differences in the phenomena of odylic light are uniformly delicate and require a very sensitive, calm, and exact observer for their observation and testing; but even more, they require a truth-loving, unprejudiced, cautious, and patient investigator. 361. They may be attributed to two causes. First, to the shorter path which the imponderables <note>In 19th-century science, "imponderables" referred to hypothetical fluids or substances that were believed to lack weight, such as heat, light, and electricity.</note> must travel when the circuit is completed by the curve alone, instead of the entire horseshoe. Second, to the stronger mutual action and the larger amount of magnetism and of odyle set in motion by the polar contact of two magnets; in this case, the magnetism is accumulated or concentrated at the poles and is less quickly carried off because of its greater quantity, which ultimately results in diminished conduction. And as odyle moves rather sluggishly through matter, this adds to the theoretical probability. However, it is currently premature to engage in such speculation; we must first collect and arrange the facts.

->AFFECTED BY THE ELECTRIC ATMOSPHERE.<-

the full <term>odylic glow</term>. We shall hereafter meet with a similar action of magnets on other <term>odylo-luminous</term> <note>Bodies that emit "odylic" light, a core concept in Reichenbach's theory of a universal life force.</note> bodies.

369. Heat was found not to increase the odylo-luminous phenomena. I placed some small bars and horseshoes on the hot stove in the dark chamber before Mlle. PAUER and Mlle. GLASER; when cold, these showed them a beautiful glow and distinct flames. When they had reached nearly blood-heat, both girls found the glow much duller and more cloudy. Mlle. ZINKEL saw a large horseshoe become gradually duller as it grew warmer, and at a temperature of 167° F., the glow was strikingly reduced; however, it returned to its previous state upon cooling. 370. When I brought a magnet into the electric atmosphere of a machine's conductor at a distance of forty inches, while the sparks were two inches long, the glow increased considerably in intensity. This happened even when the magnet was not isolated but held in the hand or lying on the table, and the effect increased as it was brought closer to the conductor. The light did not change perceptibly regardless of whether the magnet itself was electrified. These facts were established through a series of experiments with Mlle. ZINKEL using short bars, larger ones (including one five feet long), smaller horseshoes, and a large nine-bar horseshoe.

371. The effect produced by the electric atmosphere on the <term>odylic polarity</term> seems even more noteworthy to me, as it affects the colors of the glow. For example, if I turned the negative, northward, and blue-glowing side of a bar or horseshoe magnet toward the positively charged conductor, the intensity of light increased, and the blue became brighter. But if I turned the magnet around and placed the positive, southward, and red-glowing side toward the conductor, not only did the red color of the glow fade, but it soon turned blue. *The odylic polarity was reversed.* The + O, turned toward + E, was changed into — O; the blue — O of the opposite

# ODYLIC GLOW IN THE ELECTRIC ATMOSPHERE.

**372.** I reversed the experiment, giving positive electricity to the conductor. It now produced reversed effects on the <term>odylic glow</term> of the magnet; when turned towards it, the negative blue-glowing pole of the magnet changed into a positive red-glowing pole, and the opposite positive red pole changed to a negative blue one, all at a distance of forty inches. But when I stopped electrifying the conductor, the light at both poles faded within a few seconds and returned to its original colors, corresponding to the magnetic polarities. I could repeat and vary this reversal of the colors back and forth every minute. The power of electricity—merely through its <term>electric atmosphere</term>—to intensify the <term>odylic polarities</term> even of magnets that are not isolated when in a aligned position, and to reverse them temporarily when placed in an opposing position, was thus demonstrated.

**373.** Since everyone familiar with this department of physics knows that, under these circumstances, the magnetic poles of a magnet are not reversed, it is almost unnecessary to describe in detail the experiments I made to confirm that fact. Because the approach of another needle could not settle the question here—as it might possibly be affected by <term>induction</term>—I adopted another method. I hung a small needle at the far end of a bar magnet twenty inches long, so that its point was merely attached to the extreme tip of the bar; it was therefore so easily detached that a slight shaking of the floor caused it to fall. If the attracting power were diminished in the slightest degree, it would have to fall instantly, long before the power was reduced to zero. However, such a diminution—and final passage into a state of neutrality—must necessarily occur if the magnetic polarities underwent reversal. I now charged the conductor and then discharged it; the glow of the bar changed its colors due to the effect of the electric atmosphere and then returned to its original state, with all of this being repeated several times. But the needle never stirred nor fell off. The magnetic polarity of the bar, therefore, suffered no appreciable change, while the <term>odylic polarities</term>, as was shown by the colors of the glow, were repeatedly reversed.

These facts provide one of the most striking proofs of the distinction that exists between magnetism and odyle, since they prove that cases occur in which these forces are in direct opposition within one and the same bar at the same time. We shall return to this point when considering the odylic flame.

**374.** Just as the armature becomes glowing through induction, so also does an *electro-magnet*. A soft iron horseshoe magnet, the limbs of which were thirteen and a half inches long and 1.6 inches in diameter, and around which was coiled a copper wire 0.032 (about one-thirtieth) of an inch thick, was connected to a battery of six pairs of zinc and silver, based on **SMEE'S** design, with each pair having a surface of sixty square inches. All the sensitives to whom I showed this in the dark—namely, **MME. KIENESBERGER**, **ANKA HETMANEK**, **MLLE. ZINKEL**, **STEPHAN KOLLAR**, **MME. VON TESSEDIK**, **PROF. ENDLICHER**, **MME. FENZL**, **M. DELHEZ**, and others—saw the iron, as well as the armature when attached, very soon become more or less glowing. The open poles were brightest, and the light diminished toward the curve. The color of the glow was bluish at the northward pole and reddish-yellow at the southward pole, exactly as in a steel magnet magnetized by stroking. When the armature was attached, it exhibited the colors reversed: red at the northward pole of the magnet and blue at the southward pole. It had therefore been converted into an induced magnet by the induced magnet which it closed.

**375.** Not only did the soft iron, thus converted into an induced magnet, exhibit the odylic glow, but this was also the case with all those parts of the apparatus which temporarily acquired magnetism, such as the coil, the connecting wires, and even the battery itself. I only mention this here to make the section on the odylic glow complete; but I must reserve the details for a subsequent occasion.

377. We already know, from my previous treatises, that the magnet possesses the power of communicating its own inherent odylic force to other bodies. But later research first taught me *that its power of exciting the odylic glow could also be transferred to other bodies.* Mme. Kienesberger, Mlles. Even glass, such as large lenses, bell jars, etc., acquired the glow when brought near the poles of strong magnets. See § 481.

378. If we now collect, in a brief form, what has been said above concerning the odylic glow, we obtain the following condensed summary:
	a. The proper light, or glow, of all magnets—of whatever form—appears in the dark as dark grey when at the lowest degree of luminosity; it gradually rises to whitish and yellowish and generally assumes a bluish tint at the northward pole and a reddish tint at the southward pole.
	b. These colors exhibit many varieties of shade, depending on whether the poles of the magnets are open or closed, placed conformably or unconformably, or turned eastward or westward, upward or downward; that is to say, depending on how their struggle with the magnetism of the earth was carried out under different conditions. But the phenomena uniformly follow a law which decides their nature in each position, and the effects of which never fail to appear.

*c.* An electromagnet obeys essentially the same laws.

*d.* A bundle of bars or of horseshoe magnets, placed with like magnetic poles in contact, has its odylic poles reversed so as to alternate with each other.

*e.* The armature shares in these effects. As an induced magnet, it interferes both actively and passively, altering the intensity and color of the light.

*f.* A non-magnetic iron bar plays, to some extent, the part of an induced magnet formed by the influence of the Earth's magnetism, and exhibits the phenomena of odylic glow corresponding to that state.

*g.* The intensities of the odylic glow in the same magnet keep pace with the magnetic intensities. They appear in different degrees in different magnets and in different parts of the same magnet; this varies according to whether the magnets are open or closed, whether the poles are conformable or unconformable, and whether they are turned toward the east or west, or pointed upward or downward. In these different circumstances, the points of greatest intensity change their places at the magnetic poles or axes. The light is strong enough for sensitive individuals to see it reflected in ordinary mirrors.

*h.* When magnets are closed by other magnets instead of their armatures, they exhibit a shifting of the points of greatest intensity according to the same laws, but in a different manner.

*i.* The poles of magnets, when laid on any part of other magnets, produce a partial increase of intensity in the glow or brighter spots at 그곳. Crystals and hands produce the same effect.

*k.* The electric atmosphere intensifies the odylic glow.

*l.* It has such a powerful action on the odylic light that it can produce a reversal of the odylic poles even where no change in magnetic polarity occurs.

*m.* Heat diminishes the odylic glow in steel magnets.

*n.* The odylic glow is transferable from the magnet to other non-magnetic bodies, such as copper wire, etc.

*o.* Although odylic intensities run parallel with magnetic intensities, their polar values do not always do so. There are frequent cases in which positive magnetism (+M) appears associated with negative odyle (—O), and vice versa. These contrasts afford strong proof that magnetism and odyle are not identical.

<header>THE ODYLIC FLAMES</header>

## II. THE ODYLIC FLAMES OVER STEEL MAGNETS.

379. In the preceding experiments on the glow, the flames flowing from the magnetic poles followed the same course everywhere. This phenomenon represents the second degree in the scale of <term>odylo-luminous</term> appearances, and consists of a light which, to those who are less sensitive, appears as a vague gleam over the poles, but which the more highly sensitive—according to the degree of their perceptive power—saw gradually transitioning into the appearance of a real flame, which is the name they used to describe it. There are magnets that exhibit the glow without the flame, but none that possess the flame yet fail to exhibit the glow. The glow is always the first luminous appearance. I once had a horseshoe magnet which had become so weak that it could no longer support its armature, but it still retained perceptible traces of magnetism. I showed it to Mlle. ZINKEL in the dark chamber at a time when she was very highly sensitive to <term>odylic</term> light. She saw the entire magnet glowing, but could perceive no flame over its poles, only a faintly luminous smoke. When the <term>odylic</term> intensity is increased, the flame is added. We are entitled to assume that the flame exists everywhere, but we can only speak of it where it becomes visible. We shall study its characteristics, as far as I have been able to extend the investigation into these beyond what has been previously described. Let us go through the experiments which I have conducted with magnets on this branch of the subject.

380. For the sake of continuity, I must refer to the details given in the first treatise, § 3 to 20. A year later, in 1845, I conducted a series of studies with Mlle. ATZMANNSDORFER, who was then living in my house. These studies partly confirmed and partly expanded upon those previously described and must be added to them. She saw flames on all magnets without exception, varying in size or in intensity; the size according to the physical size of the magnet, and the intensity according to the amount of magnetic or <term>odylic</term> charge of the magnets, also varying according to how the fluctuations in her state of health heightened or depressed her sensitive abilities. 382. Let us now consider some of the properties of these flames; and first, *their extent*.

We have seen that the size of the flames depends, objectively, in part on the size of the magnets and in part on their intensity or amount of charge; but that, subjectively, the perception and recognition of them is determined by the state of sensitivity of the observer. Just as among people, in reference to ordinary vision, there exist such differences that while one man does not recognize his brother as he passes, another, with a falcon-like gaze, counts the larks in the sky; as, further, there are persons who can see nothing even in a moderate degree of darkness or obscurity, while others find their way in the darkest night; as there are patients, suffering from intense <term>hemeralgia</term> <note>night blindness</note>, who only see in the brightest light and become quite blind in a feeble light, and are thus directly opposed to sensitives; as there are Albinos and persons affected with what is called <term>Daltonism</term> <note>color blindness</note>, who are insensitive to certain colors—indeed, some persons who are insensitive to all colors, and

This is the case not only with different people, but with the same person on different days and at different hours; indeed, the variation often occurs in a surprising manner from one minute to another, so that, for example, in three successive moments, the same odylic flame may be at first imperceptible, then visible but small, and immediately afterward large and strong, without any change in the object itself, resulting from variations in the observer's sensitivity to the light. But at that moment, the flame over the poles was not at its largest; on the contrary, it was at its smallest and at first hardly perceptible. However, it immediately began to appear—small at first, then growing, and soon reaching its stationary maximum. This required about a minute in total. Some months afterward, **Miss ZINKEL** gave me exactly the same account of the phenomenon.

### ODYLIC FLAMES OF MAGNETS.

*East, in its relations to odyle, stands to some extent on the side of north; and west, in the same way, on that of south.* See § 536.

392. In a similar way, I tested, in numerous experiments with the most sensitive subjects, the effect produced by the magnetic inclination on the character and size of the odylic flames on steel magnets. Most of these experiments were conducted with Mlle. **ATZMANNSDORFER**, Mlle. **REICHEL**, Mme. **KIENESBERGER**, and the healthy sensitive Mlle. **ZINKEL**. It first appeared that the results reached in § 11 are not unconditionally, but only conditionally, accurate. I stated there, on the authority of Mlle. **REICHEL**, that the magnetism of the Earth appears to have no noticeable influence on the size of the flames. This is correct when, as was the case in these first trials, *the changes of the poles and of inclination are made rapidly, and when time is not allowed for the development of the flame.* At that time, I was not yet aware of a certain slowness with which nature produces odylic changes; these require a short interval for completion in all cases—half a minute, a full minute, and sometimes several minutes, as I shall frequently have opportunities to point out. When the experiments in § 11 were conducted more slowly and observed carefully, it certainly appeared that the flames changed gradually, not only in their size but also in their form, becoming smaller or larger according to the position; and that the magnetism of the Earth undoubtedly exercised a slow but very definite and significant influence on them. The suspended needle, as is well known, instantly changes its position when the Earth’s magnetism acts on it, and this action immediately produces its full effect. I at first assumed that this applied equally to odyle, and my first experiments were conducted under this impression; however, longer experience has taught me that it is not so, and that the effects of odyle only slowly reach their maximum. When I later varied the experiments with Mlle. **REICHEL**, so that the bar magnet was not held in my hand as before—which complicates and distorts the polar flames—but was supported by a wooden stand, which allowed

*Other properties or influences, besides those of magnetism, which affect odyle and its characteristics.* I shall describe what I have succeeded in ascertaining up to this time when discussing the odylic colors (§ 489, et seq.); but here, where I only treat the effect of the Earth’s magnetism on the flame of the needle when placed in the inclination, I shall content myself with stating the results mentioned above.

393. When I used *horse-shoe magnets* in these experiments, the result was altered. When both poles pointed to the north in the inclination, the blue flame of the northward pole was at its full length, but the opposite southward flame appeared suppressed, cloudy, bluish-red, and smaller. When the poles pointed to the south, the red flame of the southward pole was now the larger, while that of the northward pole was now smaller, duller, and reddish-blue. When both poles were pointed upwards, the northward flame increased and the southward diminished. (This confirms the results in the preceding paragraphs.) This went so far as to yield a fact of importance for the practical observation of the phenomena; namely this: that frequently the odylic flame of the unconformably placed pole was entirely suppressed; that is, it became invisible to the observer, as if only one pole possessed a flame. My journals are full of such instances; and there is hardly one among my numerous sensitives with whom it has not frequently happened, under the proper circumstances—especially in those less sensitive to the luminous impressions, or in imperfect darkness, or when the observer had not remained long enough in complete darkness. # MOTION AND DIRECTION OF ODYLIC FLAMES.
<page-num>316</page-num>

399. *The restlessness and continual motion that prevail in the odylic flame were confirmed in many new experiments* by Miss ATZMANNSDORFER, Miss ZINKEL, Mrs. KIENESBERGER, Miss WEIGAND, Miss DORFER, FRIEDRICH WEIDLICH, Mr. RABE, Baron VON OBERLAENDER, Miss SOPHIE PAUER, Mrs. VON PEICHICH, Baroness VON NATORP, Baroness VON VARADY, Mrs. VON TESSEDIK, Prof. ENDLICHER, Mr. DELHEZ, Baroness VON AUGUSTIN, Dr. NIED, JOHANNA KYNAST, JOHANN KLAIBER, and others. The first and last mentioned individuals compared it to some degree to the positive luminous bundle of an electric machine, but said it was more delicate and fuller; the northward flame was bluer, but equally moving and flickering. They found it cool and of feeble light, sometimes almost <term>moniliform</term> <note>shaped like a string of beads</note>. It was affected by the slightest motion of the air in which it appeared.

400. *The direction taken by the flame was frequently studied.* Instead of providing many statements, I shall limit myself to two that encompass all the rest. I placed the nine-bar horseshoe on a chair in front of Miss ATZMANNSDORFER, with the poles facing south. She saw the flames flowing out to the length of an arm—first horizontally, extending the line of the limbs for a distance, then curving upward until they formed a <term>quadrant</term> with their points directed upward. Miss ZINKEL observed the same with horseshoes and bars. The flame, therefore, leaves the poles with a certain force of a projectile nature, which carries it away from the poles; but it has, on the other hand, an innate tendency to rise in the air, and its material substance must therefore be lighter than air at the earth's surface. From the combination of these forces results the rising quadrant of the flame. However, this experiment only succeeds with very powerful magnets, the flames of which are long. When the flames are short, they are always seen to proceed in the line of the magnet's limb. From the various directions we can give to magnets—toward different points of the compass or at various degrees of inclination to the horizon—combined increases and decreases of the flame arise, depending on whether these positions are more or less consistent with the normal one.

401. I must mention here a series of experiments with several sensitives, the object of which was to determine the effect that different odylic flames might have on one another when brought into contact. This might provide further information regarding the relationship of the magnet to the odylic flame. We consider positive and negative magnetism to have a strong tendency to attract each other and, through mutual interpenetration, to neutralize each other or produce an equilibrium. However, it would appear that the odylic flame—considering the rising quadrant mentioned in the previous paragraph and the phenomena described in § 392, where it appears to oppose the magnetic inclination—has no such inherent attraction. Here we find distinctions between the two forces in their specific manifestations. To Miss von Weigelsberg, Miss Winter, and Mrs. Anschuetz, all in delicate health, and to the healthy sensitives, Miss Ernestine Anschuetz, Mr. Anschuetz, Mr. Delhez, Mrs. Fenzl, Mrs. von Peichich, Mr. Hochstetter, Dr. Nied, and Baroness von Augustin, I showed two bar magnets in the dark chamber. Both were four inches long, and I held them horizontally in the magnetic parallel with their opposite poles turned toward each other at a distance equal to twice the length of the bars. I took the essential precaution of holding the southward pole of one in my right hand while I held the northward pole of the other in my left, with the opposite poles projecting from my hands; the reasons for this will soon become clear. All the observers saw that upon placing the bars opposite each other in this way, the flames of both became narrower and longer, as if striving to meet. When I moved them closer, the flames returned to their former shorter but thicker shape, which intensified as they were brought nearer. At the same time, the intensity of the light increased. When I finally joined the poles, both flames nearly disappeared, but at the far ends, they immediately became stronger and nearly twice as long as before. Mr. Hochstetter and Dr. Nied also stated that the thickness or width of the flames far exceeded that of the bars when the poles were near, and that they were brightest when the poles were at their closest. 407. All of this makes it highly probable that the <term>odylic</term> flame is a real projection of something that, near the outer surface of the magnet, is charged with <term>odyle</term>, becomes luminous because of it, and is then projected. If it meets obstacles, it is turned aside or forced back. An opposing current of flame can act as such an obstacle. But upon contact of the poles, this obstacle is removed and the enveloping flames appear. They are the result of the residue of <term>magnetism</term> and <term>odyle</term> gathered at the poles which, due to imperfect contact, cannot be conducted away quickly or completely enough. Now, the closer the opposite poles remain to each other, the more easily the currents will pass through them and be maintained; we have already frequently seen that they do not have perfect continuity. And the better the polar ends fit one another—with more numerous and close points of contact—the more perfectly the <term>magnetism</term> appears to be conducted away and confined to its own internal circulation, and the feebler the intensity of the luminous phenomenon becomes, both inverted and

408. When the flames of bar magnets, whether positive or negative, pass close to each other crosswise, or even touch each other without coming into full contact, there appeared neither attraction nor repulsion. We previously saw something similar with the flames of horseshoe magnets, which flowed from the two poles and remained parallel, neither attracting nor destroying each other. But when two unequal flames actually met, Mlles. Reichel and Atzmannsdorfer both observed that the stronger *carried the weaker with it*, but only when its projectile force or current was stronger. However, according to numerous observations by both of these sensitives, the stronger propulsion is always found in the flame which is nearest to its source; and that flame, which at the point where they cross happens to be most distant from its pole, is carried along by the other. It does not matter which is larger; a small flame, if crossed near its pole by that part of a larger flame which is more remote from its own pole, will carry the latter with it and determine the direction of their united course.

**411.** If we now view, collectively, the observations from § 399 to the present point, we have many and various proofs that the odylic flame is not itself magnetism, as has been repeatedly stated. It does not obey the laws of magnetic attraction and repulsion and is material enough that it can be moved about, like an ordinary flame, by currents of air. It appears instead as a *phenomenon that accompanies magnetism*, but follows the magnetic current only in part. It resembles a projectile which, once thrown out, pursues its own course in the direction of the impulse originally given to it and is affected by the obstacles and new impulses it encounters.

**412.** It seemed interesting to me to make *observations on the effects produced by stroking steel bars with magnets* and to apply to them the collected results obtained regarding the odylic glow and the odylic flames. These lights must necessarily appear in many forms and degrees and should provide many confirmations of what has been described. It was also hoped that we might obtain new information about what occurs during the process of making steel magnets, and in general, regarding the transfer of magnetism and of <term>odyle</term> from one body to another. With this view, I conducted the following research with Mlle. ZINKEL.

The first result was that the magnet used for stroking, whenever it was held perpendicularly to the bar, caused the latter to exhibit a much brighter odylic glow around the point of contact.

->Fig. 6.<-

<image-desc>A diagram illustrating a magnetic experiment. A horizontal grey rectangle represents a steel bar. A vertical grey rectangle, representing a magnet, is placed perpendicular to the horizontal bar, touching its top edge at the center. Therefore, the pole of the magnet acted with its full magnetic and odylic force so strongly on the steel bar that it caused the bar to shine more brightly wherever it touched it. Figure 6 shows this more clearly. 

This luminous spot appeared at any and every part of the bar. Because it immediately disappeared when the magnetic pole was moved from the spot, it follows that in stroking the bar from one end (or pole) to the other, the bright spot also traversed the bar from one end to the other, constantly accompanying the pole of the magnet. Now, since the bar—as we have seen—exhibits a bluish glow on its northern half and a reddish glow on its southern half when placed in the <term>meridian</term>, the moving spot also appears bluish on the northern half and reddish on the southern half. Therefore, the effect of drawing a magnetic pole along a steel bar appears obviously to be a local one, attached to the immediate presence of the magnet's pole as far as the odylic glow is concerned. It does not, at least not visibly, spread over the entire extent of the bar. In this, it apparently differs from the actual magnetic effect, which with every stroke is spread over all parts of the bar, and not only appears in all parts but adheres to them.

In these experiments, I used two bars: the magnetic bar, or "stroker," was twenty-four inches long, and the steel bar to be stroked was eighteen inches long. Let us now follow the results—first in the steel bar, then in the magnetic bar—initially with reference to the glow, and then with reference to the flame.

In the meridian was a steel bar that was hardly magnetic at all. It had a faint glow in the dark; its northern half appeared gray instead of blue, and its southern half appeared whitish-yellow instead of yellowish-red. The light of both was cloudy and dull.

e. When the northward pole of the magnet touched the south end of the bar, the blue glow extended to the middle. The red glow was now much brighter and more intense.

### **417. D.** *Odylic flame of the magnetic bar* :—

Its blue northward flame, originally four inches long, was extinguished upon contact with the bar. We only have to consider the red southward flame, therefore. In all these experiments, the magnet lay in the magnetic parallels, with its southward pole toward the west.

*a.* When the two northward poles were in contact, the red flame of the magnet was 2.8 inches long.

*b.* At one-fourth of the length of the steel bar, the red flame of the magnet had fallen to two inches.

418. We now come to the application of these laws to the case of the *conversion of a horseshoe bar into a magnet* by stroking it with a magnet.

I used as the magnet in these experiments a powerful five-bar horseshoe magnet, along which I drew a simple horseshoe bar that had lost almost all the magnetism it once possessed. I laid the five-bar magnet on the table so that its poles projected over the edge, with the curve toward the middle of the table. It was heavy enough to remain firmly in this position while the stroking was performed, and so powerful that it held the single bar fast in every position in which the latter was placed in contact with its poles. I held the single bar vertically, with the poles pointing upwards.

Originally, the single bar—in the dark, and of course this applies only to the visual perception of Mlle. ZINKEL at that time—had a small blue flame of about 0.4 inches on its northern pole, and only a reddish smoke on its southern pole. The five-bar magnet had a blue northern flame as long as a hand, and a red southern flame the length of a finger. Both horseshoes had a bluish <term>odylic glow</term> on one side and a reddish one on the other; it was duller on the single bar and very much brighter on the five-bar magnet. This glow was hardly

The single bar adhered firmly in a vertical position, with its limbs and poles projecting above the poles of the five-bar magnet. The result was that:

419. A. *The odylic glow of the single bar* became brighter at the curve, dividing into two halves, red and blue—the former on the part attached to the northward pole, and the latter on the part attached to the southward pole of the five-bar magnet. At the same time, both limbs of the single bar acquired a brighter glow, with the colors being on the same sides as before, but more intense. When I now slowly drew the single bar downwards until the poles of the two magnets came in contact, the glow of the curve in the single bar increased, and the two colors met and mingled in the middle; meanwhile, in both limbs, the glow diminished, becoming duller and more gray, though the colors still remained in their places. The northward limb of the single bar always had a blue glow, and the opposite limb a red glow, and the *quality* of the glow remained unchanged; that is, blue on the northward side and red on the southward side, whether the single bar was free, or in contact at its curve with the poles of the five-bar magnet, or finally, when the poles of both were in contact. However, the distribution of magnetic and odylic force, regarding amount and intensity, was not the same in these three positions.

420. B. *The odylic flames of the single bar*, when its curve closed the five-bar magnet like an armature, rose rapidly from its original size of 0.4 inches on the northward pole to 4.8 inches. Meanwhile, the reddish smoke of the southward pole changed into a red flame 1.2 to 1.6 inches long, with a thick yellowish-grey smoke above it. In later experiments, when the single bar had become quite strongly magnetized by the earlier ones and had, in its free state, a blue flame 2.4 inches long, it rose in this position to 4.8 inches on the blue side and to 2.4 inches on the red side.

On drawing the single bar slowly downwards, its polar flames gradually diminished; the southward flame soon vanished, the northward flame became shorter and duller, while the glow at the curve became brighter. When the poles of both magnets were brought into contact, all flames disappeared.

In this experiment, and in every phase of it, the colors of each limb remained constantly the same in every position. The two lateral portions of the curve, the limbs, above or below the points of contact, the flames over the poles, the sparks, the fiery threads, and the luminous downy flames around the limbs, continued throughout blue on the northward and red on the southward half of the single-bar horseshoe. At no point did the quality of the odylic light vary, but only its intensity, corresponding to the amount of odylic charge.

421. C. *Odylic glow of the five-bar horse-shoe.* As soon as the poles were joined by the curve of the single bar, the glow at its own curve became brighter, while that of the limbs, and still more of the poles, became duller, the northward limb acquiring a grayish blue, the southward a yellowish red color. Here also, both colors met and passed into each other on the curve. On drawing the single bar slowly downwards, the poles of the other became gradually brighter in their glow. They were brightest when the poles came into contact, but still inferior in brightness to the curve. The glow, therefore, in the five-bar magnet, pursued a course nearly the reverse of that observed in the single bar; which is in accordance with the general laws already ascertained.

When I removed the single bar, the curve and limbs of the other horseshoe became less bright, but its poles again became brighter. We cannot here consider the odylic flames of the five-bar magnet, because, as the poles were never free, no such flames could appear.

Here then, as in the case of the glow (§ 371), *a reversal of the odylic polarity had taken place*, without any such reversal of the actual magnetic polarity. When I now reversed the electric polarity by charging the conductor negatively, I obtained the same <term>odylo-luminous</term> phenomena, but of course reversed. The <term>odyle</term> passed into + O, and that at the negative magnetic pole.

437. To bring out these facts still more distinctly, I repeated them using bar magnets instead of horseshoe magnets. Two bars—one twenty-six inches long and the other five feet long—were placed on a table, uninsulated, in the magnetic parallels, and at forty inches from the conductor. When their blue negative flames were turned toward it, they lengthened out toward the conductor to three and four times their former length. But when their red positive flames were placed nearest the conductor, the flames were at first rendered turbid and less luminous, and then, after a struggle between the forces acting here—shown by the playing of small flames back and forth on the bars—they were changed into blue and increased within one or two minutes to a considerable length and breadth. As often as I stopped the rotation of the machine or discharged the conductor, the flames were again reversed and returned, in all respects, to their former state. The small struggling flames played over the surface as before, until all was again brought under the dominion of the magnetism of the bars.

438. b. 443. If this view were correct, then we should obtain confirmation of it from a control experiment. The effect of the flames of magnets and crystals when opposed to each other ought to coincide with what we have seen of the flames of two magnets when made to approach each other in § 401. To test this, I placed a six-inch bar magnet before Mlle. ZINKEL, aligned with the magnetic <term>meridian</term>, and brought the negative pole of a gypsum crystal (which had a blue flame about two inches long) toward its south pole. As soon as the poles were about one foot apart, with the magnet and the crystal in a straight line, both flames became narrower and longer and seemed to struggle to meet each other. But when they were close enough for this meeting to have occurred, it did not take place; instead, they became broader and shorter, contracted around their own poles, and finally disappeared upon contact. However, when hostile—that is, similar—poles were brought near each other, no lengthening of the flames toward each other was observed. They became compressed and, upon contact, were turned back over their own poles; all of this is in perfect agreement with the phenomena exhibited when two magnets are brought toward each other.

These have, until now, weighed like a nightmare on what is called <term>animal and mineral magnetism</term>; and, without clearing these away, it was absolutely impossible to obtain consistent or trustworthy results. Every observer of <term>animal magnetism</term>, or the effects of magnets on the human system, saw a different phenomenon, and every day brought a new one that differed from the day before. ## The odylic flame, as we see, gives us no information as to the direction of the magnetic force; no lines of magnetic force,

<note>protocol, she often declared that she spoke the truth, for she *could* see nothing under such perverted arrangements—not because she lacked the power to do so, but because experiments conducted blunderingly and without knowledge of the subject made it impossible for her to exercise that power. But, at last, she occasionally saw something, gave confused statements, and was therefore called a liar and an impostor. Let us examine the statements of these gentlemen and see where the lies and imposture actually lie. Mlle. REICHEL was three to six paces from the magnet and generally had a doctor on each side to watch her; these guards often held both her hands. Opposite them sat another doctor, holding the heavy horseshoe magnet in his lap and moving it back and forth. Close to him, on each side, stood a fourth and fifth doctor who were to control the movements of the magnet. The sensitive girl was then required to tell how and where the magnet emitted light when it was shifted here or there. She was urged to show her skill; she was laughed at and treated with scorn when she failed. In this way, she was irritated and exasperated, so much so that she struck out at the doctors and was on the verge of boxing one of them on the ear, etc.

Now, in the first place, it is quite impossible that a sensitive person of moderate power, as Mlle. REICHEL was at that time, could see any magnetic light in a darkness frequently interrupted by spectators coming and going. In the second place, three to six paces is far too great a distance from the magnet. Such a sensitive person cannot perceive magnetic light with any certainty at a distance greater than forty inches. In the third place, the magnet—a heavy nine-bar horseshoe—was between the doctor's hands and held close to his body. The light was, therefore, completely obscured from the observer's view. *All this made it a threefold impossibility for her to see any luminous emanations from the magnet.* Three enormous blunders were therefore made, each of which alone was enough to make the sensitive perception of light impossible.

In fact, the girl saw nothing but scattered and uncertain gleams of light here and there—no doubt from a hand, a head, or two heads held together, or hands and heads in contact, or hands touching the magnet and strengthened by it, or eyes, or breath, or the pits of the stomach, or the knees of the doctors sitting close together, etc., etc., where these things accidentally met and mutually strengthened each other's odylic power. Although I had fully and minutely detailed in my work how much light was emitted by all these living organs, the experimenters mostly paid no attention to it. They shifted and hid the magnet in all directions, and when she saw a light, it occurred to none of them that they had faces, eyes, hands, hypochondria, etc., etc., all of which emit light—and, generally, more strongly than the magnet. In this utter confusion of all the conditions of scientific research, the poor tormented girl, as can be easily understood, knew not what to do or how to satisfy the demands with which she was overwhelmed; and when the result of such poorly designed experiments was inconsistent answers, the gentlemen, instead of confessing their own ignorance, did not hesitate to protect themselves with the unconscionable and slanderous assertion that the sensitive patient was an impostor. Mlle. **Reichel**, for example, is said to have secretly crept toward the magnet held by one of the doctors and felt for it with her hands to discover its position. This story contradicts itself. For if she saw *no light*, she could not find the magnet, because it might be held above the head, under the feet, to the side of, or behind the person who had it. She could not, therefore, even know where to feel for it, but would certainly have grabbed the experimenter’s body, head, or feet, or thrust her hand into his eyes. It is painful to think that similar cases have also occurred in England. The spontaneous somnambulism and apparent shifting of the senses in Miss **M'Avoy** received exactly the same treatment; as did the very interesting facts that occurred in the case of **Dr. Elliotson's** patients, the **Okeys**. There was the same predisposition to find the patient an impostor, the same total lack of any convincing evidence, and the same reckless, unjustifiable, and unmanly accusation of fraud brought against people of good character—apparently because the authorities chose to assume the facts were impossible. It is the duty of every lover of truth and science to protest strongly against the system of reckless accusations of fraud made against people of blameless character just because their statements seem incredible to us, or—as has often happened—because we lack the scientific knowledge to distinguish between what is real and what might be imaginary or deceptive in the results.—W. **453.** *b.* A condensed retrospect of the observations in the flame teaches us:

*a.* Weakly magnetic steel exhibits a glow without a flame. When the intensity of the magnetism rises beyond a certain point, luminous emanations are added, which appear first nebulous, then vaporous, and then as flames—more especially at the poles of magnets—and frequently appear to the eyes of even healthy persons to be five or six feet high.

*b.* The magnetism of the Earth has a great influence on the size and color of the odylic flames. According to how magnets are placed with one or the other pole toward the north, west, south, or east, upwards or downwards, in the magnetic inclination, or in any other position, the flames in each case have a more or less different aspect.

*c.* Bars of soft iron, under the influence of the Earth’s magnetism, behave like weak magnets.

*d.* In compound magnets, the odylic flames are found in colors that are alternately stratified, just as the glow is.

*e.* The odylic flame has a tendency to rise in the air.

*f.* Magnetic flames from opposite poles, when placed opposite

*o.* Heat weakens the odylic flame.

*p.* Crystals and animals (such as the human hand) act on the odylic flame as magnets do; they strengthen or weaken it, reverse its colors, or extinguish it, both through contact and merely by being nearby.

*q.* The magnetic curves produced in iron filings when placed over a bar magnet exhibit to the sensitive eye a starry host of miniature magnets, emitting odylic flames and glittering in rainbow hues.

*r.* The odylic flame is a material substance; most probably a body rendered luminous; but it is not magnetism.

# ODYLIC LIGHT IN THREADS OR FIBERS.

**458.** When I attached the armature to horseshoe magnets, which, when open, were clothed in the downy light, it instantly diminished but did not disappear. According to Mlles. ATZMANNSDORFER and ZINKEL, it became less than half of its former length and size, and grew especially duller and more cloudy. Where it had been yellow or red, it was now grayish yellow or quite colorless and gray. This also happened when I closed a horseshoe magnet, not with its armature, but with another horseshoe magnet. Dr. NIED, who saw a strong downy light on a single-bar horseshoe magnet, lost this and saw only the dull glow of the steel when the armature was attached. His sensitivity is not great. In all cases, therefore, it would appear that the conduction through the armature is imperfect, and consequently a part of the current of <term>imponderables</term> residing in the magnets continually passed off into the air. From all these observations, we may be more than sufficiently satisfied of the accuracy of the original observations of Mlle. REICHEL <note>the impostor of the Vienna Doctors, W. G.</note> on this point, as described in Part I.

**459.** These downy envelopes are very probably constant but weak <term>odylic emanations</term>, extending over the whole magnet, which, due to the low intensity of their light, are generally visible only to the most highly sensitive people, and hardly or not at all visible to those of lower sensitivity.

They are locally concentrated currents of <term>odyle</term> within the general <term>odylic</term> current: blue from the negative pole and red from the positive pole.

### IV. ODYLIC SMOKE.

462. The next phenomenon, after the <term>odylic flame</term>, is a peculiar luminous vapor or smoke which rises from the magnet and is seen in the dark by <term>sensitives</term>. I have said little of it in the earlier part of this work, but as I pursued my research, it was unavoidably forced upon my attention, as it appeared always in the same way and under similar circumstances; therefore, I was compelled to regard it as an essential part of the phenomena and to direct my attention to it.

# LUMINOUS ODYLIC SMOKE

**468.** *How faint the light of the odylic smoke must be* is shown by some experiments I made on the reflection of <term>odylic</term> light by mirrors. Neither Mlle. Atzmannsdorfer nor Mlle. Zinkel could see the image of the smoke. Both were in their ordinary state. Only Mme. Bauer, during pregnancy, was able to perceive it. In the case of the two girls, the loss of light through absorption was enough to make the image invisible to them.

**469.** The <term>odylic</term> smoke appears stronger in a vacuum (an exhausted receiver). This was seen by many sensitives; among others, by Mlle. Pauer, Mlle. Zinkel, M. Hochstetter, Mlle. Glaser, etc. We shall return to this in § 480.

# OVER THE FLAMES OF MAGNETS.

471. That which is testified here by more than thirty witnesses not only agrees essentially with itself in all details, but also harmonizes with what we already know of the <term>odylic</term> flame, with which the <term>odylic</term> smoke is most intimately connected. It therefore bears the obvious mark of truth so certainly that it can only be denied by those who talk recklessly and illogically, as unfortunately many do, who would gladly be [recognized as experts]. 

What I do, before asking a single question, is to remove to a certain distance both from the person and from the object, in order to avoid disturbing the result by the <term>odylic</term> influence of my own person, which would confuse them and render them utterly worthless. Instead of observing similar precautions, these gentlemen actually placed a doctor on each side of **Mlle. REICHEL**, and they generally held her hands—an arrangement, moreover, which no <term>sensitive</term> can endure—and then placed the magnet in the lap of a doctor opposite, and so on. It is impossible to resist smiling when we read of research conducted in such a style. The girl, thus tortured, was expected to justify the reckless statements of the ignorant person who had placed her in such a false position, and whom every negative answer from her exposed to shame. She was also expected to satisfy the excited expectations of those assembled, who incessantly irritated her with expressions of abuse and scorn, and by their contemptuous treatment drove her into outbursts of anger. In this general confusion and restlessness, she was expected to solve with precision the most delicate problems which can be proposed to the senses of touch and sight; and that, under physical and moral conditions which rendered their solution absolutely impossible!... What could possibly be the result of such a mode of investigation but the pitiful hodgepodge presented by the answers of the persecuted girl in the record! In such circumstances, it is not worth while to enter into the individual statements, whether they be truly or falsely recorded, understood or not understood by the investigators. The whole resolves itself into a hopeless mass of confusion and misapprehension.

**Mlle. REICHEL** was, in her time (that is, in her then state of health), an admirable <term>sensitive</term>; the best that could be desired for scientific purposes. The senses of touch and sight were wonderfully acute; she was very obliging, persevering, exact, and truthful in her statements, very modest and humble in her behavior, and intelligent in understanding questions rightly framed. But we must not trample with jackboots on so delicate an instrument for delicate research. Neither did the doctors understand their own object, nor did the girl and her helpless conductor understand what they had to do. Science cannot be promoted this way; but folly may be shown in making such experiments, and then it is cloaked by the contemptuous slander of a defenseless woman.
