# RETROSPECT OF OBSERVATIONS ON

...called natural philosophers, but who often have no trace either of logic or of natural science. If we now compare all the above observations, scattered over a period of more than three years and made by so many different persons, we arrive at the following propositions:

*a.* All magnets—whether permanent magnets of hardened steel, induction magnets of soft steel or iron, magnets produced by the induction of the Earth's magnetism, or electromagnets—give out, in profound darkness, along with the <term>odylic</term> flames at the poles, a luminous, nebulous, or *smoky thin vapor*. This is also emitted by their surface generally, although it is much weaker and often imperceptible there. The strength of this emanation diminishes from the poles toward the axis, where it is relatively small but still detectable.

*b. The size of this smoky light* is directly proportional to the size of the associated flame. When the latter is only an inch or two in height, the length of the smoke does not much exceed this. When the flame rises to three or four feet, the smoke extends to five or six feet or more. Its size is also directly proportional to both the size and the intensity of the magnet from which it flows. Large magnets of low intensity (such as my nine-bar horseshoe magnet was when it was weak) produced relatively long flames with abundant vapor. It should not be expected that I should produce exact measurements at this early stage of such an investigation.

*c.* The <term>odylic</term> smoke is *propelled from the magnet with a certain force* which gives it its initial direction, but after that, it exhibits *a constant tendency to flow upward*. When it reaches the ceiling, it spreads out, flows over it, illuminates the painting on it, and lasts for a short time, not exceeding a few minutes. Whatever material substance may lie at the foundation of this phenomenon, it is either lighter than air or is in some way repelled from the earth so as to be forced to rise.

*d.* The smoke differs according to the pole which yields it. At the positive southward pole, it is reddish-gray or yellowish-reddish-gray and thicker, inclined to form heavy masses of clouds; the negative northward pole yields it as blue-gray and

Finally, the fact that <term>sensitives</term> who have remained with me in total darkness for several hours initially saw only smoke, then flame and smoke after an hour, and after several hours saw large flames and great rolling clouds of smoke on all magnets, makes me suspect that the flame and smoke are perhaps the same phenomenon. They may vary in intensity on one hand and be perceived differently on the other, depending on the sensitivity of the observers or the development of an observer's perceptive power—whether due to variations in their natural state or the effect of long exposure of the eye to perfect darkness. 

The first degree of the phenomenon would then be a dimly luminous nebula; the next a more distinct vapor, either duller or brighter, which appears first grey, then yellowish-reddish grey on the positive side and bluish-grey on the negative side. A third or fourth degree would be the appearance of flame covered with vapor—first the blue flame, then the red flame. Finally, above these, and especially over the red flame, there would be the abundant rolling upward of thick clouds of smoke toward the ceiling of the room. 

I say I feel compelled to maintain this suspicion because I wish to keep all my theoretical views completely distinct from the observed facts. I have recorded these facts from the consistent statements of so many <term>sensitives</term>, and they are, in any case, more certain and safe than any speculation of mine, however simple. So long as we do not know the nature of these <term>odylic</term> phenomena in general—and, as far as I can judge, there is not much prospect of our soon penetrating very deeply into the essential nature of that essence, considering the prejudiced dislike of such inquiries which prevails in the minds of so many natural philosophers—so long as the whole nature of these beautiful phenomena remains mysterious to us, we shall be unable to come to a settled decision regarding the identity or diversity of their many forms. Therefore, for the present, we must stick to the shapes in which they appear to our senses in our descriptions, our understanding, and our naming of them.

### V. ODYLIC SCINTILLATIONS.

473. Besides the four forms of odylic light just discussed—the glow, the flames, the fibrous or downy flames, and the smoke—there is another that is less extensive but very intense. This consists of *scattered sparks or scintillations* which appear in the smoke and move about independently within it. **Mlle. REICHEL** first noticed them and saw them often, not only in the smoke from magnets (which is our only focus at present) but in many other odylic lights from other sources, a subject I will return to later. The first signs of them are very slightly indicated in *Figures 1 and 2 of Plate I*; in the flame illustrated there (quite inadequately), they were most distinct when viewed from the side. In this form, they were very clearly seen by **Baron VON OBERLAENDER**, who compared them to the sparks of burning pine charcoal <note>These sparks are mainly produced by the charcoal of the bark, as is clearly seen when charcoal burns in oxygen gas.—W. GIRTLER** called them little scattered stars. **Mlle. WINTER** saw them flying about in large numbers near the wall, rising up with an angular or zigzag motion. NOWOTNY** saw the largest number of them coming from the magnet, and **Mme. KIENESBERGER** not only saw them rising nearly to the ceiling in the smoke of the nine-bar magnet but also coming from the body of the electromagnet itself. **FRIEDRICH WEIDLICH** and **Mlle. STURMANN** saw them in the smoke of both small and large magnets. **Dr. NIED** and **M. RABE** saw them streaming upward in the vaporous emanations of the nine-bar magnet,

The same thing, reversed of course, occurred at the positive pole. They became abundant in the electric atmosphere, in which all odylo-luminous emanations are increased and intensified. They were more numerous and brighter the nearer the magnet was to the conductor. See § 436.

They were so bright that she could not conceal her astonishment that I was not able to see them as well.

476. Finally, something similar was observed when I suddenly detached the armature of a horseshoe magnet, and this occurred more strongly the greater the intensity of its magnetism. At the moment of separation, Mme. **Bauer**, Mlle. **Zinkel**, Mlle. **Reichel**, Mlle. **Dorfer**, and others, saw numerous sparks flash forth and instantly disappear; after which the flame began to appear and to develop itself.

I do not allow myself for the present to form any conjectures as to its nature, or even the relation which it bears to the other phenomena of magnetism or of odyle with which it is associated. 478. Having now become somewhat acquainted with *the various kinds* of luminous emanations from the magnet, let us turn to *differences in the circumstances* in which the magnet may be placed while emitting them, and strive to investigate the influence which such differences may exert.

---

### LIGHT FROM THE MAGNET IN DIFFERENT EXTERNAL CIRCUMSTANCES.

#### ODYLIC LIGHT IN DIFFERENT MEDIA.

479. We *know* how different the luminous phenomena of electricity are in air, in a vacuum, or even under diminished atmospheric pressure. In order to test the effect of the air on odylic-luminous emanations, I frequently placed magnets *under the exhausted receiver of the air-pump* in the presence of sensitive persons. I used small and large horseshoe magnets, with the poles pointing upwards, standing in large tumblers under the bell-jar, so that every change was easily visible, as well as small bar-magnets that could lie horizontally under the bell-jar.

480. Even the blind man Bollmann solved the question. When all was ready, but before starting the exhaustion, I led him to the air-pump. He saw nothing. To be certain that he was looking in the right direction, I placed his hand on the bell-jar, but he still saw nothing. The magnet sent out too little light to affect his vision through the glass. I then began the exhaustion. Very soon, when it was about half completed, he saw light. And as the rarefaction increased, this light also increased, and reached its maximum size and brightness for his damaged organs of vision when the mercury in the gauge stood at 0.12 to 0.16 of an inch—the highest degree of exhaustion, unfortunately, which could be obtained with my air-pump. 481. These observations, collected and compared, yield the following results: *The <term>odylo-luminous</term> phenomena are affected by changes in atmospheric pressure. Under diminished pressure, they increase considerably in brightness.* Magnets, invisible in the open air or under the full jar, acquired a bright <term>odylic</term> glow and very distinctly visible flames on their poles and between their limbs when the air was half-exhausted. These emanations, bluish and reddish on the opposite poles and mixed with rainbow colors, increased as the exhaustion became more complete. Then the jar became so charged with <term>odyle</term> that it, as well as the external knob, acquired the glow. The flame did not pass through the glass but was deflected by it as an ordinary flame would have been—and as Mlle. Reichel often described the <term>odylic</term> flame to be, as in the glass case of Schweigger’s <term>multiplicator</term> (§ 434) and by the approach to a large lens (§ 20), like fire on the bottom of a pan held over it. The smoke also appears and increases, but only up to a certain point of rarefaction, beyond which it diminishes and probably disappears in a perfect vacuum. The glowing jar produces no smoke externally.

483. As a medium presenting a *greater density than air*, I selected *water*. I showed to the following four sensitives a small and freshly-magnetized horse-shoe, whose flames flowed brightly in the dark, alternately in air and in water at different times. Mme. However, he declared that the flame had not entirely vanished, but that one small point, as if on a corner, was left. Whenever the magnet was taken out of the water, it exhibited the two-inch-long flame, even though it was dripping wet. The same appearances were observed at every repetition. Mlle. ATZMANNSDORFER, in whose presence I made the same experiment, saw the magnet instantly lose its flames, but retain its glow, which was brightest towards the poles. Mlle. This point was on the side next to the opposite pole, and from it proceeded an exceedingly slender thread of light, which was found to be the cross-edge of the pole near the other pole. In the dark, I marked the pole where this spot appeared.

In many repetitions of this experiment, Miss **Zinkel** saw—especially during her menstrual period—traces of similar light at the negative pole, though they were less bright and visible. 484. Therefore, a denser medium such as water destroys the flame and smoke—whether the water absorbs them and thereby becomes magnetized (or rather, <term>odylised water</term>), or whether it prevents their development beyond a bright point and a bright thread on the inner corner and edge of a horseshoe pole. Miss **Nowotny** had already identified such a thread as the lowest degree of <term>odylic flame</term>. § 3.

485. I have not tested solid bodies as another kind of medium. In such a trial, it would be advisable to use an induction magnet hermetically sealed in glass of considerable thickness, or rather placed in close contact by melting the glass around it. If a permanent magnet were used, it would be necessary to restore its magnetism from the outside, as the heat of melting glass would demagnetize it. But there would be no great difficulty in doing this. I have performed some experiments with copper wire that were similar to this, yet essentially different. I wished to test whether the <term>odylic charge</term>—which, as we know from § 45, can be transferred to other bodies by magnets and is recognized by its effect on the nerves of touch—might also be made perceptible through luminous emanations, thus providing further insight into this difficult matter. With this goal in mind, I made an irregular coil of copper wire one-twelfth of an inch thick with ten or fifteen turns, forming a kind of net or basket. I pressed this flat and placed it on the northward pole of a nine-bar magnet standing vertically. It fitted quite closely on the pole, and the end of the wire projected about eight inches sideways toward the east. 486. These experiments—to which, if it were necessary, I could add many similar ones that entirely confirm them—teach us with consistency and gradually increasing clearness *that the conduction of <term>odyle</term> through other bodies*, which we have learned in the seventh treatise to recognize by its effects on the sense of touch in sensitive persons, *is also accompanied by corresponding luminous phenomena*; that just as the force which the magnet emits and uses to saturate all other bodies, the flames proceeding from it may also be absorbed by other substances and released by them again, exactly as they are from the magnet itself. The <term>odyle</term>, or its essence, or its substratum, therefore, when transferred, carries with it not only its power of acting on the <term>animal nerve</term>, *but also its property of emitting light into other solid media; its glow, its flames, its smoke, with their fluidity and mobility, their light and their colors*; and, as we already know, their power of exciting the peculiar sensations of coolness, warmth, oppression, and refreshing lightness.

487. A review of the contents of the present section shows us:

*a.* The luminous emanations from the magnet—the glow and the flame—are strongest, largest, and brightest in highly rarefied air, and would probably, <term>in vacuo</term>, become even a little more intense.

*b.* That the <term>odylic smoke</term>, in its greatest intensity, seems to be connected with a certain definite density of the air, on either side of which it diminishes.

*c.* That ordinary atmospheric pressure considerably lowers the intensity of the <term>odylic</term> luminous phenomena.

*d.* That the density of water so much limits the development of the <term>odylic flame</term> as to almost destroy it entirely, without, however, affecting the <term>odylic glow</term>.

*e.* That the density of solid bodies, such as glass, absorbs and to a certain extent retains and gives out <term>odylic</term> light.

*f. In short, odylic light is affected differently by different media.*

488. From what we have discovered so far, it seems somewhat probable that <term>odylic smoke</term> is *odylized air*, just as what is called magnetized water is *odylized water*—that is, air and water charged with <term>odyle</term>. For water also, when odylized—whether by a magnet, crystals, the hand, or chemical action—acquires an <term>odylic glow</term> and becomes visible in the dark where it was previously invisible, just as odylized metals acquire a glow or show an increase in their naturally weaker glow when odylized in the same manner.

### THE COLORS OF ODYLIC LIGHT.

489. The nature and sequence of the colors shown by the different forms of <term>odylic light</term>, when closely studied, become a highly important branch of the subject. From my further research, it appears to be not accidental and irregular, as it seemed at first, but subject to very regular physical laws. Thus, its intensity, tints, and shades serve as a kind of measurement or means of estimating the polar quality and strength of the odylic emanations on one hand, and the degree of sensitiveness in the observer on the other. This investigation also leads, or promises to lead, to most interesting disclosures regarding <term>magnetism</term> itself and its internal distribution. <term>Odylic light</term>, at its lowest intensity, appears on a magnet as a faint gray—that is, a colorless nebula—visible only after the observer has been in absolute darkness for hours; he can only confirm its reality when the magnet emitting it is slowly moved back and forth. Thus, M. EDUARD HUETTER, using a high-intensity pocket horseshoe magnet, saw the light from the north pole as such a faint gray in the blackness of the deepest night that he momentarily doubted whether

Proceeding higher in the scale of objective intensity (or of subjective sensitiveness), the part of the smoke nearest the steel acquires the appearance of flame, while the upper part remains smoky. The smoke is always thickest at the point of the flame and decreases further off, passing gradually into vapor and <term>nebula</term>, thus becoming constantly feebler and more delicate until it is lost at its upper extremity. When all factors combine to permit its steady development, the variegated play of moving colors arranges itself into determinate forms and follows fixed laws. Similar nonsense is not infrequently met with in the course of the report. Who would have the patience to wade through 200 pages of it?—R.

I have waded through it and experienced nothing short of disgust in doing so. **Dr. von Eisenstein** would indeed find it difficult to explain his most absurd experiment, which could not, by any possibility, have any bearing on the research of the author, inasmuch as he had expressly declared that he avoided making experiments on persons in the <term>magnetic sleep</term>. But even if he had made experiments on persons in that state, it is inconceivable how a man of ordinary education could imagine that such experiments as those of **Dr. E.** could prove anything, or how he could make them in the manner described in the report.—W. 502. But besides this simple Iris, we have to consider a complex kind of compound Iris.

There had occurred, as has been formerly alluded to, a certain variability of the colors of *odylic light*, which often threatened to introduce confusion into the results. This induced me to undertake a long special investigation of the point, consisting of numberless experiments made with the utmost attention, and from which I endeavored to deduce the laws regulating the phenomenon. I shall here detail the most essential parts of this investigation.

503. A magnetic bar, with the poles in the line of dip or inclination, always emitted colors different from those seen when it lay horizontally in that of the meridian; and when a northward pole was turned toward the north or toward the south, its flame was at one time more blue, at another more red and gray. Another uncertainty consisted in this, that when I placed a northward pole vertically upward, the observers generally described the flame as bright blue, but sometimes as gray, occasionally even yellow, with other similar inconsistencies.

As soon as she moved further away, it became bluish. Now, Mlle. PAUER is nearsighted. This peculiarity, therefore, had an influence on her perception of odylic light, and it was thus proved how much the apparent variation of color at different distances depends on subjective causes.

506. Similar observations made with Mlle. ZINKEL at different times, and in all different directions, yielded proof in the same way that there is only one fixed distance, differing for each individual, at which the color of the odylic flame is pure and distinctly visible; *but that at this distance it remains constant for the same individual, and does not vary at all; whereas, at other distances, less or greater, it exhibits different shades, being dull yellow at small distances, and bluish-gray and gray at greater distances.* In order, therefore, to obtain unmixed results, we must always attend to the proper distance for the eye of each observer.

507. In fact, before I had been led to make the last-mentioned investigation, I had sometimes found myself in no small perplexity, since one observation had yielded an azure blue color, while another, apparently made under precisely similar circumstances, had given a gray or a yellow color to the odylic flame. As long as we do not see our way out of such confusion, these researches—in which we cannot perceive the phenomena with our own senses, but must obtain information by asking questions of another person unacquainted with the subject, and this in the dark—frequently become wearisome and exhausting to an indescribable degree; occasionally, it required all the charm of so interesting a subject to support my wavering patience.

I mounted the same two-foot bar magnet by its center in a wooden Guido's support equipped with a universal joint, so that it could be positioned in any direction. 509. If we examine the colors of this circle, we find there a new iris, the colors of which are arranged in a circular form, or rather follow each other around the circumference.

510. It is very remarkable that the position of greatest magnetic intensity—namely, that of the *inclination* at an angle of 65° with the horizon (in Vienna)—is precisely that in which all the colors disappear, and nothing but *dark gray* is left. Does this gray represent white, the sum of all colors, or black, the absence of all color? I have not yet been able to decide this with certainty; further research will soon settle the point, but I am inclined toward the latter opinion.

511. It is also remarkable that the colors which stand diametrically opposite to one another are *not complementary colors*. For here we find blue opposite *red, not yellow*; opposite violet blue, we find *flame red, not green*; opposite yellow, we find *gray, not blue, etc.* The circle appears divided into sectors of 90°, the zero point of which must be placed in the line of magnetic inclination. Opposite to this zero, at a distance of 180°, stands golden yellow; and on each side at 90° from these two points, we find red and blue opposite each other—that is, again, 180° apart. Under the magnetic equator, where the polar line (or meridian) and the inclination coincide, the direction and order of the colors would be different. I hope to see the time when someone might try these experiments there, which should not be difficult, for surely no ship ever crosses the equator without one or more sensitive persons being found on board.

512. Another peculiarity appears in the fact that the observer continued to describe *a narrow streak of red between the gray of the northward pole (pointing downward in the line of inclination) and the violet blue*. This remarkable fact had occurred in former experiments; for we have seen that **Mme. KIENESBERGER** often spoke of a narrow red streak above the blue in the beautiful Iris of the electromagnet, passing into the gray of the smoke. **Mlle. GLASER**, **STEPHAN KOLLAR**, **Mme. BAUER**, and **Mlle. PAUER** all observed the same thing. It would appear, therefore, that from the blue or the violet, the red is developed again so strongly as to appear as an independent red at the other (the violet) end of the Iris; consequently, red closes the spectrum at both ends—at least certainly the odylic spectrum or Iris.

513. *Those colors which lie in the lower semicircle—that is, for 90° on each side of the inclination—differ strikingly in light intensity from those of the upper half, or 90° on each side of the golden yellow.* The upper half, occupying the space parallel to the arc a c b, is bright, strongly luminous, lively, and brilliant; the lower half is dull, cloudy, and feebly luminous. *The greatest intensity of light lies in the golden yellow; the greatest darkness lies in the gray of the inclination.* We might call

The earth's action on odylic flames is opposite to that of the heavens.* §§ 536, 356.

514. When I used the southward pole of the same magnet instead of the northward pole, I prepared myself for a great difference in the results. But my expectation was not fulfilled. In the general result, it was almost immaterial which pole was made to revolve in the vertical circle in the plane of the meridian. There were, however, some minor modifications. The colors, which were almost exactly the same from both poles when in the same direction, always appeared somewhat later when the southward pole moved from the downward position in the inclination towards the north, and so on around the circle. It was always necessary to advance the pole a few degrees further than in the case of the northward pole in order to obtain the same color report from the observer. This delay of the colors on the southward pole was the same throughout the circle, so that the gray of the inclination was seen in a position where the bar formed a smaller angle with the horizon than that which gave the same result with the north pole—an angle, as stated above, of 65°, which is the magnetic dip in Vienna. See § 534.

515. terrestrial poles. It is obvious that the aligned and unaligned positions of the magnet's poles made their influence felt here as they had always done. The northward pole, exerting its full power when aligned, was weakened by the direct opposition of terrestrial magnetism when it was unaligned—that is, when pointing to the south. *516. The circular Iris is therefore divided twice by external influences into two halves, regarding the intensity of light and purity of color. In one case, this division is that of a horizontal section; in the other, it is that of a (nearly) vertical section. In the first case, the influence of terrestrial polarity predominates; in the second, the polarity of the bar magnet itself is dominant.*

535. The agreement which might be expected in *those points where the vertical circles cut the horizontal circle*, and thus form nodes, is demonstrated in a most satisfactory manner. The alignment along the north line produced blue; the south line, red; the west, yellow; and the east, gray—exactly as they occurred in the same positions on the two previous circles. Therefore, these three sets of observations mutually verify and confirm one another.

536. The observations made in the vertical circle of the parallel and those made in the horizontal circle are more difficult than those in the meridional vertical circle. This is mainly because, in the first two, north and south—which exert the strongest influence on the magnet—act equally on its poles throughout the entire revolution. Meanwhile, east and west, which represent much weaker points of the compass, must contend alone against "above" and "below," which correspond with south and north. The size of the bar, its intensity, and so on, all exert a greater influence on those colors produced by these weaker forces, which are less strongly supported. However, a slight difference does occur between the colors in the east and west. In the east, the gray of the northward pole had a blue tint, while that of the southward pole had a violet tint. In the west, the yellow of the northward pole was mixed with red, and the southward pole exhibited the fullest and brightest yellow, with a shade of red. This indicates a similarity between the effect of the west and that of the south, and between the east and the north. Thus, through a different path, we arrive at the same result found in section 391: namely, that *generally, in reference to <term>odyle</term>, east inclines toward the north, and west toward the south.* And as we already knew (see section 356 and section 531) that east and "below" harmonize in their effect, as do west and "above," we arrive at the comprehensive result: *that north, east, and the earth (below) form a general contrast, in <term>odylic polarity</term>, to south, west, and the heavens (above).*

553. And thus we have proven beyond a doubt *the existence of transversality in odylic phenomena*, just as it has long been known to exist in magnetic phenomena since the first researches of M. PRECHTL. The difference, as far as my researches have extended and as can be seen from the details I have provided, consists chiefly in this: *magnetic* transversality has greater independence, while *odylic* transversality exhibits more dependence on the threefold polarity of the earth.

These colors are always called into existence and made to appear separately by the influence of the corresponding point of the compass, when the apparatus is arranged so that the colors can separate from one another and each can develop freely on its own. We might say, in other words, that every magnetic pole is thus shown to possess a sort of double <term>odylic transversality</term>, depending on the polarities of the earth.

565. I now tried the effect of a circular surface or disk. It was suspended by a small hook in the middle, horizontally above the pole of the magnet, and could be fixed at any height. I could then lower it onto the north pole of the magnet, which stood vertically. In this way, it formed a widely extended flat cap or termination—or, in other words, an <term>induction magnet</term> with a length as small as the thickness of the plate, but a thickness as great as the diameter of the disk.

# ON A DISC SHAPED MAGNET.

566. I first showed Mademoiselle GLASER the disc by itself. It had a pale whitish-gray glow, but no colors could be observed. I now lowered it onto the pole, and it instantly acquired <term>odylic light</term>. In the center point of the upper surface, a blue spot appeared; the surface became bright, and the border was colored gray on the east, and blue, yellow, and red on the north, west, and south respectively. These colors blended into each other where they met.

567. Madame BAUER saw the same thing; however, the surface was not merely gray; the colors were seen not only on the border but for a considerable distance inward from it. When I used the south pole of the magnet, the colors were the same, but feebler and less clear.

568. I showed the disc, resting on the north pole, to Mademoiselle PAUER. The <term>odylic glow</term> instantly spread over it. The colors developed as might have been expected: a blue spot on the upper center and a red spot on the lower center—in contact with the magnet—both more than two inches in diameter. They passed into a surrounding yellowish zone, which was faintly tinged with red on the underside and with green on the upper surface, and this zone again faded into a gray zone. This last zone continued to the border, where it was surrounded by a kind of downy fringe of light, 0.6 inches thick, and colored gray, blue, yellow, and red in the east, north, west, and south respectively. In the northwest, southwest, and southeast, she saw green, orange, and gray-red respectively; in the northeast, she saw violet with a short patch of red. These colors formed a continuous wreath of tints passing into each other, thus creating a kind of circular rainbow.

569. Mademoiselle PAUER saw a blue flame, two inches high, rising from the upper center; it transitioned above into sulfur yellow, and then into gray. This, of course, could not be observed below, where the disc rested on the magnet. However, the whole disc was surrounded by a downy, <term>nebulous light</term>, only clearly seen in profile, which was bluish above and reddish-gray below. It had a slow, undulating movement and flowed gently along both surfaces toward the center. She could disturb it by blowing on it, at which point it became momentarily brighter, but it soon recovered its former state.

# ON A SPHERICAL MAGNET.

# THE PHENOMENA OF THE ODYLIC LIGHT

ANKA HETMANEK saw the ball in a white odylic glow before it was connected to the battery. When connected, it became much brighter, with colored streaks running from one pole to another. The colors were blue on the north, yellow on the west, red on the south, dark gray on the east, and green on the northwest. The poles were the brightest parts: the upper was blue and the lower was red.

When she looked down on it, the north side appeared blue, the west yellow, the south red, and the east gray; she also saw green between the north and west, orange between the west and south, and violet between the east and north. The west side was the brightest and the east the darkest. The colors shaded imperceptibly into one another. However, the most intense light appeared at the points corresponding to the poles of the enclosed <term>electro-magnet</term>, which served as the poles of the ball. The upper pole had a blue spot and the lower a red spot; the former was connected to the silver and the latter to the zinc of the battery. Each spot was four inches in diameter and transitioned at its outer border into yellow, which then faded into gray. At both poles, flames appeared—blue at the top and red at the bottom—standing about four inches high. The entire surface was covered with a delicate gray nebulous veil, seen most distinctly in profile, which was about 0.4 of an inch high. This veil appeared to her to flow gently from the equator toward the poles and was disturbed if one blew on it. Around the entire equator, she saw a brighter, narrow, whitish-yellow ring.

### PHENOMENA OF THE ODYLIC LIGHT

...exhibited the appearance of a fine comb with countless short teeth, pointing toward the poles, and at right angles to the equatorial girdle itself.

579. The light over the surface, its odylic glow, was described by her—as it was by Mme. BAUER—to be continuous, but within this continuity it was formed of an infinite number of distinguishable *fibers*, which appeared to be the thickness of a small knitting needle and ran perpendicularly from both poles to the girdle. She considered these not as independent threads of light, but rather as lines of greater intensity, alternating with lines of less intensity, and thus giving the appearance of threads running from the poles. They all had the color of their position: blue on the north both above and below the equator, yellow on the west, and so forth.

The blue and red polar spots had the significant diameter of six inches, or a radius of three inches from the poles. They then divided and formed the threads which passed over the remaining zones to the equator. This gave the polar spots the appearance of stars, which were more clearly defined by the different intensities of the various colors; this caused some points to apparently project further than others and thus form a star.

580. The intensity of light in these phenomena diminished from the poles toward the equator, so that, in the tropical zones, they became gradually duller and finally disappeared very near the luminous equator.

581. The colors around the sphere, which thus formed a spherical Iris, blended into each other everywhere, such as blue through green into yellow, yellow through orange into red, etc. These transitions were formed in this way: each of the meridional threads had a color very slightly different from that of the threads on each side of it; no two were perfectly alike, and the difference was marked enough to be distinctly seen by the observer. Thus, the ball appeared as if composed of a thousand colored threads, which gave it such a great charm that Mme. BAUER and Mlle. ZINKEL declared that they had never seen anything so beautiful.

Thus, there was a bundle of dark blue and a bundle of azure-blue luminous threads. The green, which developed from the azure blue, first showed a bundle of blackish-green threads, then one of a grass-green color. The yellow, red, and gray were also divided into principal shades in this way. The gray had a dark gray bundle in the middle, 0.8 inches wide near the equator. On each side of this lay a bundle of whitish, light-gray threads, 1.2 to 1.6 inches wide. Before the violet developed from the gray toward the north, the often-mentioned strange phenomenon of a narrow portion of red appeared. It was quite sharply separated from the dark gray and transitioned quite rapidly into dark violet-blue. Its width at the equator was no more than one-fifth of an inch. This remarkable red streak was very brightly luminous and intensely red, much brighter than any part of the red on the south side of the ball. *Red, therefore*, occurred at both ends of the spectrum, beginning and ending the series of colors. It was formed on one side from the yellow, and on the other from the blue; thus, we perceive very clearly *what is to be thought of the violet of the spectrum generally: it is not a distinct color, but in fact only a mixture of blue with the neighboring pure and independent red of the streaks so often mentioned.* Why this red—which in the ordinary spectrum appears only as violet within a portion of the blue—stands out independently in the *odylic spectrum* is a fact whose causes can only be determined by further research of a different kind.

The lower half, with its red pole, was brighter in its blue and gray parts, and cloudy in its yellow and red. 584. Such were Mlle. Zinkel's descriptions of the odylic glow of the ball. Let us now attend to the *odylic flame* as seen by her. At each pole, a flame streamed out perpendicular to the surface of the sphere, 2 to 2.5 inches high and 1.2 to 1.6 inches thick, *which then spread out and positioned itself on all sides parallel to the spherical surface* to the extent of a radius of 3.2 inches around the polar or central point. It divided into bundles of fibers or single fibers and flowed like the fibers of the odylic glow in the air, above and parallel to them, over the ball to the extent just mentioned. Above each pole, therefore, there appeared a luminous mass 6.4 inches in diameter. The observer compared the whole flame to a loosely bound sheaf of grain standing on the ground, the ears and stems of which hang over on all sides, horizontally or curved downwards. The bundles of flame were not still but flickered and sparkled continually back and forth, shortening and lengthening, and shooting out rays like the bundle of electric light at a positively electrified conductor. *The resemblance of this phenomenon to the polar light of the earth or aurora borealis (and aurora australis) is so obvious that it must occur to everyone who may take the trouble to read these lines. The ball in my experiment is, in fact, a terrelle or miniature earth, analogous to the magnetic one created by Barlow.*

->CONSISTENCY OF THE PHENOMENA.<-

**589.** However, such explanations are not required for those who have read these researches with some attention. The entire course of them, continued as they have been for more than three years, shows on every page that the same threads of physical law may be traced throughout the approximately sixty persons included in the investigation. Every new branching off or subdivision has only supplied new proofs of the accuracy of the observations and new guarantees for the consistency that prevails in the connections between the observed facts. Thus we have seen—to take the example of the last-mentioned investigation (§ 525)—that a yellow <term>odylic flame</term> flows from the end of a vertical bar of soft iron, but that from the <term>magnetic pole</term> an <term>Iris</term> arises (§ 517). The colors of this <term>Iris</term> lie in horizontal layers above each other, with red appearing a second time above the violet. A horizontal line, forming the end of a vertically placed <term>magnetic pole</term> (§ 560), produced an <term>Iris</term> arranged in vertical layers along the horizontal line. Bar magnets showed (§ 517) colored flames at both poles, with certain primary colors in uniform contrast; one such contrast in the meridian, and another in the parallels. Four-cornered ends exhibited at the corners (§ 539, etc.) the four primary colors at once. But it was found possible to isolate and separate the colors even more perfectly at either pole. A two-pointed end gave the two opposite colors of the meridian when the points lay in that line, and the colors of the parallels when they lay in them (§ 561), just as a bar magnet showed them at its opposite ends. And a four-pointed end yielded (§ 562) all four colors perfectly separated and unmixed on either pole. Thus, a double <term>transversality</term> was demonstrated at the same time with the most beautiful distinctness and precision. A disc exhibited (§ 565) all four colors at once on a horizontal surface, and also all the mixed and transition tints. Lastly, a hollow sphere, uniting all these appearances (§ 571 et seq.), exhibited each distinctly and all collected on a single field of action: the surface of the sphere, on which a single glance perceived them all in their mutual relations. To produce these effects, I sometimes used <term>terrestrial magnetism</term>, and sometimes the <term>magnetism</term> of steel bars, at

# RETROSPECT OF THE COLORS OF

...at other times that of an electromagnet, but in the end, they all follow the same principle, as is easily seen. We have seen, through countless variations in this section, that (to summarize it briefly):

590. *a.* The light emitted by magnets, which is visible in the dark, is perceived by sensitives in different colors at different distances; however, the color remains constant for the same eye at a specific fixed distance, though this distance varies from person to person.

*b.* This light takes on not only different forms, but all known colors.

*c.* These colors encompass the entire spectrum, including its mixed colors and transition tints, as well as white and black combined in every shade of gray.

*d.* The colors often appear individually to the sensitive eye: generally blue at the northward or negative pole, red at the southward or positive pole, or gray at both.

*e.* But in most cases, especially in instances of high intensity, several colors appear together; frequently, all of them are seen.

*f.* When this occurs, and when the colors can arrange themselves freely, they always follow the order of the rainbow and the spectrum.

*g.* When layered horizontally one over the other, red is always at the bottom and blue at the top.

*h.* Above the blue, and connected to it by violet (which is an intermediate or transition color produced in this way), a pure red appears once more. Thus, the <term>odylic spectrum</term>, which begins with red and passes through orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet, also ends in red.

*i.* These colored light phenomena are produced, according to the same laws, by the magnetism of steel bars, electromagnets, and the earth.

*k.* The last of these—terrestrial magnetism—which is immovable relative to us, imposes certain laws on the phenomena. These laws produce different results for every point on the earth where they are observed.

*l.* Terrestrial magnetism produces these phenomena in any bar of soft iron.

*m.* In all observed cases, and probably in all cases, they consist of an Iris, except perhaps in certain directions where only gray occurs.

### COLORS OF ODYLIC LIGHT.

*n.* Within this *Iris*, one color usually—or more rarely, two—predominates in size and intensity. Often, this prevailing color is the only one seen by the sensitive, while the weaker associated colors escape their notice.

*o.* In general, when directed downwards along the line of dip or inclination, they are heavily tinged with gray. They are blue toward the north, yellow above, and red toward the south. They are further yellow toward the west and gray toward the east. This applies with equal accuracy to the vertical meridional circle, to the vertical circles in the parallels, and to the horizontal circle.

*p.* When the magnetism of bars or electromagnets comes into conflict with the Earth's magnetism due to their non-aligned position, the tints are weakened and discolored. When the magnets are aligned, the colors become stronger and more vivid. Intermediate positions produce intermediate tints and shades.

*q.* The <term>odyle</term> of crystals, of the animal body, and of every source of that influence, acts on the <term>odylic light</term> of magnets or other bodies when brought into conflict with it, just as the Earth's magnetism does.

*r.* A bar magnet revolving on its axis, with flames at both ends, does not exhibit—in any vertical or horizontal circle, nor in any other position—flames at its poles whose colors are complementary, even though they stand in polar opposition.

*s.* The colors of the upper semicircle have greater light intensity than those of the lower. All the colors on the northward pole are brighter on the semicircle toward the north and duller on the opposite side. This is reversed for the colors of the southward pole.

*t.* These colored flames may be transferred from the magnet to other bodies.

*u.* Magnets ending in several points divide the colors among them, so that each has a color corresponding to its position on the compass; in this way, the *Iris* of every flame may be analyzed into its elementary colors.

*v.* A four-cornered iron plate thus exhibits both magnetism

# ODYLIC LIGHT

## IN THE MORE LIMITED SENSE OF THE TERM.

591. It is hardly necessary to explain that we must accurately *distinguish <term>odylic light</term>* from <term>odylic glow</term>, <term>odylic flame</term>, <term>odylic luminous fiber</term>, <term>odylic scintillations</term>, and <term>odylic smoke</term>, and that these are all to be viewed as sources of <term>odylic light</term>. All this is included in the fact that these phenomena are seen. For according to the structure of our eyes, we can only see that which gives out light; when we see any object, therefore, it emits luminous rays, or whatever name may be given to its emanations. # REFLECTION OF THE ODYLIC LIGHT.

596. I must mention an observation here, made with Professor ENDLICHER. Since he was accustomed to wearing spectacles, he kept them on in the dark chamber. When I placed the magnet before him, and he did not see it as well as I expected based on what I knew of his sensitivity, Dr. FENZL, who was present, suggested that possibly the spectacles were interfering. Mr. ENDLICHER took them off. Immediately he saw the flames very distinctly, just as I had supposed he would from my knowledge of him. The glasses had reflected one part and absorbed another of the light, and what was ~~transmitted~~ was such an insignificant residue that it only ~~sufficed~~ for a faint perception, while the whole light, ~~as given out~~ by the magnet, was quite easily seen and ~~formed~~ a flame four inches high.

597. It ~~having been thus~~ shown that the odylic light of magnets is transmitted through glass, and its passage is subject to absorption, reflection, and refraction like those of ordinary light, it was necessary to test the former by a mirror and compare its action on odylic light with its action on ordinary light. It was possible that odylic light might be absorbed, and thus be unfit for producing catoptrical phenomena, since the odyle from which it originates is easily absorbed by all kinds of matter.

She saw in the mirror the image of the odylic glow of the metal, but not that of the flame—not even a trace of it—even when she carefully looked for it during different very dark nights. 599. I had already resigned myself to this and had no hope of having the flame observed in the mirror, when, in a repetition with Mlle. ZINKEL, during her <term>catamenia</term>. She also now saw a reflected image of the flame, which she could not perceive before. Lastly, I tried it with Mme. BAUER. She saw many glowing objects in the mirror quite easily; and she perceived the flames of the magnet so well as to be able to distinguish the blue and red flames of the opposite poles. But she also said that the image was, beyond comparison, duller and feebler than the flame itself. In the latter, she could see, at both poles of a seven-bar magnet, traces of the Iris, yellow and violet, as well as smoke. These were indeed feeble, but on the image they had disappeared entirely.

601. Now, an eyelid is strongly translucent. If a candle is brought near anyone standing in the dark with closed eyes, they become immediately aware of the arrival of light. This translucency is so great that no one can endure looking at the midday sun through closed eyelids for more than a very short time. *The <term>odylic light</term>, weak as it is, still has enough force to pass through the closed eyelids and become perceptible to <term>sensitives</term>.* We shall see hereafter that this circumstance, apparently insignificant, is not without importance when we have to explain certain other rather striking phenomena observed in <term>sensitives</term>.

### THE NORTHERN LIGHTS, OR AURORA BOREALIS.

602. I may now be permitted to return for a moment to the subject mentioned in § 2 and § 21, at the very beginning of these researches. Even then, at a time when I knew far less concerning <term>odylic light</term>, I expressed the opinion that it was nothing other than the same phenomenon which, on a large scale, appears as the <term>aurora borealis</term>, or rather as the <term>polar light</term>, both south and north. This opinion, during the long period that I have since devoted uninterruptedly to the subject of odylic phenomena, has not only not lost any of its probability, but has acquired additional strength and security from many parts of the investigation. The observations on the behavior of <term>odylic light</term> under the more or less exhausted receiver of the <term>air pump</term>, the development of colors in it so often seen in my later experiments, the motions which we can communicate to it at will, and the discovery that there are a large number of perfectly healthy persons to whom it is visible—these and other important facts not only do not oppose my original view, but all of them lend it new and powerful support. The theory of <term>Sir HUMPHRY DAVY</term>, that the aurora is not so much a magnetic as an electric phenomenon—a slow, tranquil equalization or neutralization of the <term>atmospheric electricity</term>—

...tricity, at heights where the atmosphere is highly rarefied, and replacing the rapid process of neutralization of storms in our lower latitudes and at lower atmospheric heights, meets with many difficulties upon a full consideration of the subject. First, during winter, the meteorological phenomena of rain and snow occur without storms in the temperate as well as the arctic zones, while in the former, no appearance similar to the aurora is produced by atmospheric electricity. Secondly, according to the numerous observations made on the aurora since the time of Davy, the aurora does not occur more frequently in winter than in summer. Thirdly, according to the knowledge we have acquired of the laws of electricity from other sources, such an accumulation of electricity as would be necessary to fill with light—as often happens—half a quadrant of the sky during perhaps more than half the night for nights on end, cannot be easily imagined to take place in our atmosphere, given its state of constant motion. Lastly, we can see no reason why such an accumulation of atmospheric electricity, even if it could exist, should occur exactly around the magnetic terrestrial poles.<note>It is not observed that those accumulations of electricity with which storms are certainly connected have any such tendency towards the magnetic poles. —W. G.</note> Davy’s suggestion has been admired as a very ingenious thought, but it has obtained no firm footing among the established laws of natural science because it does not provide a sufficient account of cause and effect in these remarkable phenomena. *But now that we know, from the preceding research, that flaming lights exist over magnetic poles, larger than the magnets from which they flow; when we learn that these flaming appearances are movable, undulating, and often moving in serpentine windings, like those of a ribbon tossed by the wind, becoming at every moment larger or smaller, shooting out rays, scintillating, variegated in color, and often nebulous, vaporous, and cloud-like; when we find that with our breath we can cause it to flicker back and forth; when we observe that it increases at a rapid rate in size, intensity, and brilliance in rarefied air; and lastly, when we see it followed at every step by a play of rainbow colors, etc., etc.*

The waves and serpentine twists that the aurora borealis often displays are, assuming the two lights are identical, naturally and simply explained by the motion of the wind. This wind causes the light of the earth to wave back and forth in more or less rarefied layers of air, just as our breath does with the <term>odylic light</term> of magnets. We might now venture to add that, in both cases, the amounts and intensities of the <term>odylic light</term> will most likely relate to each other in the ratio of the different masses of the two spheres. As is well known, mass increases as the cube of the diameter, while the surface area increases only as the square of the diameter. According to the laws which regulate it, the <term>odyle</term>, when it reaches the earth’s surface, not only flows toward those parts where the <term>odylic</term> charge is currently weaker, but it immediately becomes polarized; that is, the current sets toward the poles and there increases the intensity of the phenomena caused by the <term>odyle</term> inherent in the mass of the earth. The inequalities in the state of the surface—depending on whether it is covered with clouds or not (the <term>odylic</term> rays being arrested in the atmosphere in the former case and falling on the solid mass of our planet in the latter)—and the different positions of the sun and moon in regard to the earth, according to whether they act in combination with or in opposition to one another; all these things necessarily cause fluctuations and irregularities in the occurrence of the polar light, just as they do in the weather or in meteorological phenomena generally. The differences in the intensity of the <term>odylic light</term> between the poles of the <term>terrelle</term> and those of the earth are thus explained and, to a certain extent, accounted for.

actually has magnetic poles, whether its magnetism proceeds alone from the surface and the sun’s rays falling on it, as modern philosophers think they are justified in assuming, or is also derived from the internal conditions of the whole planet. But in reference to this last opinion, there is a circumstance favorable to it, which, so far as I know, has not yet been taken into account in physics. I shall here venture to explain it. It is now generally admitted that meteorites have a planetary origin and are small stars, tracing their origin from the same source and orbiting in their paths around the sun in the same way as the larger and smaller planets. And indeed, the distance is no greater from the mighty Jupiter to the small Vesta or Astræa—hardly larger than the island of Ceylon—than from these asteroids to the huge meteorites of Senegal, which are said to form small hills of iron. From such meteorites, through those of Bahia, Durango, or Zacatecas, which are masses of iron weighing many tons, to that at Aix-la-Chapelle of a few tons, and to our ordinary meteorites of a few pounds, the transitional links are found everywhere.*<note>Baron von Reichenbach has long paid much attention to the subject of meteorites and possesses a magnificent collection of them from all parts of the world, which is probably superior to any other collection in Europe.—W. G.</note> From Jupiter, therefore, to the smallest meteorite, there is an unbroken series. There is no difference between a planet and a meteorite, except that of size. If this is admitted—and indeed we can hardly now avoid admitting it—then the structure of meteorites gives us a highly valuable key to opening up considerations and doctrines concerning the true internal condition of our earth. The law that governed the formation of meteorites and determined their structure and composition also governed, according to this theory, the formation of our globe. Now, meteorites consist chiefly of either metallic masses—most commonly iron with a portion of nickel (cobalt, etc.)—or of stony masses, almost always heavily mixed with the same kind of iron. # STRUCTURE OF METEORITES. 451

...consists of a coherent network of cells pervading their mass. This can be seen with the naked eye in the meteorites of Krasnojarsk and of Atacama, in the original iron mass of Bittburg, in the meteorites of unknown origin analogous to these in the museum at Gotha, and in many others. But even those more finely mixed, such as those of Smolensk, Seres, Blansko, Taber, Barbotan, etc., have the same structure. We can remove the stony parts and obtain a coherent network of iron cells. The specific gravity of these stones varies from 3 to 4 and 5. That of the Earth is about 4.7, and it is therefore probable that it has an internal constitution like that of a meteorite with a coherent mass of iron cells; that it contains, throughout its stony mass, a pervading web of metallic iron, like the large majority of meteoric stones. *But it is in all probability this iron in which the magnetism of the Earth resides.* The inequality of its distribution, as seen in every meteorite, and as we must also suppose to exist in the Earth, makes the fourfold polarity of the Earth easily conceivable.

605. This view of the constitution of our globe, which geology has not yet utilized but which, as we see, rests on a foundation of fact in natural history, is not in contradiction to the generally admitted supposition that liquid strata of melted matter may still exist under our lowest geological formations. Such liquid strata exist as certainly as the fact that meteorites, when they reach the Earth, are still hot and have a *crust* of slag, recently melted. The remarkable meteorite of Clairborn in Alabama was, when I received it, encrusted all around with a slag from one-fifth to one-third of an inch thick. The meteoric iron mass of Caryfort, Decalb county, North America, came to me with a crust about one-sixth of an inch (0.016 inch) thick. I possess the aerolite of Nanjemoy in Maryland, which is covered in parts with a porous slag about one-seventh of an inch (0.014 inch) thick. But from such a covering to the *igneous fusion of the mass throughout is a long way.* The Earth certainly has a red-hot or still fluid covering, several leagues thick, analogous to the coating of slag on the meteorites. <header>STRUCTURE OF METEORITES.</header>

proofs of this to permit us to doubt it; but we are far from being entitled to conclude from this that it must therefore be in a state of fusion through its whole mass, as is generally, but rather hastily, assumed. It is beyond all comparison more probable that it has the internal structure of a meteorite—and indeed of one containing iron, possibly of several combined—as it daily unites before our eyes with new meteorites.

606. Some philosophers, and among them Dr. **FARADAY**, have asserted that the Earth could not be magnetic throughout its mass because it is internally in a state of igneous fusion, and because we know that high temperatures are not reconcilable with the presence of magnetism in bodies. This argument has weight only so long as we regard *the whole mass as a lava*. But not only is there no strict proof of this, but many considerations are strongly opposed to it, of which I shall refer here only to the one derived above from the analogy of meteorites. All of them are melted only on the surface, but internally they are crystalline formations resulting from a force which can be shown to have operated entirely at a low temperature. A moment has come for each meteorite in which excessive heat has acted on it externally, has melted the surface, and formed lavas on it. But this has only been a moment, and a very short one, which has only been able to melt the surface to a very limited depth. Such a moment once existed for the Earth, but it could melt down only a thin crust of its mass, which now forms the red-hot liquid stratum below its congealed surface; it is from this molten fountain that Geologists suppose our volcanoes, our basalts, trachytes, and porphyries to have flowed, and its existence, if admitted, satisfactorily explains the fact that in every shaft and pit the heat increases as we descend. The hypothesis of the existence of this fluid stratum has been generally received with favor, as being founded on sufficient data. But such a mere crust of glowing or fused matter, even if several miles in thickness, is altogether insufficient to destroy, or even materially to diminish, the effects of the magnetism of the vast, cold, iron-pervaded sphere, 8000 miles in diameter.

According to what has been stated here, then, there does

This internal composition explains the Earth's magnetism, which would be destroyed if the entire globe were in a state of igneous fusion.</summary>

# METEORIC IRON IS CRYSTALLIZED.

actually exists a magnet, passing through the earth, exactly as I passed one through my <term>terrelle</term> (although of a different form), in imitation of it, and thus endeavored to place the small sphere in conditions analogous, to a certain degree, to those of the terrestrial globe.

607. But this iron, which I hold we must assume to be interwoven with the whole internal mass of the earth, as it is in meteorites, *is also uniformly crystallized.* When meteoric stones are cut, polished, and very slowly etched by diluted nitric acid, crystalline figures appear on every portion of iron, however small, and can be distinctly recognized under the microscope. These have been shown to be the same appearances which, on masses of meteoric iron, are called the Widtmannstetten figures, and they are nothing else than crystalline forms of the metallic constituents. I have examined many meteorites in my own collection, and have uniformly found the <term>reguline iron</term> crystallize exactly in the same way, and according to the same laws, as the large masses of meteoric iron. I have picked out of the Blansko meteorite small portions of iron which, when polished and etched, notwithstanding their small size, exhibited not only cleavage planes, but crystallized pyrites enclosed in the iron, exactly as in the large masses. Meteorites, therefore, include a twofold source of magnetic and <term>odylic</term> polarity; *they consist in part of cellular but yet coherent masses of iron; and these metallic masses are crystallized, and perhaps form, in each case, a single large crystal, externally indeed irregular, but, internally, cohering according to the laws of crystallization.* But we know, from § 55, that all crystals permanently pour out odylic light from their poles. Here, therefore, the presence of iron and the crystalline form act together in producing magnetico-odylic poles in the earth, and these are the reasons which make it probable to me that the magnetism and the <term>odyle</term> of the earth are to be ascribed, not only to external causes, such as the solar rays, but also in great part, perhaps for the most part, to internal causes. In following these out further, the facts,

608. In connection with this part of the subject, an old remark made by the Swedish philosopher WILKE deserves to be recalled to memory: namely, *that disturbances of the magnetic needle always PRECEDE the appearance and the motions of the aurora borealis.*\* This, as we have seen, agrees most exactly with the phenomena of <term>odylic</term> light; for these always occur later and more slowly than the associated magnetic or electric effects, which are followed by the <term>odylic</term> effects only after an observable pause. The same facts I have ascertained in my dark chamber were, therefore, noticed many years ago in the wide expanse of heaven by other observers.

609. Lastly, I may here cite the observation of WARGENTIN, *that the polar lights make the needle less acute and delicate in its indications, or "blunt" it.* This is now naturally explained. The aurora borealis is an <term>odylo-magnetic</term> emanation, whether ponderable or imponderable, material or immaterial. Where it issues from the North Pole of the Earth, it is positively magnetic. But the *northward* pole of the needle is negative. Therefore, when +M passes over the needle from north to south, as the aurora does, the effect is the same as if a very feeble southward pole of a magnet were drawn uninterruptedly along the needle, from north to south, during the entire duration of the aurora. The effect of the aurora must be the same as that of the ordinary reversed stroke of a weak magnet. And everyone knows that a needle thus

The <term>terrelle</term> exhibits the phenomena of the polar light very perfectly in miniature.

# APPENDIX.

## A.

When I became acquainted with the research of the author in 1845, through the publication of Part I, I was naturally eager to have an opportunity to observe the phenomena presented by sensitive persons for myself. I was deeply convinced of the truth and accuracy of Baron von Reichenbach, but it was impossible not to feel a desire to become personally acquainted with these interesting facts. I therefore inquired for such persons affected by nervous disease as were likely to be sensitive in a high degree, and I very soon found one who would certainly have ranked very high on the author's list. This was a young woman who had recently given birth to a healthy child at one of the charitable institutions in this city. She appeared to be in perfect and vigorous health and was nursing a thriving child. But I was informed that she was so excessively nervous that if another person's hand were placed on her head, she was very soon thrown into convulsions; upon the cessation of these, she was found to be in a state of somnambulism. I was also told by eyewitnesses of intelligence, education, and truthfulness that, in this state, she exhibited the phenomena of the transference of one of the senses. As it was obviously not prudent to induce convulsions in order to produce the somnambulistic state, I did not see her in that state at all. Neither was it found practical to make observations in the dark, so I was limited here to her sensations. I tried making <term>passes</term> over her with various weak magnets—the only ones in my possession at the time—and, in every detail, she described the same sensations as the sensitive persons examined by the author, without any questions being asked. Specifically, she felt different apparent temperatures from the same end during the upward and downward pass, so that she could instantly tell which pole or which pass was being used. These sensations were very vivid and

Another lady, a member of my family who was occasionally subject to very severe headaches and who very clearly felt the effects of magnets and crystals—even those of small size and weak intensity—was also able to find a small rock crystal by its light in the same manner.

A boy, nine or ten years old, the son of a gentleman living near Ambleside, whom I saw playing on the lawn in perfect health, was called in and shut into a short passage between two drawing rooms that could be reasonably, though not perfectly, darkened. He held one end of a copper wire ten or twelve feet long, which passed through the keyhole. When the other end was placed on one pole of a weak horseshoe magnet, he soon described a warm sensation passing up his arm from the wire. When I dipped the end of the wire in weak nitric acid, the sensation changed. The wire soon felt hot, and after a moment, the boy called out, "I see a fire." Upon further questioning, he described this in his own words but found it difficult to compare it to anything he knew; finally, he said it was *a shining green cloud or smoke*. I had, of course, carefully avoided telling him anything at all about the phenomena. It is most interesting to see that this young boy—who likely did not know what kind of wire he held and certainly was not aware that copper and its compounds tint ordinary flames green—described a green flame at the tip of the wire or surrounding it. This is a fact the Author always observed in the <term>odylic light</term> when copper was used.

Using various crystals—rock crystal, rock salt, gypsum, heavy spar, galena, and Iceland spar—the same boy instantly detected the warm and cool poles along the lines of the crystallographic axes, pointing out three pairs of such poles in some crystals. Without him knowing, I marked these and tested him again in the dark; he consistently identified the same poles as warm or cold.

I was unable to devote the necessary time and effort to further study these cases. I had seen enough to confirm what I already knew of the Author’s minute accuracy. I have recently been informed of the following case. A lady, during her final illness and while she was, I understand, speechless (probably due to some brain condition <note>cerebral affection</note>), was observed by her family to have moved herself across the bed shortly after being, as they supposed, comfortably arranged and settled. After trying in vain for a long time to counteract this tendency, her relatives very sensibly turned the bed at right angles to its former position. From that time until she died—although she remained in precisely the same state—the patient never changed her position again as she had done before, and she showed signs of satisfaction at the change. Her relatives had no idea what caused this, and it occurred several years before the *Abstract* was published. However, upon recently seeing that work, they immediately recognized the facts they had observed and obtained a natural explanation for them.

## B.

The experiments to be briefly noted here were conducted by a gentleman well-versed in science on a lady while she was in a mesmeric sleep. This lady exhibited various remarkable phenomena, including clairvoyance in different forms; however, I will not discuss those here, as they are outside the specific scope of this work. All sleepwalkers <note>somnambulists</note>, whether spontaneous or otherwise, are highly sensitive; therefore, we will consider this lady simply in reference to her <term>odylic</term> sensitivity while in a mesmeric sleep. It will be seen that her descriptions coincide perfectly with those of others examined by the author in a normal state (a point of great interest); these, in turn, agree in all points with those given by Mlle. ATZMANNSDORFER in a spontaneous sleepwalking state, as recorded in section 480. It is clear that the only difference regarding these phenomena between the normal state and that of somnambulism is that in the latter, the sensitivity is more intense.

April 13.—A rock crystal, two inches long and half an inch thick, was convulsively grasped in the hand, and the arm rose and became rigid. A bilateral crystal of selenite (gypsum), four inches by one and a half inches, exhibited in the diffused daylight a "soft and somewhat dim light, but the summit was very bright with yellow and red rays." The light soon became too intense and "made her eyes water; she could not bear it." A short time later, the flame above the crystal was one to two inches higher, the light being as intense as before. She saw five points of light (still in the ordinary light of a room with the blinds drawn) on the tips of Mr. F.'s fingers.

April 17.—A large translucent double crystal of quartz, each crystal being five inches by one and a half, gave off a light too brilliant to be endured when held at a distance of three feet. At six feet, it was "pleasant and very beautiful—a light, yellow, and white light rising two inches above the crystal and flickering. There was a glow of light all over it." Water was charged by these crystals and was greatly enjoyed by the patient. It was somewhat different from water charged by the hand; it tasted warm and like peppermint, though without actual flavor. A crystal of fluorspar charged water less powerfully, but still distinctly.

April 20.—The light of the gypsum crystal was too intense to be endured at less than six feet. At six feet, the colors were "beautiful and varied: white, yellow, green, and blue." It soon became too powerful even there. When a hand was placed in the way, the crystal could not be seen, only a strong light diffused all around it. Even three or four feet further away, in front of an open window, it became too powerful and was removed because of the over-excitement it caused. Passes made with the quartz crystal were felt very vividly.

## ### *Familiar Letters on Chemistry.*

### By **JUSTUS VON LIEBIG.** New Edition. Complete in 1 vol., fcap. 8vo. 6*s.*, cloth.

The present edition is so considerably enlarged that it may be regarded as almost a new work. The object of the author has been to present a sort of bird's-eye view of Chemistry in all its various aspects and relations, to show its importance as a means of unfolding the secrets of nature, and also to show the influence which it exerts, through its various applications, in manufactures, agriculture, and medicine, on the present social condition of mankind.

A large portion of the work is devoted to the consideration of the subjects of fermentation, putrefaction, the use of manures, nutrition, and respiration, with results of the author's researches on dietetics, and observations on the comparative nutritive value of different articles of food.

---

## ### *Railway Economy,*

### Or, **THE NEW ART OF TRANSPORT.** Its Management, Prospects, and Relations, Commercial, Financial, and Social; with an Exposition <unclear>of</unclear> the Practical Results of the Railways in operation in the Unite<unclear>d</unclear> Kingdom, on the Continent and in America. By **DIONYSIUS LARDNER**, D.C.L. 12mo. 12*s.*

<margin>71</margin>
This work is intended to fill a void in our industrial literature. Nothing has hithe<unclear>rto</unclear> been published in which the management, prospects, and relations of railways in gene<unclear>ral</unclear> are regarded in a high and general point of view, and in which their commercial <unclear>and</unclear> social relations and effects are investigated.

The volume opens with two preliminary chapters; in one of which, the influen<unclear>ce of</unclear> improved transport on civilization is discussed; and in the other, a short histor<unclear>ical</unclear> retrospect is given of land-transport to the present time. These are succeeded <unclear>by an</unclear> analysis of the business of the chief departments of a railway establishment. <unclear>In</unclear> these is considered in a separate chapter.

The circumstances which determine the durability of a railway, and the p<unclear>arts</unclear> which, under given conditions, the superficial structure of the road may be exp<unclear>ected to</unclear> require renewal, are discussed in the first of these chapters, and a view is taken <unclear>of the</unclear> gradual development of railways in England, and of the capital they have absorbe<unclear>d.</unclear>

<margin>72</margin>
The chapter on locomotive power contains an exposition of the manner in wh<unclear>ich a</unclear> record should be kept of the performance of the locomotive stock, illustrated by exam<unclear>ples</unclear> drawn from several foreign railroads. The average daily work of locomotives in Engla<unclear>nd</unclear> and on the Continent, their average consumption of fuel, the fabrication and cost of coke, and other expenses attending the locomotive stock, are explained.

In the chapter on the carrying-stock, the average work obtained from the variou<unclear>s</unclear> classes of vehicles on the railways of England and the Continent are examined, and the average distances which they severally run, the amount of stock necessary to work a given traffic, etc., are investigated. The questions of the maintenance and reproduction of the rolling stock are discussed at length in a separate chapter.

These chapters are succeeded by two on the stations, and on the clearing-house, in which the details of the business comprehended under these important heads are discussed. A detailed analysis of the passengers' and goods' traffic is given in the next chapter.

## ### *The Inventions of the Ancients.*

### **PNEUMATICS OF HERO OF ALEXANDRIA.** Fcap. 4to., cloth, 12*s.* 6*d.*

<margin>2-3</margin>
This work comprises descriptions of many of the elementary parts of all steam engines, while those of most other machines are also mentioned. ## ### *Familiar Letters on Chemistry.*

### By **JUSTUS VON LIEBIG.** New Edition. Complete in 1 volume, <term>fcap. 8vo.</term> 6 shillings, cloth.

The present edition is so significantly enlarged that it may be regarded as almost a new work. The author's goal has been to present a bird's-eye view of Chemistry in all its various aspects and relations; to show its importance as a means of revealing the secrets of nature, and also to show the influence which it exerts, through its various applications in manufacturing, agriculture, and medicine, on the current social condition of mankind.

A large portion of the work is devoted to the consideration of the subjects of fermentation, decay, the use of fertilizers, nutrition, and respiration, with the results of the author's research on dietetics and observations on the comparative nutritional value of different articles of food.

---

## ### *Railway Economy,*

### Or, **THE NEW ART OF TRANSPORT.** Its Management, Prospects, and Relations, Commercial, Financial, and Social; with an Exposition <unclear>of</unclear> the Practical Results of the Railways in operation in the Unite<unclear>d</unclear> Kingdom, on the Continent and in America. By **DIONYSIUS LARDNER**, D.C.L. <term>12mo.</term> 12 shillings.

<margin>71</margin>
This work is intended to fill a gap in our industrial literature. Nothing has previously been published in which the management, prospects, and relations of railways in general are viewed from a broad and comprehensive perspective, and in which their commercial <unclear>and</unclear> social relations and effects are discussed.
